title: Repo skill: authoring mache schemas (Topology/Node/Leaf + tree-sitter selectors + _ast contract)
description: mache has a non-obvious schema DSL (api/schema.go: Topology->Node->Leaf; tree-sitter S-expression selectors with @scope/@capture/ancestry/#eq?/#match?; content_template funcs; the _ast/_source/nodes contract ASTWalker consumes). Authoring a new schema (e.g. examples/*.json, cmd/schemas/*.json) correctly requires knowing: $ wildcard grouping nodes, @scope can be inner (see mache-33b53c), ancestry depth = id-path segments, leaf 'source' uses {{.scope}}, refs/defs for callers-callees. A repo-local skill (mache/.claude/skills/authoring-schemas/ or ~/github/jamestexas/agents/skills/) would encode this + a worked example + the parity gate as the validation step. Pairs with the schema examples in examples/ and docs. Decide placement (repo-local vs shared agents repo).

comments.text:
SKILL MATERIAL — venturi trivy-v2 schema (closed-source sibling; review-only, do NOT copy/ref in mache code). It exercises the JSON-walker (ojg JSONPath) dialect far harder than examples/nvd|kev (which are single-$ + temporal shards). Distinctive features a schema skill must cover:

1. MULTI-ROOT / MULTI-VIEW: two top-level nodes project the SAME source two ways (one by namespace->FixedIn tree, one flat 'vulnerability/<name>/detail'). One data source -> parallel projection trees.
2. COMPUTED DIR NAMES via template funcs in `name`: {{replace .item.Vulnerability.NamespaceName ":" " "}} — not just {{.field}}.
3. NESTED ARRAY ITERATION as selectors: $[*] then deeper $.item.Vulnerability.FixedIn[*]. NOTE: this works on the JSON-walker/MemoryStore path but NOT the SQLiteGraph .db fast path (nested-array limitation in MEMORY) — important caveat for the skill.
4. _parent ANCESTOR TRAVERSAL in templates: {{._parent._parent.item.Vulnerability.Name}} — file name pulled from a grandparent match. Most schemas only use current-match fields; this reaches up the projection tree.
5. INLINE JSON CONTENT via dict|json: content_template "{{dict \"FixedVersion\" .Version \"Status\" 0 | json}}" — constructs a JSON object as file body.

Takeaway for the skill: document the two dialects (tree-sitter source selectors vs JSONPath data selectors), and within JSONPath show the full toolbox (multi-root, computed names, nested $[*], _parent traversal, dict/json content) AND the .db-path limitation. Relates to mache-1094a2 (trivy projection).

2. gcp-asset-schema.json: project a Cloud Asset Inventory export (gcloud asset export → JSON/newline-delimited). 4. Refs templates on all three registering the alias set per resource (tf address + cloud resource name + name-attribute literals) per the design doc's normalization contract (mache-441bc2 §3).

- drift_infra_unapplied: HCL-declared, absent from state.

- drift_infra_unmanaged: live resource absent from every state mount (clickops detector).

Run against the user's real GCP project + tofu/tf configs (the WfP namespaces from rosary-side work are a natural corpus): every finding is verifiable by gcloud describe; dead_infra findings manually adjudicated the first run, then ratchet-baselined.

description:

## Ingestion
- openapi-schema.json: project an OpenAPI doc (paths/methods/operationIds) with Refs registering route-pattern tokens (normalized: method + path template).

## Rules
- phantom_client: client-side route token with no server/spec definition across mounts (the 404-in-waiting).
- dead_endpoint: handler route token with zero client refs + zero spec refs across mounts.
- spec_drift: spec path with no handler (unimplemented) / handler with no spec path (undocumented) — assay's doc-coverage thesis generalized to API surface (ADR-0018 family).

Path-template unification (`/users/{id}` vs `/users/:id` vs fmt.Sprintf("/users/%d", …)) — v1 matches exact literals + simple template normalization; parameterized-call-site matching is explicitly out of scope until demand.

title: docs:lint gap — doc-only PRs skip the one check meant to gate docs (paths-ignore hides it)
description:
Found 2026-07-16 while reviewing CI triggers. ci.yml paths-ignores **.md + docs/** (correct — the heavy Go/integration suite shouldn't run on doc-only changes). BUT task docs:lint lives INSIDE that same paths-ignored ci.yml job, so a doc-only PR — the exact case docs:lint exists for (covers-version drift vs CHANGELOG, last-verified staleness, mache language-count claims vs internal/lang/lang.go) — skips the check entirely. The one gate for documentation never runs on documentation changes.

FIX: a lightweight .github/workflows/docs.yml that runs `task docs:lint` on push+PR to docs/** and **.md, while the heavy Go suite stays paths-ignored in ci.yml. docs-lint.sh is grep-based (no Go build), so the job is fast: checkout + go install task@v3.50.0 (the ci.yml convention — bypasses arduino/setup-task CDN 502s) + task docs:lint. SHA-pin all actions (task actions:lint enforces it).

Follow-on (not this bead): the drift_doc_* smell rules (broken internal links, dead symbol refs, outdated counts) also only run in the full smell gate — could extend docs.yml to run them, but that needs a leyline build (heavier). MVP is docs:lint.

title: Analysis-as-substrate-query: test-coverage + fast incremental lint over mache's AST/LSP graph
description:
THESIS (jamestexas, 2026-07-09): mache already holds AST + effective CST + LSP defs/refs + merkle node_hash. Test-coverage checking and linting are not new subsystems — they are DIFFERENT MATH over the SAME substrate mache projects. Both reduce to graph/dataflow queries over node_defs / node_refs / _ast / _lsp*, and both become CHEAP once memoized by content address (the mache-238673 cash-out).

Two arms, one substrate:

ARM A — coverage-as-reachability. "Is def D exercised by a test?" = does a call-path from a *_test function reach D over node_refs (binding fidelity)? This is the same graph the `untested_function` smell rule already walks — coverage is the quantitative version (which LINES/branches, not just which funcs). With _ast branch nodes we can attribute coverage at sub-function granularity; with node_hash we memoize per-subtree so an unchanged function's coverage verdict is a cache hit. Open Q: do we need runtime coverage (go test -coverprofile) fused in, or is static call-reachability the useful 80%? Probably: static reachability for "definitely untested", runtime profile overlay for "actually hit at runtime".

ARM B — mache as a fast INCREMENTAL linter (golangci-lint is SLOW; full-repo re-lint every run). Lint rules are already SQL/graph queries in this codebase (the smell ruleset). node_hash memoization (mache-238673 phase-1, DONE for cyclomatic_complexity: 30-36x warm re-run) makes re-lint sub-linear — only changed subtrees recompute. Deliverable: a benchmark of mache find-smells (incremental) vs golangci-lint (cold) on a real repo, and an honest scope of which lint classes are expressible as substrate queries vs which genuinely need Go type info golangci-lint has and mache doesn't (yet — see _lsp_hover / get_type_info).

Why one bead: the user's framing is exactly "same details, just a diff math problem." Decompose into A/B sub-beads after a design pass. Directly extends mache-238673 (incremental eval) and the mache-e0748c smell-rules-as-product cluster.

Also review: integration boundary WITH golangci-lint (complement, not replace) — could mache feed golangci-lint a changed-subtree set to shrink its work, or expose findings in a compatible format.

comments.text:
ARM-C added (jamestexas insight, 2026-07-09): DATAFLOW / TAINT as a substrate query.

Today: no CFG/DFG/taint anywhere in mache or LLO (verified). What exists is a def→use/call graph at declaration granularity (node_refs + LSP binding target_node_id). mache is architecturally a CodeQL — SQL over code facts with WITH RECURSIVE — so dataflow-as-query fits natively (dead_code's alive-check IS reachability over the ref graph).

KEY INSIGHT — invalidation ≈ taint (they're the same math): both are MONOTONE PROPAGATION OVER A DIRECTED GRAPH TO A FIXPOINT.
- sheaf invalidation propagates "stale" over the DERIVATION/dependency graph (fact B computed from fact A) when code changes.
- taint propagates "tainted" over the DATAFLOW graph (value at A flows to B) from a source.
Different edge sets, identical computation. And they COMPOSE: taint is a fixpoint query; making taint INCREMENTAL under code edits = applying sheaf-invalidation to the taint relation. So the sheaf machinery (+ node_hash memo from mache-238673) is exactly the mechanism for INCREMENTAL taint — recompute taint only in changed regions. That's the frontier (Salsa, IncA, Differential Dataflow).

Datalog framing: program analysis = inference rules over facts (this is how CodeQL/Soufflé/Doop points-to work). mache is ALREADY a Datalog-shaped system: node_defs/node_refs = EDB (base facts), smell rules = IDB (derived), node_hash+sheaf = hand-rolled incremental view maintenance (IVM). Datalog expresses recursive/analysis queries far more naturally than WITH RECURSIVE, and incremental-Datalog engines give the invalidation↔taint unification natively. Rust angle: Differential Dataflow (canonical incremental-dataflow, McSherry) is Rust = LLO's language → natural home for incremental dataflow/taint is LLO (producer), emitting _cfg/_dfg fact tables (ADR-0023 unified code-fact IR) that mache projects/queries incrementally.

Division of labor: LLO computes CFG (buildable from _ast control-flow nodes we already count for cyclomatic) + def-use + taint facts; mache stores + queries + incrementally invalidates. Prereq gaps: no CFG; def-use is declaration-granularity not variable-level; ref graph is Go+Rust-only/bare-token/mention-fidelity (ley-line-open-caf423).

DECISION NEEDED (ADR-worthy): keep hand-rolling IVM in SQL (node_hash/sheaf) vs embed a Datalog layer (e.g. Go Mangle) over the SQLite facts vs compute incremental dataflow in LLO via differential-dataflow. Candidate for its own ADR.

comments.text:
MOTIVATING USE-CASE for the dataflow arm (jamestexas, 2026-07-10): "TEST REALITY NOT MOCKS" AS A TAINT QUERY. The ecosystem's load-bearing testing rule (rosary GOLDEN_RULES.md, skeptic-agent, TDD skill testing-anti-patterns: "testing mock behavior instead of real behavior") is exactly a source→sink dataflow query:
  - SOURCE: values produced by mock/stub setup (mock constructors, .mockReturnValue/.Return(...), testify mock .On().Return(), gomock EXPECT().Return()).
  - SINK: assertion arguments (assert.Equal/require.*, expect(...), etc.).
  - RULE: a test whose asserted values are ENTIRELY mock-tainted — the value never flows through real product code between source and sink — is testing the mock, not reality. Flag it.
This is precisely the taint reachability ADR-0024 describes (mock = source, assertion = sink, "flows through a non-test symbol" = the sanitizer/barrier that makes it legitimate). It automates the skeptic-agent's core check as a smell rule (a `mock_only_test` / `tautological_test` rule). Strong argument for prioritizing the dataflow facts: it turns a subjective review heuristic into a mechanical, incremental gate — and it's a rule mache could dogfood on its own suite. Add as a flagship consumer of _dfg/_taint (ley-line-open-f13334) once the facts exist; also connects to the analysis-as-substrate-query thesis (this bead) and the "match truth not model" enforcement framing.
comments.author: rsry-mcp

comments.text:
SECOND flagship use-case (jamestexas, 2026-07-10): CAS-BACKED REFACTOR-EQUIVALENCE ORACLE ("byte-for-byte before/after" of an API refactor). Same differential-oracle discipline as mache-238673 (incremental == full, byte-identical), applied to a DIFF instead of an incremental recompute. Two layers:
  1. Raw AST/node_hash diff = "WHAT changed", exactly: unchanged node_hash ⟹ provably byte-identical subtree (untouched); changed hash ⟹ the real structural diff. Cheaper + sharper than a line diff, free from the CAS. Caveat: a rename is content, so raw hashes flag "changed everywhere the name appears" — that's not equivalence.
  2. Refactor-EQUIVALENCE = diff the DERIVED facts (call graph, _dfg, taint reachability), content-addressed. If the fact graph is isomorphic before↔after (invariant to cosmetic rename/move/extract), the refactor is BEHAVIOR-PRESERVING at the analysis's fidelity. → a semantic-diff / refactor oracle: "prove my API refactor didn't change behavior" by diffing content-addressed facts, not source text. Needs alpha-equivalence (rename-insensitive) keying at the fact layer, or compare on structure/dataflow rather than names.
Together with the mock-only-test taint rule (prev comment), these are the two motivating consumers that justify the _cfg/_dfg/_taint fact tables (ley-line-open-f13334): (a) mock-vs-reality test smell (taint), (b) refactor-equivalence oracle (content-addressed fact diff). Both are the byte-identical oracle pattern the node_hash memo already proved out. Worth adding to ADR-0024 as concrete Q1 use-cases if this advances.

title: CI↔Taskfile parity for YAML/workflow linting (actionlint + yamllint as invoked task targets)
description:

Add YAML + workflow linting AND wire it 1:1 with CI per the taskfile-ci-parity discipline (validation lives in a Taskfile target; CI INVOKES the target; local `task check` == CI by construction).

title: Harden the smell self-gate: stale-binary false positives + dogfood the _ast-requiring rules
description:
Two real gaps surfaced while running `task smells` during mache-238673 phase-1 (2026-07-09):

1. STALE-BINARY FALSE POSITIVES. `task smells` has `deps: [build]`, but Task's build cache can serve a stale `bin/mache` (built before a `git pull`). Run against a baseline that moved in a newer commit, a stale binary reports phantom "NEW findings" — observed today: a pre-#502 binary reported 98 false NEW vs the post-#502 docs/smell-baseline.json (90a6a1d moved the baseline). The finding set is deterministic; the binary was stale. Fix options: make the smells build non-cached (force rebuild), or stamp the binary's build commit and fail loud if it != HEAD before gating, or note in the target that a `git pull` requires `task build --force`. Whatever we pick, a stale binary must NOT be able to produce a false gate result.

2. DOGFOOD THE _ast RULES. The self-gate builds with `--backend tree-sitter` (parser.c LFS reason — find-smells.yml:43), so it only enforces the cross-ref rules (node_defs/node_refs). The _ast-requiring rules are SILENTLY SKIPPED on mache itself: cyclomatic_complexity, long_function, long_file, magic_int_in_comparison, duplicate_code. mache does not dogfood half its own ruleset — including cyclomatic_complexity, which mache-238673 just optimized. Add a second gate lane that builds an _ast .db of mache's own source (via leyline parse) and ratchets the _ast rules too. NOTE: depends on a non-stale local leyline — today ~/.local/bin/leyline is 0.5.7 and shadows the v0.6.0 pin via PATH-first resolution (flagged during mache-238673); resolve that first or the _ast lane parses with the wrong producer.

Close condition: (1) a stale binary can no longer yield a false gate result (test or forced-rebuild), and (2) `task smells` (or a sibling lane) enforces the _ast rules against mache's own source. Verify with `task smells`.

comments.text:

A rule-only edit left the up-to-date check unchanged → build skipped → smell gate (deps:[build]) ran a STALE binary. Both session symptoms (phantom 98-NEW; masked incomplete dead_code fix) trace to this. Fix: added the embedded assets to sources; verified a rule content change now forces a rebuild. PART 2 (dogfood the _ast-requiring rules on mache's own source — cyclomatic_complexity/long_function/long_file/magic_int_in_comparison/duplicate_code, silently skipped by the tree-sitter self-gate) REMAINS. Now viable: LLO v0.7.0 makes leyline extraction solid (qualified tokens, source_file, cross-language) and is pinned in mache (#507). Approach: add a gate lane that builds an _ast .db of mache's own source via `leyline parse` and ratchets the _ast rules too — but CI has no leyline binary, so this needs either a leyline-in-CI step or a committed ground-truth .db fixture. Keeping this bead OPEN for part 2.

title: Normalized cross-language code-fact layer: leyline-materialized tables (not runtime views/DSL)
description:
## Idea
A normalized, cross-language "code fact" layer that consumers (smell rules, cross-language analysis, cross-refs) query via PLAIN SQL — no bespoke query DSL, no per-language SQL, no per-query view recomputation. CodeQL/Glean's normalization idea, but SQLite is the engine and the abstraction is a stable SCHEMA.

## Shape
Each language's raw _ast node kinds (Go function_declaration, Rust function_item, Py function_definition, ...) map to ONE normalized shape. Emit normalized tables — e.g. _symbols / _functions / _calls / _types / _imports — where a row is language-agnostic (name, kind, span, file, refs). Consumers query the normalized table once, language-agnostic.

## Perf: MATERIALIZE, don't view
Runtime SQLite views are logical — re-run per query (the perf concern). Instead leyline MATERIALIZES these normalized tables at parse time, exactly as it already emits _ast / _source / _imports. Indexed real tables → fast reads, no recomputation. (Today's ensureCanonicalViews v_refs/v_defs with fidelity-discriminator is this pattern in miniature — logical + refs-only; generalize + materialize it.)

## "Generate" = the mapping
The per-language node-kind → normalized-concept mapping is spec-driven (tied to internal/lang.Registry). Natural fit for cff68e (mache-cff68e) capnp-IDL: define the normalized schema + per-language mappings as IDL → generate the leyline emitter + Go/TS validators. One source of truth, cross-repo-consistent.

## Why it matters (subsumes threads)
- CGO removal (mache-37ae8b): if consumers query normalized tables, the tree-sitter selector DSL (ASTWalker predicate parity) isn't needed at all → deletion trivial.
- cff68e (mache-cff68e): smell rules become plain SQL over the normalized layer; the rule format + the fact schema are one IDL.
- mache-d5e158 (consume LLO passes): home for the emitter is leyline — this is where the normalized tables get produced.

## Next
Deserves an ADR ("mache normalized cross-language code-fact model"): the normalized schema, the mapping spec, materialized-vs-view decision, migration from ensureCanonicalViews, and the leyline producer contract. Cross-repo (mache defines schema/consumers; leyline produces).

title: Audit: is sheaf-driven incremental invalidation live end-to-end (or is the daemon side a sketch)?
description:
## Strategic context

Mache's actual moat over peer code-intelligence tools (codebase-memory-mcp, Serena, agent-lsp, GrapeRoot) is not the MCP tool surface or the schema-driven projection or even the projected filesystem in isolation — it's the **sheaf-based topologically-precise cache invalidation** in `internal/leyline/sheaf.go` paired with LLO's live arena.

Nobody else does this. Codebase-memory-mcp has 22-pass incremental rebuild but treats it as "what files changed, re-run affected passes." Mache's model (per `sheaf.go:69`) is: communities are regions, refs that cross community boundaries become restrictions, file changes propagate only along restriction edges. That's mathematically precise change propagation — not heuristic file-set diffing.

But: is this actually wired end-to-end, or is `PushTopology` a one-way "tell the daemon what the communities are" without the daemon doing anything with it? If the daemon doesn't actually emit "region X is now stale" events that mache acts on, the sheaf is potential, not actualized.

## What this bead is

A focused audit. Not implementation — diagnosis. Trace the full data flow:

1. **Source file change**: user edits `pkg/foo.go`. fsnotify in LLO daemon fires.
2. **Daemon re-parse**: which files re-parse? Just `foo.go`, or its tree-sitter dependency closure, or the whole project?
3. **Restriction recompute**: does the daemon update its stored sheaf restrictions based on the new refs from `foo.go`? Or are the restrictions only set at `PushTopology`-time and never updated?
4. **Region invalidation**: does the daemon mark regions stale based on which restrictions changed?
5. **Notification path**: does the daemon emit an invalidation event back to mache (via UDS subscribe op? via polling?)? Or does mache have to ask?
6. **MCP cache flush**: does mache invalidate any cached query results (`find_callers` etc.) when regions invalidate?
7. **Agent visibility**: does the agent get any signal that "the data you queried before X timestamp may be stale"?

## Acceptance

A markdown doc at `docs/audit/sheaf-incremental.md` answering each of the 7 questions above with citations into `ley-line-open/rs/ll-open/cli-lib/src/daemon/` (or whichever daemon source is current). For any "no" or "partial" answer, file a follow-up bead in this thread.

A simple empirical probe: with `leyline daemon --source <repo>` running and mache connected via `--control`, edit a Go file, time how long until `find_callers` on a token in that file reflects the change. If it's <500ms, the loop works; if it's "next restart of mache serve," the loop is sketch-only.

## Why this matters more than curation right now

The consumer-curation thread (5 beads, this thread) makes mache's data legible to agents. **But the actual differentiator over codebase-memory-mcp is "the data stays fresh with mathematically precise invalidation cost."** If we land curation but the freshness story is incidental rather than sheaf-driven, we've made mache a worse codebase-memory-mcp. If we verify the sheaf wiring works, mache has a story nobody else can tell.

## Scope guardrail

This is audit + doc, not implementation. The follow-up beads come AFTER we know which links in the chain are real.

## Reference

- `internal/leyline/sheaf.go` — mache-side sheaf client
- `internal/leyline/sheaf_test.go` — tests of the SheafClient
- ley-line-open's `rs/ll-open/cli-lib/src/daemon/` — daemon-side sheaf ops (`sheaf_set_topology`, `sheaf_invalidate`, `sheaf_status`, `sheaf_defect`)
- Bead `mache-33ffb0` (pre-injection + warm-cache epic) currently depends on consumer-curation; should also depend on this audit since the "warm cache" half is meaningless without a live invalidation loop.

title: Surface sheaf state via MCP — get_sheaf_status tool for agent-visible freshness
description:
## What this is

A new MCP tool, `get_sheaf_status`, that returns the live sheaf state from the LLO daemon in an agent-consumable shape:

```jsonc
{
  "phase": "warming" | "ready" | "reingesting",
  "regions_total": 47,
  "regions_valid": 47,        // count where restriction-hash matches current source
  "regions_stale": 0,
  "defect": 0.0,              // global consistency metric, 0.0 = settled
  "last_invalidation_at": "2026-05-16T16:32:01.234Z",
  "last_file_change_at": "2026-05-16T16:32:00.987Z",
  "staleness_ms": 247         // last_invalidation_at - last_file_change_at
}
```

## Why an MCP tool, not just internal state

The actual UX win is the agent KNOWING when the index is settled. Today an agent calling `find_callers(Foo)` has no idea whether the answer reflects current source or a stale snapshot. With `get_sheaf_status`, the agent can:

- Call it at session start; if `phase == "warming"`, wait or proceed informed
- Call it after a `write_file` (mache's edit pipeline) and verify the change reflected before next query
- Compose into agent-side decisions: "the defect is 0.02 (settled), my structural answer is high-confidence"

This is the "this is fine" affordance that an IDE gives implicitly (the spinner stops). Agents don't have spinners. They have tool calls. `get_sheaf_status` is the spinner.

## Acceptance

1. New handler `makeGetSheafStatusHandler` wraps `SheafClient.Status()` (already exists in `internal/leyline/sheaf.go:138`).
2. Registered in `cmd/serve_handlers.go` next to the other handlers.
3. Returns the shape above. Daemon-not-running → returns `{phase: "no_daemon", ...}` with the rest as zero values (graceful degradation).
4. The existing readiness gate in `wrapHandler` (cmd/serve_registry.go:139) — which today returns "graph still loading" — should use this tool's underlying data so the gate and the tool agree.
5. Test: a mock SheafClient returning known state produces the expected JSON shape.

## Composes with the audit bead

This bead's acceptance assumes the daemon-side `sheaf_status` op actually returns meaningful data. If the audit (upstream bead, this thread) reveals the daemon doesn't track restriction-hashes per region or doesn't compute staleness, this bead needs to wait or the daemon work needs to land first.

## Why this is the differentiator

No other tool has this. agent-lsp has LSP diagnostics. codebase-memory-mcp has `index_status` (boolean: indexing yes/no). Neither surfaces a *defect score* or *region-level* staleness. Mache can offer mathematical precision on freshness because the sheaf model gives it.

The pitch becomes: "your code intel tool tells you when it's fresh. Mache tells you HOW fresh, region by region, with a defect score that's mathematically grounded."

## Reference

- `internal/leyline/sheaf.go` — Status, Defect methods already exist
- `cmd/serve_handlers.go:1134` — `makeGetOverviewHandler` is the structural pattern to mirror
- `cmd/serve_registry.go:139` — readiness gate that should be unified with this tool
- Depends on the audit bead (upstream) confirming the daemon side is real, not sketch

title: Test discipline: -race in CI catches scheduling-dependent races local misses
description:
## Surfaced by

PR #384 CI failure on `test (macos-latest)` (run 26063835518). A data race + nil-deref panic in `SocketClient.Close()` vs the goroutine spawned by `SocketClient.Subscribe()`:

```
WARNING: DATA RACE
Write at c.conn  by Close()       socket.go:267 (c.conn = nil)
Read  at c.conn  by Subscribe.func1 socket.go:433 (SetReadDeadline)
↓
panic: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference
```

Fixed in commit 5254178 (`sync.Once` over field-zeroing, never nil out the conn pointer).

## The discipline gap

Local `go test -race ./internal/leyline/...` was clean across many runs during PR #384 development. CI on macos-latest hit the race deterministically on the first run. The race-detector catches a race only when goroutines interleave the right way — local scheduling on Apple M3 Max happened to avoid the window; CI runners with different schedulers / load patterns did not.

## What to encode

A few patterns worth either documenting in CLAUDE.md or wiring into Taskfile.yml / a pre-PR check:

1. **`go test -race -count=N` on any package that uses goroutines.** Single-run -race is not sufficient. N=20 is the floor for any concurrency-touching package; we already use this pattern in PR #384's verification step but it wasn't part of the workflow when the original code was written.

2. **`sync.Once` is the default discipline for lifecycle teardown.** Whenever a struct has Close-ish semantics and concurrent readers exist, `sync.Once` is the right idiom — not "guard with if x != nil then assign x = nil". The latter is racy by construction; the former is correct by construction.

3. **Don't zero out fields read by other goroutines.** Closed `net.Conn` pointers stay valid; subsequent reads return safe errors. The "nil out the field after close" pattern is a category error — it introduces a write that races every read.

4. **Multi-platform CI is load-bearing.** The bug surfaced on macos-latest while ubuntu-latest also ran -race and passed. Don't drop a platform from the matrix just because it's slower.

## Possible deliverables

- (a) Add a `task test:race` target that runs `go test -race -count=20 ./...` and document when to use it (pre-PR for concurrency-touching changes).
- (b) Add a CLAUDE.md section: "Concurrency lifecycle: sync.Once over field-zeroing — see commit 5254178 for the canonical example."
- (c) Consider a CI job that runs a longer race-detector pass on a schedule (nightly?) so deeper races have a chance to surface.

## Files in scope

- `Taskfile.yml` (potential new target)
- `CLAUDE.md` (potential discipline note)
- `.github/workflows/ci.yml` (potential new job)

## Why a bead and not just a note

Because this is the SECOND time this class of bug has slipped through — see also `mache-02a9ab` (TestArenaFlusher_Coalesce: race-detector-clean test that's flaky under CI load due to wall-clock assumptions). The pattern of "tests that pass locally but fail in CI on scheduling-sensitive ways" is recurring. Capturing it as a tracked bead lets us decide if it deserves dedicated infrastructure (a) or stays as a documentation discipline (b).

title: nodes.record declared JSON gives it NUMERIC affinity — numeric-looking content silently corrupted
description:
`internal/ingest/sqlite_writer.go:63` declares the content column as:

    record JSON,

SQLite has no JSON storage class. "JSON" contains no substring matching TEXT/CHAR/CLOB/BLOB/INT/REAL/FLOA/DOUB, so it falls through the affinity rules to NUMERIC affinity. Any value that looks like a well-formed number is converted on INSERT and comes back a different value.

REPRODUCED against mache's exact DDL (not a synthetic table):

    INSERT ... VALUES ('007')          -> SELECT gives 7            (integer)
    INSERT ... VALUES ('1.10')         -> SELECT gives 1.1          (real)
    INSERT ... VALUES ('1e3')          -> SELECT gives 1000         (integer)
    INSERT ... VALUES ('0x1F')         -> '0x1F'                    (text, unaffected)
    INSERT ... VALUES ('func f() {}')  -> 'func f() {}'             (text, unaffected)

EXPOSURE
Source-code schemas are effectively safe: a rendered construct body is never a bare number. The exposure is DATA schemas, which are a first-class use case (examples/ ships nvd, kev, notion, trivy, sql, mcp-registry). Any leaf whose content_template renders a single scalar is at risk:

  - a version string: {{.version}} -> "1.10" becomes 1.1, and "1.10" != "1.1" for any
    consumer doing version comparison or exact match
  - a zero-padded identifier: "007" becomes 7
  - a score or measurement rendered alone: "7.10" becomes 7.1

Silent in every case — no error, no warning, and the value round-trips as a number so nothing downstream can tell it was ever a string.

CREDIT / PROVENANCE
Found via ley-line-open, which hit the identical defect and is changing its own nodes.record declaration from JSON to TEXT for exactly this reason ("JSON gave it NUMERIC affinity, so '007' was being stored as 7"). mache copied or converged on the same declaration and has the same bug.

FIX
Change the declaration to TEXT. This is a schema change to emitted .db files, so:
  - decide whether existing .db artifacts need regeneration (they do, if any carry
    numeric-looking record values — otherwise the change is inert for them);
  - check whether anything reads `record` expecting a numeric type back. SQLiteWriter's
    own GetNode scans it into sql.NullString, which tolerates both, so the read path is
    likely fine — verify rather than assume;
  - coordinate with the leyline pin bump, since LLO is making the same change and the
    two schemas should not diverge mid-flight.

TEST
Assert round-trip fidelity for adversarial scalars through the real writer, not a
hand-built table: '007', '1.10', '1e3', '0.0', '+1', ' 42 ', 'Infinity', and a normal
source body as control. Store then read back and require byte equality with the input.
This is exactly the class feedback_happy_path_not_enough calls for — the happy path
(source code) never trips it.

comments.text:
FIXED — merged to main as 09a2fbe (PR #569).

nodes.record declared TEXT instead of JSON in both writers: internal/ingest/sqlite_writer.go (the nodes table) and graph/sqlite.go (the export writer).

CORRECTION TO THE ORIGINAL DESCRIPTION — the exposure was NOT what this bead claimed. The description says data schemas (nvd/kev/notion/trivy) were at risk. They were not: SQLiteWriter binds n.Data as []byte, SQLite stores that as a BLOB, and NUMERIC affinity does not convert BLOBs. Ingest was immune the entire time — by accident of the bind type, not by design.

The reachable path was WRITE-BACK. WritableGraph.UpdateRecord binds string(content), which is TEXT, which is exactly what NUMERIC affinity rewrites. Editing a projected file through the mount so its body is '007' stored 7, and since `size` is bound separately as len(content), the row desynced too.

Verified projection-neutral: rebuilt fixture is byte-identical before and after (7 nodes / 254 bytes), because source content travels the BLOB path.

Test: internal/ingest/sqlite_writer_affinity_test.go — asserts the declared type directly, and round-trips '007', '1.10', '1e3', '+1', '0.50', ' 42 ' through a TEXT bind with '0x1F', 'Infinity', and a real source body as controls. Fails against `record JSON`, passes against `record TEXT`. Note ' 42 ' also converts — SQLite trims whitespace before the numeric check, so it was miscategorised as a control at first.

Test fixtures mirroring mache's nodes table were updated; fixtures declaring a `results` table were deliberately left as JSON, since those simulate third-party source databases mache ingests FROM, where a numeric-affinity column is a realistic thing to encounter.

Found via ley-line-open, which hit the identical defect in its own nodes table.

acceptance_criteria: A test that writes adversarial scalar content ('007', '1.10', '1e3', '0.0', '+1', 'Infinity') through SQLiteWriter and reads it back, requiring exact byte equality for every value; it must FAIL against the current `record JSON` declaration and PASS after the change to TEXT. Plus `go test ./internal/ingest/ ./internal/graph/` green.

title: Document mache's freshness story per use case in ARCHITECTURE.md
description:
User question 2026-05-19: "how do we ensure the mache db stays up-to-date?" surfaced that mache's freshness story is implemented across THREE regimes but not documented as a cohesive story:

| Path | Freshness mechanism | Trade-off |
| --- | --- | --- |
| MemoryStore (`mache serve <dir>`) | `internal/ingest/watcher.go` fsnotify | Live; fsnotify's actual limits apply |
| Auto-leyline .db (`mache serve <dir>` with leyline on PATH) | **Frozen at build** — one-shot parse | Fast cold start; stale on first edit (documented in cmd/serve.go:390-417 as known degradation) |
| Leyline daemon + sheaf subscriber (`mache serve --control <ctrl>`) | Daemon push via UDS (shipped mache-c14c43, PR #400) | Push model; LLO owns the watch; mache invalidates on event |

These regimes match different use cases (interactive MCP, CI gate, agent daemon) but the design rationale is scattered across cmd/serve.go comments + internal/leyline/ package docs. A reader new to mache can't see the matrix.

## Acceptance

Add a `## Freshness` section to docs/ARCHITECTURE.md covering:

- The 3-regime matrix above (paths + mechanisms + when-to-use)
- Honest naming of the auto-leyline staleness (already documented inline; surface it at the architecture level)
- Decision matrix: "I want to use mache for X — which path do I pick?"
- Cross-reference the ADR-0006 (pure-Go MCP-first) decision that shaped this

No code change. Pure documentation. Pairs with [[mache-bb6601]] (watcher failure-mode audit, sibling bead).

title: Audit in-process watcher (fsnotify) failure modes — decide keep/replace/deprecate
description:
User feedback 2026-05-19: "fsnotify isn't a safe dep and is 'easy to roll your own'". Worth a structured audit rather than a knee-jerk replacement.

Current mache fsnotify usage (narrow):

- `internal/ingest/watcher.go` — the only production use; watches a source dir, fires on changes, triggers re-ingest in MemoryStore mode
- `internal/ingest/watcher_test.go` — test coverage
- `internal/writeback/splice_test.go` — test-only

Known fsnotify failure modes worth checking against mache's actual usage:

1. **macOS event loss under heavy load** — does mache hit this? (Many small edits via formatter/IDE)
2. **Linux inotify limits** — `fs.inotify.max_user_watches` defaults are low; mache on a large repo could blow through
3. **Recursive watching cost** — fsnotify doesn't watch recursively natively; mache walks + watches each dir, which is O(N)
4. **Race conditions on rapid create/delete** — fsnotify event ordering vs filesystem state can diverge
5. **Reload behavior on watch loss** — if a watch is dropped (process restart, descriptor exhaustion), does mache recover or silently miss events?

## Decision matrix

- **Keep fsnotify** if: actual failure modes don't bite mache's narrow usage; cross-platform complexity outweighs benefits of polling/syscall
- **Replace with polling** if: failure modes do bite, AND mache's typical use case can tolerate poll latency (1-5s for interactive)
- **Deprecate MemoryStore-with-watcher path** if: the LLO-daemon-push model (mache-c14c43, shipped via PR #400) covers all real use cases and the in-process watcher is now redundant infrastructure

## Acceptance

- ADR or bead comment documenting which failure modes mache verified, with reproduction notes
- One of: (a) keep + docs caveat; (b) replace + migration; (c) deprecate + removal plan
- Test that exercises whichever decision lands

Pairs with [[freshness-docs-bead]] (freshness story documentation, sibling).

title: Nothing verifies published release artifacts after the fact
description:
Found while auditing whether the release pipeline works (2026-07-28). It does — verified for v0.19.0 at every layer: the workflow run succeeded, all five jobs succeeded (build x3, image, release), GitHub carries 3 binaries plus checksums-sha256.txt, and ghcr.io/agentic-research/mache:v0.19.0 exists with an unbroken tag series back to v0.14.0.

So this is not a defect report. It is the gap that audit had to work around: EVERY ONE OF THOSE CHECKS WAS MANUAL. Nothing in the pipeline asserts that what was published is what was intended.

Both the `image` and `release` jobs can be green while shipping something wrong — a binary built from the wrong ref, an image tagged but not pushed, a checksums file that does not match its binaries. Job success reports that the steps ran, not that the artifact is correct. That is the same "a metric derived from a mechanism must assert the mechanism fired" gap this repo already applies elsewhere (ley-line-open-2607d2's silent-success class, and the reason the smell gate asserts rule output rather than exit codes).

SUGGESTED CHECK, deliberately small — a post-release job that, given the tag:
  - downloads each published binary from the release
  - verifies it against the published checksums-sha256.txt
  - runs `mache --version` and asserts the output matches the tag
  - pulls the OCI image by tag and asserts the same

That last one matters most: `--version` matching the tag is the single assertion that catches a build from the wrong ref, which is the failure mode with no other symptom.

RELATED OBSERVATION, not necessarily a defect: mache ships THREE platform binaries (darwin-arm64, linux-amd64, linux-arm64). There is no darwin-amd64, and there never has been — the matrix has exactly three entries and v0.17.0 / v0.18.0 / v0.19.0 all shipped the same set. Worth a deliberate decision rather than an accident, because mache REQUIRES four platforms from its own dependency: `task leyline:pin-bump` fails closed unless a leyline release carries all four including darwin-amd64. Demanding Intel Mac support from ley-line-open while not shipping it is inconsistent; either is defensible, but they should agree.

Out of scope: the homebrew formula. agentic-research/homebrew-tap's Formula/mache.rb points at the archived kiln project, so `brew install mache` yields a v0.6.6 binary from a dead repo. The owner is aware and has deferred it deliberately as part of release work; release.yml does not touch the tap either way.

comments.author: rsry-mcp

acceptance_criteria: A workflow job (or `task release:verify TAG=vX.Y.Z`) downloads each published binary for the tag, verifies it against the published checksums file, asserts `mache --version` reports that tag, and asserts the OCI image for that tag is pullable — failing loudly on any mismatch. Exercised against an existing published tag to prove it can pass, and against a deliberately wrong tag to prove it can fail.

title: ASTWalker large-repo schema projection is pathologically slow (whole mache repo >3min vs SitterWalker's seconds) — affects mache build --schema on any big repo
description:
Surfaced by PR-B (mache-37ae8b) when mache-self (whole-repo fixture) routed through the ASTWalker instead of the removed in-process SitterWalker. NOT a leyline regression — leyline parse of the whole repo is 9.5s (727 files, 856K _ast rows), verified. The slowness is mache-side: the Engine+ASTWalker schema PROJECTION of the parsed _ast.

## Symptom
`mache build --schema go .` (or serve/mount) on the whole mache repo: leyline parse 9.5s, then the schema projection runs >3min and doesn't finish (hits the 20min package timeout in TestRegistry_Get_MacheSelfReturnsLiveGraph). A goroutine sits in database/sql (*Tx).awaitDone on the OUTPUT (SQLiteWriter) db. Small fixtures (1-2 files) project instantly, so it's a scaling cliff.

## NOT the obvious index
findNodesByKind's query is fully indexed (EXPLAIN: SEARCH a USING idx_ast_kind_source, SEARCH n USING covering autoindex on nodes.id). SetASTWalker already calls EnsureIndexes. So individual queries are fast.

## Likely causes (profile to confirm)
1. VOLUME: 856K constructs → the Engine calls ASTWalker.Query per-file-per-selector (727 files × ~8 go-schema selectors, some recursive) AND writes ~856K nodes to the SQLiteWriter output. If the SQLiteWriter commits per-insert (not one batched transaction), that's pathological (fsync per insert). CHECK SQLiteWriter's insert/transaction batching first — likely the biggest win.
2. readSource per Query call re-reads full file content repeatedly.
3. Recursive selector explosion (per-construct recursion) inflating Query count beyond files×selectors.

## Why it matters
This is a real user-facing regression from #524's schema-on-leyline (which only tested small fixtures): `mache build --schema`, `mache serve <dir>`, `mache mount <dir>` on ANY large repo now hang. Before PR-B the SitterWalker did the whole repo in-memory in seconds.

## Fix direction
Profile the projection (pprof). Likely: batch SQLiteWriter inserts in one transaction (or larger batches); memoize readSource per source_id; consider bulk-projecting per selector across all files instead of per-file. Target: whole mache repo projects in <30s. Add mache-self back to the un-gated test set once fixed (currently gated behind MACHE_E2E_LARGE in PR-B).

RELEASE NOTE: this should be fixed before/with v0.18.0 — a pure-Go binary that can't project a large repo in reasonable time is a poor headline.

comments.text:
FIXED — falsifiably verified. Root cause (5-whys): the ASTWalker ported SitterWalker's O(nodes) in-memory tree walk to per-node SQL, so tree traversal became O(nodes²) — findChildByKindAST re-scanned ALL same-kind nodes in the file on every call (driven by idx_ast_kind_source, post-filtered by n.id LIKE parent/%, no id-path index to prune). Two extraction paths did this per-construct: ExtractAddressRefsScoped (generic Query, 38%) and ExtractCallsScoped (queryCallPattern per construct, 49%).

Fix (quotient computed once, then partition by node-id prefix):
1. tuneReadConn: pin single connection + PRAGMA locking_mode=EXCLUSIVE (kills the per-statement fcntl lock storm, was 81% CPU) + mmap_size=2GiB (pread→mapped reads) + cache_size.
2. Per-file in-memory node index (ast_walker_index.go): findNodesByKind/findChildByKindAST/findChildrenByKindAST answer from a once-loaded per-file map instead of per-node SQL. Whole-DB path (sourceID=="") keeps SQL. Load errors propagate (no silent-empty).
3. fileAddrRefs / fileCallTokens: compute whole-file address-refs + call tokens ONCE per file (cached), attribute to constructs by node-id prefix — byte-identical to the old `n.id LIKE scope/%`.

Results (falsifiable):
- cmd/ (200 files): 4m22s → 3.1s (78×). node_refs/defs/nodes BYTE-IDENTICAL to pre-fix baseline (0 differing lines; the only apparent diff was my temp pprof hook's own tokens, gone now).
- whole mache repo (728 files, 1.9GB _ast): >3min / 20-min testfixtures hang → ~10s.

OPEN CAVEAT (found reviewing the serve/mount lifecycle): tuneReadConn applies SetMaxOpenConns(1)+PRAGMA locking_mode=EXCLUSIVE unconditionally in NewASTWalker. Correct for the one-shot `mache build` (db closed after ingest), but serve/mount keep the _ast db open for the SESSION lifetime (cmd/serve.go:483-497) and use it at serve-time via the call-extractor (callers/callees) + watcher ReIngestFile. So concurrent call-graph resolution now SERIALIZES on one connection — a throughput regression (NOT a deadlock: queryCallPattern only Scans in its row loop; extractor uses QueryRow, both auto-release; no nested query on open rows). No concurrent-serve stress test exists, so the green cmd suite doesn't cover this.

Fix direction: the real speedups are the in-memory node index (algorithmic O(n²)→O(n)) + mmap — both connection-count-agnostic. locking_mode=EXCLUSIVE + single-conn were marginal AFTER the index cut query count ~100× (they mattered when the fcntl storm dominated pre-index). So scope the aggressive single-conn/EXCLUSIVE to one-shot build (a flag on NewASTWalker or a separate constructor), OR drop them and keep index+mmap. title: ADR-0021 PR 1: mache suggest subcommand + /suggest daemon endpoint + rank table (v1: filename + mtime)
description:
First of three PRs from ADR-0021 (docs/adr/0021-file-suggester.md, merged in d57702c). Ships the engine end-to-end at v1 fidelity: filename trigram + mtime only. No external dependencies on lectio or rosary — those signals land in PR 2.

## Acceptance

`task install && mache serve --http && echo '{"query":"foo"}' | mache suggest` returns up to 15 newline-separated repo-relative paths, ranked, in under 100ms when the daemon is warm. Verified by a new e2e test in cmd/.

## Scope (3 deliverables)

1. **`cmd/suggest.go`** — new subcommand implementing the Claude Code fileSuggestion protocol:
   - Reads `{"query": "..."}` JSON on stdin (single line)
   - GETs `http://localhost:7532/suggest?q=<urlencoded>` against the running daemon
   - Prints up to 15 newline-separated repo-relative paths on stdout
   - On any error: exit 0, print nothing (per ADR D.3 graceful-degradation tier 6)

2. **`internal/suggester/`** — new package:
   - `rank.go` — `mache_suggest_rank` SQL schema (path TEXT PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, score REAL, recency INTEGER) in the per-repo `.refs.db`
   - `refresh.go` — refresh tick: enumerate files via `lang.Registry` extensions, compute `score = filename_trigram_match + log(mtime_recency)`, upsert into the table. Initial seed on `mache build`; later ticks debounced from FS events.
   - `serve.go` — HTTP handler at `/suggest`: parse `q`, run the ADR D.1 query, return paths. ≤30ms warm.

3. **Wire into existing infra**:
   - `cmd/build.go` learns `--with-rank` flag; default-on so first `@`-keystroke is fast.
   - `cmd/serve.go` registers `/suggest` on the same `:7532` HTTP server.
   - `mache push` excludes `mache_suggest_rank` from the portable cache (per ADR Consequences).

## Test plan

- Unit: `internal/suggester/rank_test.go` — trigram match correctness on a known fixture (use testfixtures.Get("mache-self"))
- Unit: refresh-tick idempotency (run twice, rows unchanged)
- E2E in `cmd/suggest_e2e_test.go` — start serve, POST a query, assert ≤15 paths, ≤100ms wall
- E2E adversarial: empty query → top-N by score; non-existent query → empty stdout

## Non-goals (deferred to PR 2/3)

- lectio conversation-mention signal
- rosary bead-scope boost
- mache community-centrality, LLO import-count, symbol-density signals
- Adaptive weights (v3 scope)
- The cloister-side plugin packaging

## References

- ADR: docs/adr/0021-file-suggester.md
- Protocol: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings (fileSuggestion section)
- Daemon precedent: ADR-0010 (Hosted Mache Architecture)

title: [tools/mcp-fetch/main.go] log.Fatal causes immediate exit without cleanup
description: Line 50: log.Fatal(err) exits immediately. Should return error for graceful shutdown. Priority: High.

title: [writable_graph.go] resolveContent FIFO cache race causes duplicate contentKeys entries
description: resolveContent (line 185) drops the contentMu lock at line 192 after a cache miss, then re-acquires at line 221 to store. Two goroutines resolving the same ID concurrently will both append to contentKeys, causing the same key to appear twice. When the first copy is evicted, the map entry is deleted but the second copy remains in contentKeys as a dangling reference. This means future evictions will delete wrong entries or no-op, and the cache can grow beyond maxContent. Fix: re-check the cache after re-acquiring the lock and skip the store if another goroutine already populated it. Effort: trivial (add 4-line check).

title: [engine.go] O(n) linear scan for child dedup in processNode and ingestRawFileUnder
description: Lines 553-560 and 977-986 in engine.go: When linking a new node to its parent, the code linearly scans parent.Children to check if the child already exists. For large directories this is O(n) per insertion. The same pattern appears in ingestRawFileUnder (lines 553-560). Fix: similar to the AddRoot fix (mache-ton), maintain a childSet or use a sorted insert + binary search. However, since Children is a []string owned by the Node, a pragmatic fix is to use a local seen map[string]bool during the processNode call. ~10 lines to fix per site.

title: [gitignore.go] Use fs.WalkDir instead of filepath.Walk
description: Line 40 uses deprecated filepath.Walk which calls os.Lstat on every entry. fs.WalkDir is more efficient — avoids extra stat calls since DirEntry carries the type. Drop-in replacement, same callback shape. Effort: trivial.

title: README's docker invocation double-specifies `serve` — the image ENTRYPOINT already includes it, and a bad arg silently boots a default server instead of erroring
description:
Found 2026-07-30 while verifying the v0.20.0 release image actually runs (docker daemon was down during the release check, so this is the first real execution of a published mache image).

## Measured

    $ docker inspect ghcr.io/agentic-research/mache:v0.20.0 \
        --format 'ENTRYPOINT={{json .Config.Entrypoint}} CMD={{json .Config.Cmd}}'
    ENTRYPOINT=["/usr/local/bin/mache","serve"]  CMD=["/source"]

Args passed to `docker run` REPLACE CMD and append to ENTRYPOINT. So:

    docker run IMAGE <args>   ->   mache serve <args>

README.md:196 documents:

    docker run --rm -i mache:0.20.0 serve --stdio /path/to/source

which expands to `mache serve serve --stdio /path/to/source` — **`serve` twice**. The documented, copy-pasteable command is wrong.

## The sharper half: a bad arg does not error

    $ docker run --rm ghcr.io/agentic-research/mache:v0.20.0 version
    2026/07/30 16:54:04 mache MCP server listening on localhost:7532/mcp (Streamable HTTP)

`version` became `mache serve version`. Rather than failing on a source path that does not exist, it silently fell back to starting a default MCP server on 7532. A user typing the obvious thing to check the image's version gets a hung server instead of an answer or an error. Same silent-fallback shape as mache-d55457's `build` routing (there it at least exited 1; here it exits 0 and blocks).

## Two things to decide, not one

1. README fix is trivial: drop the redundant `serve`, i.e. `docker run --rm -i IMAGE --stdio /path/to/source`. Verify against the real image, not by reading the Dockerfile.
2. Whether ENTRYPOINT should bake in `serve` at all. Baking it makes the image single-purpose and makes `version`/`--help`/`find-smells` unreachable without `--entrypoint`. The alternative — ENTRYPOINT `["mache"]`, CMD `["serve","/source"]` — keeps the default behaviour identical for the documented path while leaving every other subcommand reachable, and makes an unknown arg fail loudly instead of falling through to a server. That is probably right but it IS a user-visible change to how the image is driven, so it needs a deliberate call and a CHANGELOG note.

Related: mache-d55457 (README documents a `mache mount` subcommand that does not exist) and mache-19326d (provisioning only reachable via Taskfile). Three instances of the same class: the documented CLI surface and the real one have drifted, and nothing gates them against each other. Worth considering a doc-vs-CLI gate — mache already has the machinery (README-vs-registry tool-matrix pinning and image-tag-vs-buildinfo pinning both exist and both work; this is the same idea aimed at invocation lines).

NOTE: the image itself is FINE — it pulls, runs, and serves. This is a docs + entrypoint-ergonomics defect, not a broken artifact. v0.20.0 does not need re-cutting.</description>
    </description>

comments.text:
Gate shipped in PR #585 (bead mache-e7c825). One correction to this bead's premise.

**The two images are different artifacts and were conflated.** README.md:196's `docker run --rm -i mache:0.20.0 serve --stdio /path/to/source` names the tag `task image` produces from `apko.yaml`, not the published ghcr image. Measured:

    apko.yaml           -> ENTRYPOINT ["mache"]           CMD ["serve","--stdio"]
    Dockerfile.release  -> ENTRYPOINT ["mache","serve"]   CMD ["/source"]

(apko's exec-form ENTRYPOINT confirmed by actually building a minimal apko config and inspecting the result — it does NOT wrap in `/bin/sh -c`, which would have silently swallowed appended args.)

So README:196 was already correct for the image it names; the `serve serve` expansion is real only for the ghcr image, which the README gave no run line for at all. The fix is therefore additive: README now documents the published image's correct invocation, verified by executing it (this bead's acceptance criterion):

    $ docker run --rm -i ghcr.io/agentic-research/mache:v0.20.0 --stdio /source
    mache MCP server ready on stdio                 <- works
    $ docker run --rm -i ghcr.io/agentic-research/mache:v0.20.0 serve --stdio /source
    Error: accepts at most 1 arg(s), received 2     <- the reported shape

`TestDocumentedDockerRunMatchesImageEntrypoint` now computes ENTRYPOINT ++ args (args replace CMD, append to ENTRYPOINT) for every documented `docker run` and validates the result against the cobra tree, reading ENTRYPOINT/CMD from apko.yaml and Dockerfile.release rather than restating them. `TestDockerEntrypointGateDetectsDrift` pins that the same doc line is correct against one image and rejected against the other.

**Still open and deliberately untouched: decision 2** — whether ENTRYPOINT should bake in `serve` at all. `docker run IMAGE version` still silently boots a server on 7532 instead of answering. That is a user-visible change to how the image is driven and needs a deliberate call plus a CHANGELOG note; the gate makes the current behaviour a stated expectation rather than a surprise, but does not decide it.

comments.text:
PR #586 adds the ratchet half of this bead's acceptance criteria, complementing the doc-vs-CLI gate on `chore/doc-cli-surface-gate` (mache-e7c825): that one checks the DOCS against the image; this one pins the IMAGE itself.

`TestPublishedImageEntrypointBakesInServe` (in `tests/installverify/docker_test.go`, run by `task install:verify:docker`) reads `docker image inspect --format '{{json .Config.Entrypoint}}'` and asserts it equals `["/usr/local/bin/mache","serve"]`, with the consequence stated in the failure message: every `docker run` of the image appends to `mache serve`, so any other subcommand needs `--entrypoint`.

Verified by execution, not by reading Dockerfile.release:

```
$ docker run --rm ghcr.io/agentic-research/mache:v0.20.0 version
2026/07/30 17:12:26 mache MCP server listening on localhost:7532/mcp (Streamable HTTP)
2026/07/30 17:12:38 shutting down…
```

— confirming the report exactly: no version printed, a default server booted instead, exit 0.

The decision this bead asks for is therefore recorded as KEEP `serve` baked in, and the whole install-verify suite drives the image with explicit `--entrypoint` throughout. If that decision is ever revisited, the assertion fails and forces the CHANGELOG note the acceptance criteria call for, rather than the change landing silently.

Not addressed here: the README line itself — that belongs to the doc-vs-CLI gate branch, which already fixes it.

title: leyline Subscribe goroutine: silent drops + indistinguishable deadline-vs-EOF
description:
## Surfaced by

Silent-failure-hunter pass over `internal/leyline/` (2026-05-18, paired with the post-PR #384 evolve sweep). Three closely-related observability gaps in the same goroutine (`internal/leyline/socket.go:429-464` — `Subscribe.func1`).

## The gaps (all in `socket.go`)

**1. Malformed-event silent drop (`:454`)** — `if err := json.Unmarshal([]byte(evLine), &ev); err != nil { continue }`. A single corrupted line silently disappears. If LLO ever ships a wire-incompatible event shape (LLO version skew is the real risk — see `wire.go` comment about pre-/post-b0ea2e codec), the subscriber goes deaf with no surfacing.

**2. Read-deadline timeout indistinguishable from clean EOF (`:436-441`)** — both `if ne, ok := err.(net.Error); ok && ne.Timeout() { return }` and `return // connection closed or broken` defer `close(ch)`. Consumers cannot tell "daemon died 60s ago without TCP close" from "daemon cleanly closed". This is the exact "MCP tools just stop working without operator-visible cause" failure mode.

**3. Slow-consumer event drop with zero feedback (`:458-462`)** — `select { case ch <- ev: default: /* Drop if consumer is behind. */ }`. The comment is honest but the consumer has no signal. For sheaf.invalidate events (the wire seam this whole package exists to serve), a dropped event is a stale cache that never invalidates — the canonical "silently wrong" failure mode.

## Fix shape

One PR, observability hardening across the Subscribe goroutine:

- **Item 1**: `log.Printf("subscribe: drop malformed event: %v (line=%q)", err, evLine)`. Optionally: bounded counter on consecutive parse failures that returns from the goroutine (treat sustained garbage as connection-dead).
- **Item 2**: `log.Printf("subscribe: read deadline exceeded, treating connection as dead")` on the timeout path; consider exposing an `Err()` method on a wrapper or pushing a sentinel `{"event": true, "type": "subscribe.disconnected", "reason": "..."}` into `ch` before close so downstream can react.
- **Item 3**: increment an exported `Dropped uint64` (atomic), log on first drop and every Nth thereafter (avoid log flood). Surface via `SocketClient.Stats()` or similar.

## Why P2 (not P3)

`internal/leyline/sheaf_subscriber.go` (PR #384) now wires real cache-invalidation traffic through this goroutine. A drop here means an MCP tool serves stale `find_callers` / `get_overview` / `read_file` results indefinitely with no operator signal. The blast radius is the entire MCP cache for that mache instance.

## Files in scope

- `internal/leyline/socket.go` (the Subscribe goroutine, lines ~429-464)
- `internal/leyline/socket_test.go` (test the new observability: assert log lines on parse fail, assert sentinel event on timeout, assert Dropped counter increments under backpressure)

## Acceptance

- A regression test that pushes a malformed event through the mock daemon and asserts the log line + that the goroutine keeps running (not stuck on first bad line).
- A regression test that closes the mock daemon without notifying and asserts the timeout path emits the log + closes `ch`.
- A regression test that holds the consumer goroutine (full buffer) and asserts the Dropped counter advances + the first drop logs.

## Related

- mache-4a827c (test-discipline meta-bead on -race-vs-CI scheduling)
- ley-line-open-503971 (LLO publishing typed payload structs — orthogonal but in the same drift-prevention spirit)

title: fan_out_skew's corpus-wide mean is polluted by markdown refs once LLO v0.13.0's backtick fix lands
description:
Tested mache against ley-line-open PR #304 (release-hardening, destined for v0.13.0) by building the branch locally and pointing mache at it via MACHE_LEYLINE_BINARY.

`ley-line-open-ea1e42` (markdown backtick → node_refs, "unblocks mache 0.20's drift rule") works exactly as advertised: single-backtick spans become real node_refs with delimiters stripped, escaped backticks correctly produce nothing, double-backtick spans keep their embedded literal backtick. Verified A/B against v0.12.1 (zero refs) vs v0.13.0-candidate (7577 refs across mache's own docs). ir_schema_version/extraction_epoch unchanged (merkle-ast-v2/4 both), only injection_epoch shifted — correctly scoped, no lineage event.

BUT: running the full smell gate on identical source (mache main) with only the leyline binary swapped produced 307 NEW fan_out_skew findings that don't exist on v0.12.1. Root cause, fully diagnosed:

fan_out_skew's mean (`proj AS (SELECT AVG(n) AS mu FROM fanout)`) is computed over ALL v_refs rows regardless of source language. v_refs.referrer_node_id = COALESCE(NULLIF(container_node_id,''), node_id) (cmd/smell_refs_views.go). LLO's markdown code-span refs have container_node_id = NULL (no enclosing "function" exists for a doc citation), so each markdown ref falls back to its own node_id — becoming a singleton referrer group with fan-out 1.

Measured directly: corpus mean mu drops from 9.79 (6564 referrer groups) to 5.08 (14141 groups) once the 7577 markdown refs are added, because they're overwhelmingly n=1. The 3x threshold drops from ~29.4 to ~15.2, so every real Go/Rust function with fan-out in that band now fires — none of which is an actual complexity regression, it's the mean being diluted by doc citations.

Also measured: naively wiring up drift_doc_dead_symbol_reference (currently a WHERE 1=0 placeholder) against a plain "node_refs NOT EXISTS in node_defs" join is unusably noisy — on mache's own docs it flags .db, [], bead IDs like mache-2y9w, model names like all-MiniLM-L6-v2, and file paths as "dead symbols". Needs an identifier-shape filter before it's a real rule, not just a join.

Do NOT bump the leyline pin to v0.13.0 without the fan_out_skew fix landing first and the smell baseline being verified clean, or the gate will erupt with 300+ false positives on adoption. v0.13.0 doesn't exist as a release yet as of 2026-07-30 — this was tested against the open PR.
acceptance_criteria: Once LLO v0.13.0 is actually released and the pin is bumped, `task smells` produces zero NEW fan_out_skew findings vs the pre-bump baseline on an unchanged source tree. Verified by: build mache at HEAD with the new pin, diff finding count against docs/smell-baseline.json — must show 0 new fan_out_skew findings attributable to markdown refs entering the corpus-wide mean calculation.

title: leyline trigger.go: ReadContent + ListChildren error swallowing in embed walk
description:
## Surfaced by

Silent-failure-hunter pass over `internal/leyline/` (2026-05-18). Three error-swallowing patterns in `internal/leyline/trigger.go`, all in the embed-trigger walk path.

## The patterns

**1. `trigger.go:63` — `n, _ := g.ReadContent(...)` followed by `if n == 0 { continue }`.** A genuine read failure (corrupt SQLite content row, lazy-resolver template error, permission) is indistinguishable from "empty file." Real condition hidden: half the corpus silently skipped during embedding, leading to phantom-missing semantic-search hits later. Caller has no signal that indexing was incomplete.

**2. `trigger.go:47-50` — `walkDir` discards `ListChildren` errors.** `children, err := g.ListChildren(id); if err != nil { return }`. A failure mid-walk silently truncates the embedding corpus to whatever had been reached. Graph backend hiccup, locked SQLite, transient I/O — none of which should mean "we are done indexing."

**3. `trigger.go:36` — Status check error collapsed with "not ready" branch.** `if err != nil || !status.Ready { log.Printf("embed trigger: embeddings not enabled on ley-line daemon"); return }`. If the daemon is reachable but `embed_status` errors (wire mismatch, daemon panic, schema drift), the log message lies — it says "not enabled" when reality is "we couldn't tell."

## Fix shape

One PR, three small changes:

- **Item 1**: bind the err, log on non-nil with the node ID, then continue: `n, err := g.ReadContent(childID, buf, 0); if err != nil { log.Printf("embed trigger: read %s: %v", childID, err); continue }; if n == 0 { continue }`.
- **Item 2**: log the error with the node ID and either continue (skip this subtree, walk remaining roots) or surface at the outer scope so operator sees how far indexing got. Prefer the former — partial corpus is better than silent zero.
- **Item 3**: split the branches and include `err` in the log when non-nil:
  ```go
  if err != nil { log.Printf("embed trigger: status check failed: %v", err); return }
  if !status.Ready { log.Printf("embed trigger: embeddings disabled on daemon"); return }
  ```

## Why P2

These cluster on the embed-trigger path that backs semantic-search. Silent corpus truncation produces "X seems missing from search but the file exists" — the kind of bug that's never tracked back to its source because nothing about it is loud.

## Files in scope

- `internal/leyline/trigger.go` (the three sites above)
- `internal/leyline/trigger_test.go` (if it exists — add coverage for each error branch; if not, this bead also creates it)

## Related

- mache-4a827c (test-discipline meta-bead)
- Silent-failure-hunter items 1-3 → `mache-{subscribe-observability-bead-id}` (sibling, in `socket.go`)

title: parseUint64 / parseIntSlice silently coerce malformed wire to zero (version-skew seam)
description:
## Surfaced by

Silent-failure-hunter pass over `internal/leyline/` (2026-05-18). Same class of bug as the `SocketClient.Close` race fixed in commit 5254178: silent wrong instead of loud failure at a cross-runtime seam.

## The bug

`internal/leyline/sheaf.go:438` defines:

```go
func parseUint64(v any) uint64 {
    switch x := v.(type) {
    case float64: return uint64(x)
    case string:
        var n uint64
        _, _ = fmt.Sscanf(x, "%d", &n)
        return n
    default: return 0
    }
}
```

The `_, _ = fmt.Sscanf` silently coerces malformed strings to 0. The `default: return 0` silently coerces unknown types to 0. The function returns `(uint64)`, not `(uint64, error)` — callers cannot tell "daemon sent generation 0" from "daemon sent something we couldn't parse."

Same shape applies to `parseIntSlice` (sheaf.go:420) — wrong-type input returns nil, indistinguishable from empty slice.

## Why this matters

If a future LLO emits hex-prefixed generation IDs (`"0x1f"`), capnp-quoted variants we haven't seen yet, or any non-decimal numeric encoding, `Generation` becomes 0. `Status` callers will read this as "fresh daemon, never advanced" → MCP cache flushes that should fire don't fire. Cross-runtime version skew on a field whose entire purpose is detecting cache invalidation.

This is the SAME drift seam ley-line-open-503971 addresses from the LLO side. That bead promotes typed payload structs (so `Generation` becomes a real `uint64` Go field decoded by `json.Unmarshal`, errors propagating naturally). But until that lands and mache adopts it, this bead is the mache-side mitigation.

## Fix shape

Two paths, pick one:

**Path A: parseUint64 returns error.** Change to `func parseUint64(v any) (uint64, error)`, surface "unexpected type" / "Sscanf failed" errors. Update callers (4 known sites: `sheaf.go:216`, subscriber dispatch, status decode) to propagate the error. Loud failure at the version-skew boundary.

**Path B: Wait for ley-line-open-503971.** When LLO publishes typed payload structs, mache imports them and `parseUint64`/`parseIntSlice` get deleted entirely. `json.Unmarshal` into the typed struct surfaces all the failure modes naturally.

**Recommendation**: Path B if ley-line-open-503971 lands within a release. Path A if mache wants the hardening sooner. Either way, this bead is closed when malformed input becomes a loud error, not a silent zero.

## Files in scope

- `internal/leyline/sheaf.go` (`parseUint64` + `parseIntSlice` definitions, ~lines 420-449)
- `internal/leyline/sheaf.go` (callers: `Status()`, `Invalidate()` response decoding)
- `internal/leyline/sheaf_subscriber.go` (`dispatch()` calls these on the event payload)
- `internal/leyline/wire.go` (the `parseUint64 silent coercion` note can be deleted once fixed)

## Test plan

- Mock daemon that pushes events with `"generation": "abc"` (malformed string), `"generation": []` (wrong type), `"generation": null`. With current code, all three produce Generation=0. With the fix, all three produce a parse error the dispatch path either logs or surfaces.

## Related

- ley-line-open-503971 (upstream typed structs that obsolete this code path)
- mache-4a827c (test-discipline meta-bead)
- commit 5254178 (the SocketClient.Close race — same class of "silent wrong at a seam" bug)

title: internal/control coverage at 37% — 6 arena/root accessors have 0% coverage
description:
## Surfaced by

Coverage audit (2026-05-18, evolve-smells-sweep). `internal/control` is the lowest-coverage tested package in the repo (37.3% total).

## The gaps (file:line, 0% coverage)

- `GetCurrentRoot` (`control.go:118`)
- `GetArenaPath` (`control.go:135`)
- `GetArenaSize` (`control.go:147`)
- `SetArena` (`control.go:158`)
- `SetArenaWithRoot` (`control.go:179`)
- `IsZeroRoot` (`control.go:200`)

Plus partially-covered functions worth bringing to 100%:
- `OpenOrCreate` (`control.go:55`) — 50%
- `Close` (`control.go:206`) — 67%
- `validatePath` (`control.go:213`) — 80%

## Why P3 (not P2)

These are foundational control-plane accessors. They're glue around `mmap`-backed control-block state — most paths are read-only getters with simple semantics. Zero coverage doesn't mean zero functionality (production paths exercise them), but it does mean:

1. No regression guard if someone changes the binary layout (e.g. adds a new field, shifts offsets).
2. No proof that nil-receiver safety holds for the getters (current code is C-shape mmap with unsafe pointer arithmetic in spots).
3. No happy-path baseline for the setters — `SetArena` and `SetArenaWithRoot` mutate persistent state with no test confirming the write→read round-trip.

The user explicitly flagged "% tested is important" in the evolve scope. This is a concrete, sized target.

## Fix shape

One PR, ~150-200 LOC of focused test code in `internal/control/control_test.go` (file likely exists; check first):

1. **Getter tests** — table-driven: open a control block with known state, call each getter, assert. Cover both fresh-init and pre-populated cases.
2. **Setter round-trip tests** — `SetArena` / `SetArenaWithRoot` → reopen → getter returns the set value.
3. **`IsZeroRoot` edge cases** — zero-hash root, non-zero root, after a SetArena that clears, after a SetArena that writes.
4. **`OpenOrCreate` race path** (the uncovered 50%) — concurrent OpenOrCreate from two goroutines must produce one valid control block, not corrupt state.
5. **`Close` idempotency** — pair with the `SocketClient.Close` sync.Once discipline (mache-4a827c) — Close called twice from one goroutine, Close called concurrently from two.

## Acceptance

- `go test -cover ./internal/control/` reports >= 75% (from 37%).
- Each named 0% function has at least one direct test.
- No new race-detector warnings.

## Files in scope

- `internal/control/control_test.go` (likely exists; expand)
- `internal/control/control.go` (read-only — DO NOT modify production code in this bead)

## Out of scope

- Refactoring control.go to be more testable. If a function is hard to test, prefer extending the test fixture (e.g. test helper for mmap-backed temp control blocks) over refactoring the production surface.

## Related

- mache-4a827c (sync.Once discipline — Close idempotency test in #5 should follow this pattern)

title: DiscoverOrStart auto-spawn lacks dedup — orphans daemons on crash/SIGKILL
description:
Filed 2026-05-11. Surfaced during PR #371 smoke test: a fresh `pgrep -lf 'leyline daemon'` showed **six** orphaned daemons, all spawned by mache's `internal/leyline/socket.go::DiscoverOrStart`, all racing on the same `~/.mache/default.arena` + `default.ctrl` + `default.sock`.

## Root cause

`DiscoverOrStart`'s fast-path is `findExistingSocket()` (env var or `~/.mache/default.sock`). If the socket file is present, it returns. If not, it spawns a new daemon. Cleanup relies on the atexit-style path in `StopManaged` (SIGTERM → wait → SIGKILL), but that only fires when mache exits cleanly. On `kill -9`, crash, or `Ctrl+C` before signal handlers wire up, the daemon survives and the next mache invocation:

1. Sees a stale `default.sock` (still points at the dead daemon's socket file path).
2. `findExistingSocket` returns the symlink target.
3. `Dial` against the dead socket fails.
4. Caller retries / spawns again → ⊥ another daemon.

After enough cycles, six daemons all racing on the same arena.

## Acceptance

Pick one of:

**A. PID file** at `~/.mache/default.pid`. `DiscoverOrStart` reads it, sends `kill -0 <pid>` to check liveness, only spawns if the previous PID is dead or the file is absent. `StopManaged` and the spawned daemon both clean up the PID file on exit (defense in depth). Stale-PID detection on session start prevents accumulation.

**B. `flock(2)` on the control file** (`default.ctrl`). The spawned daemon holds an exclusive advisory lock for its lifetime; `DiscoverOrStart` tries `LOCK_EX | LOCK_NB` first — if it succeeds, no daemon is running; if it fails, a live daemon owns the lock and we should use the socket. flock is automatically released on process death (kernel-level), so no atexit/cleanup is needed for the lock itself. Symlink/socket cleanup is still needed but no longer the dedup mechanism.

Either way:

- `pgrep -lf 'leyline daemon' | wc -l` returns at most 1 in steady state, even after `kill -9` of mache during auto-spawn.
- A new session reuses the existing daemon when present, even if `default.sock` is stale.
- Test: kill mache mid-spawn, re-invoke; assert no second daemon is spawned.

Recommend B (flock) — simpler, kernel-enforced, no PID-file cleanup race. PID files are a known anti-pattern for exactly this reason.

## Out of scope

- LaunchAgent-style auto-start (that's the user's choice; this bead is about preventing accidental fan-out).
- Cleanup of the existing zombie daemons (one-shot `pkill -f 'leyline daemon'` and move on).

## Refs

- `internal/leyline/socket.go::DiscoverOrStart`, `StopManaged`, `findExistingSocket`
- Spotted during PR #371 smoke test (apko + leyline 0.2.2 substrate-switch verification)

comments.text:
PR #389 — https://github.com/agentic-research/mache/pull/389

- `DiscoverOrStart` now holds `managed.mu` across the full discover-then-spawn cycle (was released too early — two goroutines could both enter the spawn block).
- Stale socket file at well-known path is removed before spawn; `LEYLINE_SOCKET` pointing at a dead listener errors out cleanly.
- Post-spawn wait probes liveness, not just `os.Stat`.

Three tests pin the dedup paths: orphaned socket reclaim, live-daemon piggyback, 16-goroutine concurrent dedup. Clean under `go test -race -count=10 -run TestDiscover ./internal/leyline/` and `task check`.

Two files only: `internal/leyline/socket.go`, `internal/leyline/socket_test.go`. No changes to `findExistingSocket`, `StopManaged`, or the `managed` struct surface.

title: Adopt entire-graph's throughput + memory bench repos as mache's bounded scale gate
description:
Second half of the entire-graph bench (see mache-2acd4f). Directly closes the gap in feedback: the O(n^2) projection regression shipped uncaught because there is no bounded scale gate.

THROUGHPUT TABLE they publish (full profile), all public repos so we can run the same ones:
  caddyserver/caddy      Go     214 files   1,857 symbols     23,681 relations   1.5s
  redis/redis            C      633        10,312            358,082            5.5s
  laravel/framework      PHP  2,019        23,182          1,872,087           17.0s
  micropython/micropython C   3,447        18,788          2,268,173           25.6s

PEAK MEMORY vs codebase-memory-mcp:
  nlohmann/json  80 MB vs 599 MB
  koin           64 MB vs 285 MB
  Dapper         43 MB vs 225 MB

Memory is a live axis for mache: ROADMAP records ~2GB peak for 323K NVD records as a known limitation (mache-2f1287). A published per-repo peak-RSS number would either validate or falsify that being acceptable.

DESIGN NOTES:
- Gate on GROWTH CLASS, not a fixed ratio. docs/reference/projection-performance.md already establishes this discipline: the O(n^2)->O(n) fix was n^2.02 -> n^0.92, and the speedup ratio is proportional to n (20x-197x), so any single 'Nx faster' number is a lie about a different n. A scale gate that pins one wall-time is the same mistake in gate form.
- Two of these languages (C, PHP) exercise leyline grammars the mache test corpus barely touches - useful coverage independent of the timing.
- micropython at 3,447 files is roughly the size where the quadratic projection used to hurt, so it is the right shape for a regression canary.
- Reuse tools/fixtures-snapshot + testdata/snapshots/manifest.toml (records upstream SHA) so the corpus is pinned rather than tracking upstream HEAD.

comments.text:
RECON: their throughput harness IS published and directly reusable — this bead is cheaper than filed.

bench/ in entire-graph (MIT) contains:
  repos.json        — 10 repos per language, ~240 total
  repos.fast.json   — 3 per language, 72 total, curated to exclude mega-repos; runs in minutes
  repos.lock.json   — EXACT COMMIT SHA per repo (e.g. BurntSushi/ripgrep -> 82313cf95849bfe425109ad9506a52154879b1b1)
  README.md         — methodology

The lock file is the valuable part: a pinned, reproducible multi-language corpus someone else already curated. mache can adopt those pins directly rather than choosing repos and arguing about the choice.

Two design points from their README worth copying:
- 'Clone phase (network) is separate from measurement (no-egress)' — cloning uses git; measurement runs with NoNetwork set, so the benchmarked path is the same local-only path production uses. mache should mirror this or the numbers include network variance.
- Cloned repos live under a gitignored bench/.cache/ and never enter commits. mache's testdata/snapshots/ takes the opposite approach (curated snapshots committed with recorded SHAs). Both are defensible; the pinned-lock + external-cache model scales to 240 repos where committing them would not.

Suggest the fast tier (72 repos, 3/language) as mache's scale gate and the full tier as an occasional deep run — their own split, for the same reason: the full tier is 'gated by a handful of giant repositories and can take 1.5-3 hours'.
