title: Node Properties are double-marshaled + base64'd into record — 2.3x bloat and un-queryable by SQL
description:
Measured 2026-07-22: Properties is map[string][]byte, so persisting it does TWO marshals and base64-encodes the inner JSON.

  imports map -> json.Marshal -> Properties["imports"] ([]byte)   {"fmt":"fmt","http":"net/http"}   31B
  Properties  -> json.Marshal -> record column                      {"imports":"eyJmbXQ...","lang":"Z28="}  72B  = 2.3x

Three problems: (1) double encode, (2) base64 bloat, (3) MOST IMPORTANT — un-queryable. json_extract(record,'$.imports') yields a base64 blob, so no SQL/smell rule can filter on lang/pkg/imports. That fights mache's core design of pushing extraction into SQLite via json_extract.

The  column is the precedent: it was given its own column (mache-b8fe72) precisely so it would round-trip cleanly. Options: give hot properties (lang/pkg/imports) real columns; or change Properties to map[string]json.RawMessage so values nest as real JSON; or store a queryable props JSON column. NOTE: on-disk format change — needs a compat story for existing .db files (ColumnExists pattern) and the portable cache. Surfaced while doing mache-f930b6 (user: 'Marshaling seems bad twice imo').

comments.text: Repairing a shell-quoting glitch in the description: the sentence about precedent should read — 'The context column is the precedent: it was given its OWN column (mache-b8fe72) precisely so it would round-trip cleanly to the mount.' Options remain: (a) give hot properties (lang/pkg/imports) real columns, (b) change Properties to map[string]json.RawMessage so values nest as real JSON rather than base64, or (c) a single queryable props JSON column. Any of these must keep existing .db files readable via the ColumnExists compat pattern and round-trip through mache cache push/pull.
comments.author: rsry-cli

comments.text:
DESIGN GOAL (user, 2026-07-22): "the file can decide depending on reader" — the persisted bytes should be self-describing and reader-agnostic, so SQL/json_extract, the Go graph engine, smell rules, and leyline each project as they wish. Today one writer's encoding choice unilaterally locks out every non-Go reader.

SHARPENED FINDING: the `record` column is POLYMORPHIC across three contracts:
  1. file nodes            -> rendered content (plain text)
  2. data-projection nodes -> REAL JSON, and genuinely queried as such:
                              sqlite_graph_scan.go:142 does json_extract(record, '$.<path>')
  3. construct dir nodes   -> base64 property bag (Go-only; requires knowing the double-unmarshal)

So shape (3) is base64 sitting inside a column that shape (2) treats as queryable JSON. That is why no SQL/smell rule can filter on lang/pkg/imports — not merely bloat.

ROOT CAUSE, not the symptom: Properties is map[string][]byte — an opaque BYTE BAG in memory. Storing bytes rather than values leaves the encoder nothing to do but base64 them. So the fix is likely two-part:
  (a) values nest as real JSON (json.RawMessage, or typed properties) instead of []byte; and
  (b) stop overloading one column with three contracts — give properties their own column, per the `context` precedent (mache-b8fe72), so each column has ONE contract a reader can rely on.

Constraints unchanged: existing .db files must stay readable (ColumnExists compat pattern) and the portable cache (mache cache push/pull) must round-trip.
comments.author: rsry-cli

comments.text:
INTENT GROUNDING — blog/src/content/blog/the-semantic-file.md (draft, 2026-07-20/22).

The essay states the design goal this bead violates, in its own words:

  "One value, six projections, ZERO TRANSLATION STEPS."

  "Every conventional pipeline is a chain of representational handoffs - and every
   handoff is a seam where drift, bugs, and unverifiability live. Integrity claims
   usually die in deserialization... The semantic file closes the seams by refusing
   to have them."

  "the chosen encodings (SQLite's file format, Cap'n Proto) are ones whose SERIALIZED
   FORM IS THEIR OPERATIONAL FORM, no parse step intervenes between the bytes that
   were hashed and the bytes being read."

The base64 property bag is exactly such a handoff: a translation step only a Go reader
that knows the double-unmarshal can perform.

SEVERITY IS HIGHER THAN "BLOAT": it breaks one of the six claimed projections. The
essay asserts "hand the same buffer to sqlite3_deserialize and it is a database you can
interrogate with recursive SQL" - but for construct dir nodes, lang/pkg/imports are
NOT reachable via json_extract. The SQL projection is silently partial, in a column
(record) that the scan path otherwise queries as real JSON.

IT ALSO OBSTRUCTS ONE OF THE ESSAY'S OWN FALSIFIERS: "A second, independent reader of
the arena format, built by other hands - every format becomes a platform only when
someone else targets it." A Go-only base64 convention makes an independent reader
impossible for those fields without reimplementing mache's private encoding.

So the fix is not cosmetic - it is "make the serialized form the operational form" for
node properties. Restates the two-part shape already noted: values as real JSON
(json.RawMessage / typed) AND one contract per column (properties get their own column,
per the context precedent), so every reader projects the same bytes without translation.
comments.author: rsry-cli

comments.text:
PRIORITY RECOMMENDATION: raise P2 -> P1.

Filed as P2 when it read as "2.3x bloat + un-queryable". The semantic-file intent
grounding changes the severity: this is not cleanup, it is substrate fidelity. It
breaks one of the six claimed projections (the SQL/sqlite3_deserialize one is silently
partial for construct nodes), it is a representational handoff in a design whose method
is "closing the seams by refusing to have them", and it obstructs a named falsifier
(an independent second reader of the format).

Could not change the field from here: `rsry bead` exposes no update subcommand and the
rsry MCP server was not connected this session. Flagging for a manual bump.

title: Standalone find_callers/find_callees underperform on Rust vs Go — tree-sitter extraction tier is Go-tuned; ley-line _ast + LSP enrichment is the uniform path
description:
## Real-world observation (2026-06-25)

Running mache on a Rust codebase (lectio, ~/github/jamestexas/lectio), the user reports:

- **Weak:** `find_callers` / `find_callees` "not useful in Rust vs Go" — suspected to be our extraction impl, not a fundamental limit.
- **Shines:** Go codebases; AND **any** codebase *after* ley-line parse runs — LSP enrichment then makes `find_callers` accurate and lights up `get_type_info` / `get_diagnostics`.

## The seam (same family as mache-5bb181, the kind-filter bug)

mache has two backend tiers, and quality is uneven across them:

1. **Standalone / heuristic tier** — tree-sitter SitterWalker (CGO) extracts calls/refs via per-language queries. The Go call-extraction queries (`engine_languages.go`, `sitter_walker.go`, `ast_walker_calls.go`) are mature; Rust's qualified-call / method / trait-dispatch resolution is weaker, so caller/callee edges are sparse or wrong on Rust. This tier is effectively **Go-tuned**.
2. **Ley-line / semantic tier** — once ley-line emits `_ast` (kinds) + `_lsp_refs`/`_lsp_defs`/`_lsp_hover`/`_lsp` tables, `find_callers` supplements with compiler-grade LSP refs (`serve_lsp.go`) and type/diagnostics tools work. This tier is **uniform across languages** because it's the compiler's view, not tree-sitter heuristics.

The kind-filter bug (mache-5bb181) was one symptom of this split (path-segment vs `_ast.node_kind`). The Rust find_callers weakness is another symptom: the heuristic tier is language-uneven; the semantic tier makes mache good everywhere. The CGO-removal campaign's thesis — make ley-line `_ast`+`_lsp` the universal load-bearing path and retire the Go-tuned SitterWalker — is precisely the resolution.

## What this research bead should establish

1. **Quantify the gap**: on a fixed Rust corpus (lectio), measure find_callers/callees edge recall (a) standalone tree-sitter vs (b) ley-line `_ast`+`_lsp`. Use a hand-labeled set of known call edges as ground truth (match-truth-not-model discipline).
2. **Locate the Rust-specific extraction holes** in the tree-sitter call queries (method calls `recv.method()`, associated functions `Type::assoc()`, trait-method dispatch, macro-call edges) — are they missing from the Rust query set, or mis-resolved?
3. **Decide the disposition**: fix the Rust tree-sitter queries to close the standalone gap, OR formally gate find_callers/callees quality on ley-line availability and document standalone-Rust as best-effort (consistent with the CGO-removal endgame). The latter is likely correct — don't pour effort into a tier being retired.

## Acceptance

A short findings doc with the measured standalone-vs-leyline edge-recall gap on Rust, an enumeration of the specific Rust call-edge classes the tree-sitter tier misses, and a recommendation (fix-queries vs gate-on-leyline) with rationale tied to the CGO-removal campaign.

## Cross-refs

- mache-5bb181 (kind filter: path-segment vs `_ast` — same two-tier seam)
- mache-8fab5d (get_architecture noise — ranks raw refs incl. external tokens; another facet of "heuristic tier surfaces non-defs")
- ADR-0012 (CGO-removal migration — make `_ast`/`_lsp` universal)
- LSP enrichment path: `cmd/serve_lsp.go`, `_lsp*` tables produced by ley-line-open's lsp crate

comments.text:
## Measurement scoping pass (2026-06-25) — instruments + gotchas found

Built the leyline `.db` for lectio (`leyline parse .` → `~/github/jamestexas/lectio/output.db`) and started the standalone-vs-leyline comparison. Three blockers/findings that the real measurement run must account for:

### 1. `mache serve <dir>` is NOT a pure-tree-sitter baseline
Serving the source dir auto-starts the leyline daemon (backend=auto prefers leyline when on PATH). On this machine the daemon socket failed to appear within 5s (`leyline daemon started but socket .../default.sock did not appear within 5s`) → it fell back to in-process tree-sitter, which DID return Rust callers for `run` (tree-sitter node paths). So: (a) tree-sitter does extract Rust refs; (b) the daemon-startup flakiness is the same lifecycle fragility as the "/mcp conn refused" thread (mache-823d91) and will confound any measurement that relies on the live daemon. The LSP tier needs either the daemon working OR a pre-baked `_lsp` db.

### 2. `mache build --backend tree-sitter` emits 0 refs (instrument gap)
`mache build --backend tree-sitter ~/github/jamestexas/lectio out.db` finished in 67ms with node_refs=0, node_defs=0 — the auto-FCA inference path does not apply a code-aware projection to a source dir, so no construct/ref extraction happens. To get a clean tree-sitter baseline `.db` for SQL-level recall comparison, the build must be driven with a code schema (the serve path's projection), not FCA. This is a prerequisite to the measurement and possibly a `mache build` bug worth its own note.

### 3. lectio output.db (leyline `parse` tier) inventory
`_ast`=224,915 rows, `node_refs`=20,569, `node_defs`=1,711. No `_lsp*` tables — `leyline parse` produces the `_ast` tier only; the LSP tier requires a separate `leyline lsp` enrichment pass (the `lsp` subcommand exists: "Spawn a language server, collect symbols + diagnostics, and write a .db").

### Resume plan (clean run, own session)
1. Pre-bake all three tiers as static `.db`s so the measurement is daemon-independent: (a) tree-sitter baseline via a code-schema-driven build, (b) `output.db` (already have), (c) `leyline lsp` enrichment → `_lsp_refs`.
2. Establish ground-truth: hand-label ~15-20 known call edges in lectio (free fns + impl methods + trait dispatch + macro calls) to score recall against, not just raw counts.
3. Score find_callers recall per tier on the ground-truth set; report the gap + the specific Rust edge classes tree-sitter misses (the bead's core deliverable).

Raw counts directionally: leyline `_ast` captured 20,569 ref edges on 94 Rust files; need the tree-sitter baseline count to quantify the gap.
comments.author: rsry-mcp

comments.text:
## Benchmark framing (per user): this IS a mache differential benchmark — PostHog shadow-replay method

The right frame is PostHog's SQL-parser validation (the blog behind mache-7qf0): instead of hand-labeling ground truth, run `find_callers` for the same symbols across extraction tiers and measure where the weaker tier diverges from the compiler-grade reference (LSP). The differential IS the test. Tiers: (1) mache in-process tree-sitter, (2) leyline `parse` grammar-refs (`_ast`/`node_refs`), (3) leyline `lsp` compiler-refs (`_lsp_refs`) = reference.

## LSP tier is BLOCKED on workspace indexing (de-risked via pilot)

`leyline lsp --server rust-analyzer --input <file> --merge-db output.db` ran in ~1s but returned **0 defs/0 hovers/0 refs** ("32 symbols matched to AST, enrichment: 0 refs"); only a `_lsp` (diagnostics) table was written, no `_lsp_refs`/`_lsp_defs`. Cause: rust-analyzer resolves references only with the whole-workspace project model (cargo metadata + crate-graph index); per-file invocation collects document symbols but cannot resolve cross-file refs. So the LSP reference tier needs either (a) `leyline lsp` to drive whole-project ref collection, or (b) a harness that boots rust-analyzer against the workspace root and waits for indexing. This is a real setup task (and possibly a leyline-side limitation/bead) — not a quick win. (Note: `rust-analyzer --version` reports `0.0.0` here, worth sanity-checking the binary.)

## tree-sitter baseline tier also blocked
`mache build --backend tree-sitter <dir> out.db` → 0 node_refs/0 node_defs (auto-FCA path applies a data schema, not the serve path's code projection). Need a code-schema-driven build to get a clean in-process baseline `.db`.

## Directional result available NOW — grammar tier (output.db) name-presence coverage on Rust

For fn/method defs, fraction whose token appears as a ref (a NAME-match upper bound, not target-resolved):

| kind | defs | with ≥1 ref-token | coverage |
|------|------|-------------------|----------|
| free function | 1049 | 355 | **33.8%** |
| method | 316 | 235 | **74.4%** |

Totals: 1365 fn/method defs, 1206 distinct ref tokens, 20,569 ref edges. CAVEAT: `node_refs` matches by bare token (name), so "with caller" over-counts via name collisions (any `foo()` matches any `foo` def) AND can't see calls the grammar missed — it's an UPPER bound on recall. The true recall gap (and the free-fn-vs-method Rust weakness the user observed) requires the LSP tier to resolve actual call targets, which is exactly the blocked piece. Even so, the 33.8% free-fn vs 74.4% method split is a real signal that grammar-tier free-function call resolution is the weak spot.

## Resume requirements (dedicated session)
1. Unblock LSP tier: drive rust-analyzer with the workspace project model (verify the rust-analyzer binary first). File a leyline bead if `leyline lsp` can't do whole-project ref collection.
2. Unblock tree-sitter baseline: code-schema-driven `mache build`.
3. Then: differential `find_callers` per def symbol across all 3 tiers, LSP as reference, report per-Rust-edge-class recall (free fn / impl method / trait dispatch / macro).

## Grammar-tier baseline result (lectio output.db, static SQL — no daemon)

Two clean measurements from the leyline `parse` tier on lectio (94 Rust files, 20,569 ref edges, 1,452 distinct def tokens):

### 1. find_callers name-coverage by construct kind (caller present at all)
| kind | defs | with ≥1 ref-token | coverage (upper bound) |
|------|------|------|------|
| free function | 1049 | 355 | 33.8% |
| method | 316 | 235 | 74.4% |

### 2. Name-collision / disambiguation failure rate (the upper-bound confound, quantified)
- 74 / 1452 distinct def tokens (**5.1%**) are ambiguous (same name, >1 definition).
- **13.8% of all 20,569 ref edges (2,833) point at an ambiguous multi-def token** — for ~1 in 7 call edges the grammar tier's name-match find_callers CANNOT tell which definition is the real target.
- Worst offenders are textbook Rust: `new` (23 defs — `Type::new()` constructors), `tests` (48), `sweep` (19), `resolve` (7), `label`/`source_id`/`uri_prefixes` (18 each).

The grammar tier resolves callers by bare token name, so (a) it over-counts (any `foo()` matches any `foo` def — the 33.8/74.4% are upper bounds), and (b) for 13.8% of edges it's genuinely ambiguous. This is precisely the gap compiler-grade LSP resolution closes: `_lsp_refs` resolve the actual target def, eliminating the name-collision ambiguity. **This number (13.8% ambiguous edges) is the concrete size of the prize for the LSP tier** — and the differential measurement, once the LSP tier is unblocked, should show the LSP tier correctly splitting those 2,833 edges across the right targets.

## LSP-tier blocker moved one layer deeper (daemon path, not the one-shot CLI)

Probed the daemon-based LSP enrichment (get_type_info with file=, the path the one-shot `leyline lsp` CLI is NOT). Findings, in order of discovery:

1. First it failed with "leyline daemon ... did not appear within 5s" — but that was the stale-`~/.mache`-scratch startup bug (now isolated, see mache-823d91), NOT rust-analyzer.
2. With fresh `~/.mache` scratch the daemon binds in <1s, and enrichment proceeds — then fails with: **`LSP auto-enrichment failed: tool lsp: unknown op: tool`**.

So the daemon-LSP path is now blocked at the PROTOCOL layer: mache sends an LSP-enrichment op the leyline 0.5.1 daemon doesn't recognize ("unknown op: tool"). We still never reached rust-analyzer — so the workspace-indexing question remains unanswered.

This smells like mache↔daemon protocol/version skew (the exact class mache-8kif's version-assert-on-connect targets): mache 0.9.0's LSP-enrichment op vs what leyline 0.5.1's daemon implements. Next step to unblock the bench LSP tier: determine whether (a) the op name/shape mache sends matches leyline 0.5.1's daemon op set (mache-side or leyline-side fix), or (b) a newer leyline implements it. Until resolved, the headline differential (grammar 13.8% ambiguous edges → LSP resolves them) can't run via the daemon path.

Net: the bench LSP tier is gated by, in sequence: daemon-startup reliability (823d91, mostly mache-side) → the `unknown op: tool` protocol mismatch (mache↔leyline) → finally rust-analyzer workspace indexing (untested, leyline-side). Each is a real gate; the user's "once daemon reliability lands, bench works" is true for the FIRST gate but two more remain.

title: Extract leyline pin into a CGO-free leaf package; dedupe the two regex-over-source test helpers
description:
Two test helpers (internal/ingest/leyline_ast_test_helper_test.go, internal/lattice/infer_astdb_parity_test.go) recover the pinned leyline version by running regexp over internal/leyline/socket.go SOURCE TEXT — a regex-is-a-smell (see feedback_regex_is_a_smell). mache-e34aec exported leyline.BinaryVersion, which tempts a direct import, but there is a real -tags leyline CGO trap:

internal/leyline/client.go is //go:build leyline + import "C" + #cgo LDFLAGS: -lleyline_fs. Under -tags leyline, importing package leyline (for ANY symbol, incl. the pure-Go BinaryVersion const in socket.go) pulls client.go and requires the Rust staticlib libleyline_fs.a. Under default tags it's excluded and safe.

- ingest: already imports leyline (address_refs_test.go) + cmd/* import it non-test, so the regex protects nothing there; a direct import is safe.
- lattice: imports leyline NOWHERE today. A direct import would newly require libleyline_fs.a for 'go test -tags leyline ./internal/lattice/' — a real regression.

Clean fix: move the pin const to a leaf package with only pure-Go files (no build-tagged siblings), e.g. internal/leyline/pin { const Version = "v0.8.0" }; socket.go aliases it (const leylineBinaryVersion = pin.Version). A pure-Go leaf is CGO-free under ALL tags, so every consumer (socket.go, server-json-gen, both test helpers) imports it without staticlib risk. Then dedupe the two near-identical resolvePinnedLeyline* helpers into one shared helper. Bonus: lets server-json-gen import the leaf instead of package leyline, decoupling its -tags leyline build too.

Deferred from mache-e34aec (kept the regex to avoid the lattice regression under a rushed one-liner).

So the regex test helpers (internal/ingest, internal/lattice) can now just import leyline.BinaryVersion DIRECTLY, no leaf package needed. title: Delete drift_doc_outdated_count placeholder smell rule (14->13); it structurally can't fire

title: find_smells: rule categorization + allowlist surface (group by family, per-rule excludes)
description:
Surfaced 2026-05-19 while adding `sleep_in_test` rule ([[mache-655e98]] follow-up).

Mache's `find_smells` registry is a flat `[]SmellRule` slice. With ~10 built-in rules today and external rules loadable via `$MACHE_SMELL_RULES_DIR`, the surface is approaching a point where flat listing is unwieldy:

1. **Categories**: Rules naturally cluster — `dead_code` / `untested_function` are coverage-class; `god_file` / `long_file` / `long_function` are size-class; `cyclomatic_complexity` / `fan_out_skew` are complexity-class; `magic_int_in_comparison` / `sleep_in_test` are anti-pattern-class. An agent calling `find_smells` with no rule today gets a wall of descriptions to scan. Categories would let an agent ask "what coverage-class rules apply on the current backend?" without listing every rule.

2. **Per-rule allowlists**: `sleep_in_test` doesn't currently let a Benchmark file legitimately use sleep for timing measurement; the only escape is to add `min_metric` (irrelevant) or run the rule against a different source_id (clunky). Need a structured "this file is exempted from this rule" surface — probably a sibling yaml file or `_meta` on the rule's external JSON.

3. **Tension the user named:** "eventually it's a db all over again and config mapped against it" — adding categories, allowlists, severities, ownership all push the rule manifest toward being a config-as-database. Worth evaluating the alternative: keep rules dumb-flat and let consumers filter/categorize externally (rsry tags? a sidecar yaml at the project level?). The right answer probably depends on whether mache wants to be the curation point or just the execution engine.

Acceptance:
- One ADR that names the design choice (categories-in-rule-struct vs external-tag-store)
- If categories: add `Category` field to `SmellRule`, surface in handler help payload, test
- If allowlists: pick the format (yaml? per-file `// mache:nolint sleep_in_test`?), implement skip path in `runSmellRule`

Open question: relationship between this and `coverage-thresholds.yaml` (already exists for the coverage gate). They could share the per-file exclusion surface.

This bead's broader scope (categories like coverage-class / size-class / complexity-class / anti-pattern-class + per-rule allowlists for the benchmark-sleep exception) remains open. title: find_smells: improve discoverability of MACHE_SMELL_RULES_DIR + rule-pack distribution shape
description:
Mache already supports loading external smell rules from `$MACHE_SMELL_RULES_DIR` ([cmd/serve_find_smells_load.go](cmd/serve_find_smells_load.go) — `LoadExternalSmellRules` + `appendExternalRulesFromEnv` in init()). The mechanism is hidden though — only mentioned in ADR-0013 in passing, no README/GETTING-STARTED entry, no example rule file checked in.

User feedback 2026-05-19 ("we should make it so you can load rules from a dir? ... eventually it's a db all over again and config mapped against it"):

1. **Discoverability:** Document `$MACHE_SMELL_RULES_DIR` in README + GETTING-STARTED. Surface in `find_smells --help` output. Add an example external rule file to a new `examples/smell-rules/` directory.

2. **Distribution shape:** Should rule packs ship as:
   - **(a)** Per-project `.mache/smell-rules/` directory checked into the repo (per-project policy)
   - **(b)** External git-cloneable repos pointed at via env var (org-wide policy, shareable)
   - **(c)** A new sub-module/sub-repo at agentic-research/mache-smell-rules (curated official rules outside the binary)
   - **(d)** Some combination — built-ins ship in the binary, project repo overrides via `.mache/smell-rules/`, org-wide policy via env var pointing at a shared dir

3. **Config-vs-DB tension:** The user named this explicitly. Today: rules are static JSON, no querying, no per-rule metadata beyond what's in the file. If we add categories, severities, allowlists, ownership, we're rebuilding a config system. Worth either keeping rules dumb-flat OR going full structured (yaml + schema validation + curation tooling). Pick a side.

4. **Sub-module question:** A sub-module (`mache-smell-rules` as separate repo) lets non-mache contributors propose rules without touching mache's release cadence. Cost is one more repo to maintain + the resolver story to find it. Worth weighing against just `examples/smell-rules/` in-tree.

Pairs with [[mache-655e98]] follow-up beads on categorization + allowlists.

title: MCP tools advertise readOnlyHint=false by default — read-only tools (semantic_search, find_*, get_*) show as "destructive" in /mcp
description:
## Symptom

In a client's `/mcp` view, mache's read-only tools (e.g. `semantic_search`, `find_callers`, `get_architecture`) are flagged as **destructive**, which is alarming and wrong — they only read.

## Root cause

None of the 18 tools in `cmd/serve_handlers.go` declared annotations. mcp-go (v0.55.0) defaults `ToolAnnotation.ReadOnlyHint` to a non-nil `false` (`ToBoolPtr(false)`), so every tool actively advertised "not read-only." Per the MCP spec, clients then treat the tool as potentially destructive.

## Fix (shipped)

Added explicit annotations to every tool registration:
- 17 query/navigation tools → `WithReadOnlyHintAnnotation(true)`.
- The 4 that reach the external ley-line daemon (`semantic_search`, `get_type_info`, `get_diagnostics`, `get_sheaf_status`) → also `WithOpenWorldHintAnnotation(true)`.
- `write_file` (the only mutating tool) → explicit `WithReadOnlyHintAnnotation(false)` + `WithDestructiveHintAnnotation(true)`.

## Regression guard

`TestMCPRegistry_ToolsDeclareReadOnlyHint` (cmd/mcp_registry_invariants_test.go) introspects the live `tools/list` response and fails if any tool lacks `readOnlyHint`, or if a read tool is marked mutating / `write_file` is marked read-only. `mutatingTools` is the single allowlist; new mutating tools add themselves there.

## Notes

- `server.json` (internal/mcpregistry) is unaffected — annotations are a runtime `tools/list` concern, not part of the registry manifest; `gen:server-json:check` stays green.
- Distinct from the language-tier work (mache-9108a1) and the kind-filter bug (mache-5bb181); this is pure tool-metadata correctness.

title: refactor: UDS query proxy — mache as pure MCP client, daemon owns SQLite
description:
## Problem

mache copies the arena buffer to a temp file (352MB → disk), opens it with sql.Open, runs queries in-process. This defeats the zero-copy arena design.

## Target architecture

When daemon is running (--control mode), mache becomes a query client:

Agent → mache (MCP tool) → UDS socket → daemon (sqlite3_deserialize, zero-copy) → JSON result

Mache never opens SQLite. The daemon is the single SQLite process.

## What changes in mache

1. **New UDS graph backend** — implements graph.Graph by sending queries over the socket instead of running SQL. Returns *Node, []string, []NodeStat from JSON responses.

2. **buildControlGraph uses UDS** — instead of ExtractActiveDB + OpenSQLiteGraph, connect to UDS socket and wrap in the new backend.

3. **Existing SQL path stays** — for standalone `mache serve ./data.db` (no daemon). The UDS backend is only used when --control is set and socket is available.

4. **Remove ExtractActiveDB from --control path** — no more 352MB copy to temp file.

## What changes in LLO (separate beads)

The daemon's `query` op already exists. But mache needs richer ops:
- `list_children(id)` → returns child IDs
- `list_child_stats(id)` → returns []NodeStat equivalent
- `get_node(id)` → returns node info
- `read_content(id)` → returns content bytes
- `get_callers(token)` → returns caller node IDs
- `find_definition(symbol)` → returns definition location

These mirror the Graph interface. The daemon already has the SQL — it just needs named ops instead of raw SQL strings.

## Fallback

No daemon → existing path (sql.Open on .db file). Same code, no regression. The UDS backend is additive.

comments.text:
Reconciliation note (2026-05-10): The bead description mentions "JSON result" / "JSON response" multiple times — that prose was written before the daemon capnp schema solidified.

The actual contract is now `daemon.capnp` (file ID `@0xa1b2c3d4e5f60001`), located authoritatively at `~/remotes/art/ley-line-open/rs/ll-core/public-schema/capnp/daemon.capnp`. It defines the exact ops this bead enumerates:

- `ListChildrenRequest`/`Response` → `List(Node)`
- `ReadContentRequest`/`Response` → `Text`
- `FindCallersRequest`/`Response` → `List(Ref)`
- `FindDefsRequest`/`Response` → `List(Ref)`  (covers `find_definition`)
- `GetNodeRequest`/`Response` → `Node`
- `QueryRequest`/`Response` → typed rows
- Plus `Status`, `Reparse`, `Snapshot`, `Enrich`, `Load`, `Subscribe`

All request/response shapes are capnp structs, request-response over UDS, one message per line per the schema's docstring.

When this bead is picked up: the UDS client mache builds should encode/decode these capnp structs, NOT JSON. The description's "JSON result" language is outdated. Update accordingly during implementation.

Related: `mache-3bf414` makes mache stop forking the schema and consume LLO's authoritative copy — pick that up first so the bindings this bead uses come from a single source of truth.

comments.text:
**Doctrinal resolution: the JSON-as-carrier pattern from cloister `interlace-spec/0.1.0/README.md` is the framing.**

The original reconciliation note here said *"the contract is now daemon.capnp, NOT JSON"* — which is correct but ambiguous. The interlace-spec README (lines 92-133, "Note on test-vector format (JSON-as-carrier, NOT JSON-as-spec)") gives the precise vocabulary:

- **JSON-as-carrier**: JSON is used because every target language parses it with zero tooling. Convenient transport. NOT the spec.
- **JSON-as-spec**: the canonical wire bytes the spec ratifies — could be JSON, CBOR, DER, capnp, UTF-8, depending on surface.

For LLO daemon UDS, the right read is: **the JSON wire is JSON-as-carrier; `daemon.capnp` is the schema-as-spec.** The wire stays JSON (debuggable, MCP HTTP symmetric, ADR-0014 RPC-deferral-respecting). The shape is locked to the schema via codegen on both ends.

This bead's plan now reflects that:

| Bead | Repo | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `ley-line-open-a373ba` (P1) | LLO | Generate JSON FROM typed structs (schema is SSOT); ship the typed Go bindings consumers need |
| `ley-line-open-a47d7d` (P2) | LLO | Add `find_callees` op (unblocks mache `GetCallees` stub) |
| `ley-line-open-a4e860` (P3, research) | LLO | Future ADR — when/whether to move past JSON-as-carrier to JSON-as-spec capnp framing |
| `mache-a55625` (P2) | mache | Fix N+1 (independent — no LLO dep) |
| `mache-a5ad09` (P2) | mache | Adopt typed Go bindings ⚠️ gated on LLO `a373ba` + tag |
| `mache-a5e4ea` (P2) | mache | Implement `GetCallees` ⚠️ gated on LLO `a47d7d` + tag |

The cross-repo gates are encoded in each downstream bead's description since `rsry_bead_link` is per-repo only. Pattern matches the v0.2.1 dance (`ley-line-open-41867b ↔ mache-3bf414`).

title: MCP tools: return "still loading" when graph is empty during initial parse
description:
When mache serve --control starts, the graph may be empty (daemon still parsing). Currently returns empty results or errors. Should return a helpful message: "Graph is loading — the daemon is still parsing source files. Try again in a few seconds."

Detection: check if graph has zero roots (store.RootIDs() is empty). If so, return loading message instead of empty results.

Could also implement MCP streaming (SSE) to push "graph ready" notification to the client once the first hot-swap happens.

title: Send prioritize op to daemon when MCP tool can't resolve a symbol
description:
When find_callers/find_definition/read_file fails because the file hasn't been parsed yet, mache should send {"op": "prioritize", "files": [...]} to the daemon over UDS, then retry after the next hot-swap.

Requires:
1. Detect "not found because not yet parsed" vs "genuinely doesn't exist"
2. Send prioritize op over existing UDS connection
3. Wait for next generation bump (hot-swap poller)
4. Retry the tool request
5. Timeout if still not found after retry

title: Auto-invoke leyline daemon when mache serve gets a source directory
description:
When `mache serve .` is called with a source directory (not a .db), and leyline is on PATH, automatically start the daemon instead of using CGO SitterWalker.

Flow:
1. Detect: dataSource is a directory, not .db
2. Check: is leyline on PATH?
3. Yes: DiscoverOrStart daemon with --source flag
4. Use buildControlGraph to read from arena
5. No: fall back to existing in-process Engine + SitterWalker

This is the "three tiers in one command" UX from ADR-0006.

title: Extract the Graph conformance suite so out-of-package backends can be tested
description:
The Graph conformance suite (internal/graph/graph_suite_test.go, ~505 lines) can only reach backends defined inside package graph. SQLiteWriter — the backend `mache build` actually writes through — lives in internal/ingest, which imports internal/graph, so a suite defined in package graph's tests can never test it.

That is not an oversight anyone made; it is a property of the package layout. And it is how the P0 happened: SQLiteWriter.GetNode never populates Children, no conformance test could reach it, and an engine guard that branched on GetNode().Children was live on MemoryStore and dead on the build path, silently dropping 540 constructs (mache-c725e9, mache-e3d9bb).

ATTEMPTED 2026-07-27, REVERTED — the blocker is concrete and worth recording so the next attempt starts informed.

The obvious move is to lift the runner (types + Run, roughly lines 16-336) into an importable internal/graphsuite package, leaving the factories behind in each backend's own package. I built that; the package compiles cleanly against exported graph types (Graph, Node, ErrNotFound, ErrActNotSupported, NodeStat). That part is easy.

The blocker is on the consumer side:

  graphsuite imports internal/graph.
  A test file in `package graph` (INTERNAL test package) that imports graphsuite
  is therefore an import cycle — Go rejects it outright.

So graph's own suite entries must move to `package graph_test` (external). But ALL 25 test files in internal/graph are the internal `package graph`, and they share unexported helpers with the suite file — `createNodesTableDB`, `stubRender`, `memoryStoreFactory`. Once the suite file becomes graph_test, those helpers are invisible to it, and its definitions are invisible to them. Reverting the suite file alone breaks context_roundtrip_test.go, hotswap_test.go, and writable_graph_test.go.

Three ways forward, none free:

  A. Convert internal/graph's test files to package graph_test. Cleanest end state,
     but many of them test unexported internals and cannot move. Large and risky.
  B. Duplicate the canonical fixture builder — one copy in graphsuite for external
     consumers, one left in package graph for its own tests. Small and safe, but
     two copies of the contract fixture is exactly the drift this bead exists to
     prevent, and duplicate_code will flag it.
  C. Move the canonical fixture into graphsuite as an exported helper
     (graphsuite.CanonicalNodesTableDB) and have only the suite ENTRIES live in
     graph_test, while package graph's other tests keep their local helpers for
     their own fixtures. Still duplicates a builder, but the CONTRACT lives in
     exactly one place, which is the property that matters.

C looks best. B is acceptable if C proves fiddly. A is probably not worth it.

PAYOFF, and why this is worth doing at all: once the suite is importable, internal/ingest registers SQLiteWriter with its answers (RootEmptyReturnsDir: false, GetNodePopulatesChildren: false) and the backend that caused the P0 is finally held to the same contract as the other four. Any future backend, in any package, can be too.

Note this may be overtaken by mache-e64f36 — if mache stops maintaining parallel stores and delegates presentation to ley-line's arena, there are fewer implementations to hold to a contract in the first place. Do not start the large option (A) before that call is made.

Prerequisite context: mache-e3d9bb documents the measured divergence across all five backends and the GetNodePopulatesChildren pin that now guards the four reachable ones.

comments.text:
MOOT — closing. Settled by the arena delegation decision (ley-line-open-2037b4, done; mache-e64f36).

This bead was to extract the Graph conformance suite into an importable package so SQLiteWriter — the backend the build path writes through, structurally excluded by the internal-test-package import cycle — could finally be held to the same contract as the other four.

That is no longer worth building. LLO's rationale states it directly: "you do not build a conformance harness across implementations that should not both exist." mache maintaining its own store layer is a control-plane component doing data-plane work; delegation deletes the implementations rather than reconciling them, so there is nothing left to hold to a contract.

The import-cycle finding recorded here is still true and still worth knowing — a suite defined inside package graph's tests can never reach an implementation in a package that imports graph — so leaving it in the record rather than deleting it.

NOT moot, and already shipped: the GetNodePopulatesChildren pin on the existing suite (PR #570). That guards the four backends that exist TODAY against silent drift while delegation is unshipped. Cheap, landed, keep.

If delegation stalls or is reversed, reopen this — the analysis and the three options (convert the package's tests, duplicate the fixture builder, or move the canonical fixture into the shared package) hold as written.

title: find_callers silently returns [] for type names — correctness hazard
description:
Surfaced by the Serena-style fresh-context eval (PR #373, `benchmarks/serena/results/mache_cc_fresh_eval_macherepo.md`) AND the quantitative bench (`benchmarks/quantitative/symbol_lookup_fp_rate.md`).

`mcp__mache__find_callers(token="Topology")` returns `[]` despite 141 grep hits for `api.Topology` / `Topology{` / `*Topology` in the mache repo. Same for `SocketClient` (26 grep hits → 0 mache callers), `MemoryStore` (210 → 0), `SQLiteGraph` (108 → 0).

This is a **correctness hazard, not just a coverage gap**: an agent asking "who uses Topology?" gets `[]` and confidently concludes nobody uses it. There is no warning that the index doesn't cover type references — only call-expression `<sym>(...)` invocations.

The index is doing what it was designed to (token → call-expression map per node_refs schema), but the MCP tool's contract says "who calls a symbol" which an agent reasonably interprets as "who references this." For types this fails silently.

Fix options:
1. **Document the contract explicitly** in the tool description: "returns call-expression sites only; for type references use Grep". Cheap, doesn't fix the silent-empty hazard.
2. **Make find_callers raise** when called on a token whose only occurrences in the corpus are non-call references (requires the daemon to do a fast pre-check via `node_refs` left-join `node_defs.kind`).
3. **Broaden the index** to capture type references (composite literals, receiver types, pointer types, field types). Substantial work — would need ley-line ingestion side to record kind=type-ref entries.

Recommend (2) for short-term safety + (1) for documentation, with (3) as long-term scope.

Evidence: see report sections §1 and §6 in `mache_cc_fresh_eval_macherepo.md`; §3 row "Topology" in `symbol_lookup_fp_rate.md`.

title: find_definition broken in default projection — returns "not found" for all symbols including unique ones
description:
Surfaced by the quantitative bench (PR #373, `benchmarks/quantitative/symbol_lookup_fp_rate.md` §6) and the Serena-style eval (`mache_cc_fresh_eval_macherepo.md`).

`mcp__mache__find_definition(token=<X>)` returns `"no definition found"` for **every test symbol** including `dedupSuffix` which is uniquely defined at `internal/ingest/engine.go:1351` and has no name collisions. Same for `GetCallers`, `Graph`, `Topology`, `MemoryStore.GetCallers`, `SQLiteGraph.GetCallers`, even with `fuzzy=true`.

Hypothesis from reports: the defs index (`node_defs` table) is **empty in this projection**. The corpus was projected by mache itself (no ley-line LSP enrichment baked in), so the table either wasn't populated or the find_definition handler is reading the wrong source of truth.

Two beads worth in one — investigate:
1. Is `node_defs` populated by mache's tree-sitter ingestion path, or does it require ley-line `enrich-lsp` to populate? If the latter, the MCP tool should error explicitly: "find_definition requires LSP enrichment — run `leyline enrich-lsp` against this .db" rather than returning silently empty.
2. If it IS populated and the handler is wrong, fix the handler.

Spot-check: `grep -c '^func ' internal/ingest/engine.go` confirms `dedupSuffix` is in the file; the bug isn't in tree-sitter's parser missing it. The bug is in the defs index lookup or population.

Impact: this is the **single most-frequent code-intelligence task** — find where a symbol is defined. mache failing it on every symbol invalidates a large class of agent workflows. Should be P1.

Evidence: bench reports cited above.

title: find_callees doesn't resolve receiver-method or stdlib calls
description:
Surfaced by Serena-style eval (PR #373, `benchmarks/serena/results/mache_cc_fresh_eval_macherepo.md` §1).

`mcp__mache__find_callees(id="internal/leyline/socket.go/SendOp")` returns `[]` despite the function visibly calling `c.sendRaw(...)`, `json.Unmarshal(...)`, and `fmt.Errorf(...)` in its body.

Root cause: the callees index resolves bare-token call expressions via `node_defs` lookup. For:
- **Receiver-method calls** (`c.sendRaw`): the call expression's token is `sendRaw` but the def is `internal/leyline/socket.go/SocketClient.sendRaw` — a name-path, not a bare token. Lookup misses.
- **Stdlib calls** (`json.Unmarshal`): there's no def in the local corpus's `node_defs` for `json.Unmarshal`. Daemon should ideally resolve to "external: encoding/json.Unmarshal" rather than dropping the edge.
- **Package-qualified calls** (`fmt.Errorf`): same as stdlib.

The quantitative bench surfaced a corollary phantom-target issue: `find_callers("Error")` lists test invocations like `require.Error(t, err)`, but mache's `callees/Error` resolves to `internal/graph/store.go/method_declaration` — wrong target due to cross-package token collision.

Fix scope (sketch):
1. Index call expressions with the **receiver type** when available (`SocketClient.sendRaw` not `sendRaw`)
2. When resolving a callee, prefer **same-package + same-receiver-type** matches over arbitrary token collisions
3. For stdlib/cross-module calls with no local def, emit a "external" callee entry rather than dropping silently

This is the dual of the find_callers type-ref gap (bead 1) — both come from the index being call-expression-bare-token rather than name-path-aware.

Evidence: `mache_cc_fresh_eval_macherepo.md` §1 "find_callees returns [] for `SendOp`" + `symbol_lookup_fp_rate.md` §4 phantom-target note for `Error`.

title: search role=definition filter returns [] for every pattern in source-code projections
description:
Surfaced by Serena-style eval (PR #373, `benchmarks/serena/results/mache_cc_fresh_eval_macherepo.md` §1).

`mcp__mache__search(pattern="%X%", role="definition")` returns `[]` for every pattern tried during the eval. The same patterns without the `role` filter return matches.

Likely related to the `find_definition` bead — both depend on the `node_defs` table being populated and queried correctly. Worth verifying as a separate finding because:
1. The search filter could be checking a different code path than find_definition (e.g. searching node names vs node_defs join)
2. If find_definition's bug is index-population, search-role-filter's bug is also index-population; if find_definition's bug is handler-side, search-role-filter could be either

Acceptance: `search(pattern="dedupSuffix", role="definition")` should return at least one entry pointing at `internal/ingest/engine.go:1351`.

title: Bump go test -timeout in Taskfile test target — cmd integration suite sits on the 10m macOS boundary
description:
Observed on PR #504 (2026-07-09): `integration (macos-latest)` failed with `panic: test timed out after 10m0s` → `FAIL .../cmd 600.283s`, then PASSED on re-run at 10m27s. The cmd integration suite genuinely runs right at the go-test 10-minute cap on the slower macOS runner (ubuntu passes ~9m; ubuntu `test` ~12m). This is a boundary flake, not a logic failure — the goroutine running at timeout was an unrelated NFS test (TestReadFile_BatchRejectsTotalContentOverflow).

Fix (parity-preserving per taskfile-ci-parity): raise `-timeout` (e.g. 10m→20m) in the Taskfile `test` target so it applies to BOTH local `task test` and CI (CI invokes the target — no duplicated command). Optionally also split the slow NFS/daemon integration tests into their own target so the fast unit suite isn't hostage to them.

Close condition: the cmd integration suite no longer flakes on the timeout on macOS; timeout is set in the Taskfile target that CI invokes. Verify with `task test` locally + a green macOS integration run.

Both CI jobs (ci.yml + integration.yml) invoke `task test`, so the single-source bump keeps local == CI (taskfile-ci-parity). title: get_architecture / get_communities exceed MCP response token budget on 28K-LOC repos
description:
Surfaced by Serena-style eval (PR #373, `benchmarks/serena/results/mache_cc_fresh_eval_macherepo.md` §1).

On the mache repo (28K LOC, 268 dirs, ref_tokens=2884 per overview), with the standard projection (no LSP enrichment):

- `mcp__mache__get_architecture` returned a **486K-character payload**
- `mcp__mache__get_communities(summary=true, min_size=5)` returned a **720K-character payload**

Both exceed the MCP response budget (~25K tokens) and get truncated mid-content, making them unusable on a "fresh exploration" of an unfamiliar repo. The community-detection output is dominated by per-call-site aggregations — e.g. one community contained 2089 `require.NoError(t, err)` sites — which is high cardinality but low signal.

This is a known gap from older notes (the stale "competitive_landscape" memory file flagged `get_communities` as "blows up on large codebases (103K chars)"). The current numbers say it's worse, AND it now blows up on **medium** codebases.

Fix options:
1. **Hard-limit output size** in the handler — truncate at N entries with "+M more truncated" suffix
2. **Better summarization** — `summary=true` should aggregate or deduplicate per-call-site contributions, not just take a top-N
3. **Server-side pagination** — `get_communities(offset, limit)` so agents can stream the result

This affects "first-contact orientation" — exactly the workflow the codebase-memory-mcp competitor named as their differentiator. Mache positions `get_architecture` as a similar tool but it currently doesn't work at this scale.

Evidence: `mache_cc_fresh_eval_macherepo.md` §1 entry "Architectural overview".

title: Topology template functions are undocumented — fourteen registered, zero reachable from where a schema is written
description:
Found 2026-07-29 while writing a topology schema for 0day's published artifact.

## The gap

`internal/template/render.go` registers fourteen functions for use in `name` and `content_template`:

```
default  dict  dig  first  join  json  lookup  lower
replace  slice  split  title  unquote  upper
```

plus `printf` (Go builtin) and the `_parent` accessor for reaching an ancestor node's data.

None of it is documented for schema authors. `examples/README.md` explains selectors carefully — JSONPath for data, tree-sitter queries for code — and never mentions `content_template`'s vocabulary at all. `grep -rn content_template examples/README.md docs/` returns nothing.

The functions themselves carry good doc comments in `render.go`. They are just not anywhere a schema author would look.

## What that costs, concretely

I wrote a schema knowing only what I could reverse-engineer from a Venturi schema that happened to be pasted into a conversation. Two consequences:

1. **I got `default` backwards and shipped it.** The signature is `func(val, fallback any)`. I generated `{{default "" .field}}` — value `""`, fallback the field — which always returns the fallback, so the guard was a no-op and a null still rendered as Go's literal `<no value>`. It failed in exactly the case it existed for.

   The example I learned from could not have taught me otherwise: it uses `default (dig A) (dig B)`, where both arguments are meaningful, so argument order is invisible.

2. **I did not know `first`, `join`, `slice`, `split`, `title`, `unquote`, `upper`, `lower` existed at all**, and left `printf` in a commit message as "the weakest link, inferred rather than observed". It is registered and fine.

Both were fixed by reading `render.go`. That is the right source and the wrong discovery path — a schema author should not need to read the renderer.

## Worth documenting precisely, not just listing

Two functions have signatures that are easy to get wrong from an example alone:

- `default val fallback` — value FIRST. Backwards is a silent no-op, not an error.
- `lookup val "a" 1 "b" 2 fallback` — a value-mapping switch over literal pairs, NOT a lookup into a collection. I initially read the name as array-search-by-key, which would have let a projected row resolve an id to its record; it does not, and a schema written on that assumption would render empty files rather than fail.

`dig` also already returns `""` for a missing path, so wrapping it in `default` is redundant — worth saying, because the obvious defensive habit is to wrap it.

## Suggested shape

A section in `examples/README.md` next to the selector explanation: the fourteen functions, each with its signature and the one-line example already present in `render.go`, plus `_parent` and a note that Go builtins are available. The doc comments are written; they are just not reachable from where someone is writing a schema.

## Related

- `mache-d55457` — data-source schemas cannot be driven by either documented command. Same area, different failure: that one is about running a schema, this one is about writing one.
- 0day publishes a generated topology schema for its own artifact at `https://xn--w6j.day/schema/v1/mache-topology.json`, which now uses `dig`, `default`, `_parent` and `printf`. It is a live external example if one is wanted, though it has never been mounted — see mache-d55457.
acceptance_criteria: examples/README.md documents the template vocabulary available in `name` and `content_template`: every function registered in internal/template/render.go with its signature and an example, plus `_parent` and the availability of Go builtins. `default` and `lookup` state their argument order and semantics explicitly, since both are silently wrong rather than erroring when misused. Verified by writing a schema using only the README — no reading of render.go — and having it render correctly.

title: CLI config hierarchy: viper + TOML + project/user overrides (replace flag sprawl)
description:
Surfaced 2026-05-19 by user during PR #401: "we need to expose less CLI options and have a config file (That is repo oriented and global, like how .gitconfig works hierarchically) ... not sure if that's a cobra thing so we dont repeat the world ... i also lowkey love toml."

## Problem

`mache serve / build / mount` accumulate flags as features land. The Cobra surface is approaching "flag soup" — `--schema`, `--mount`, `--http`, `--stdio`, `--control`, `--arena-size-mib`, `--backend`, etc. Many of these are stable per-repo settings ("this repo always uses the rust preset and listens on :7533") and should not need to be retyped per invocation.

## Solution shape

Use Cobra's already-existing companion library [viper](https://github.com/spf13/viper) for hierarchical config. Resolution order (highest priority first):

1. **CLI flags** (explicit per-invocation)
2. **Env vars** (`MACHE_*` — already partially used: `MACHE_NO_LEYLINE`, `MACHE_SMELL_RULES_DIR`)
3. **Project config**: `./.mache.toml` (repo root) — checked in, shared across collaborators
4. **User-global config**: `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/mache/config.toml` or `~/.config/mache/config.toml` — personal defaults
5. **Built-in defaults**

Format: **TOML** (user preference + Cobra+viper's standard).

## Example hierarchy

User-global `~/.config/mache/config.toml`:
```toml
[serve]
http = ":7532"
backend = "auto"

[smell-rules]
external-dir = "~/.config/mache/smell-rules"
```

Project `./.mache.toml` (mache-on-mache):
```toml
[serve]
schema = "go"

[mount]
nfs = true

[smell-rules]
exclude = ["sleep_in_test"] # benchmark files in this repo use sleep legitimately
```

## Implementation notes

- Cobra → viper is a one-line bind per flag: `viper.BindPFlag("serve.http", cmd.Flags().Lookup("http"))`
- Viper auto-detects format by extension; TOML lands free
- Add `mache config` subcommand to print effective resolved config + show source per key (mirrors `git config --list --show-origin`)
- Migrate flags incrementally — start with `serve` subcommand (the most used) and the smell-rules dir lookup (currently env-var-only)
- Document `.mache.toml` in README + GETTING-STARTED

## Open questions

- Should `.mache.toml` live at repo root or in `.mache/config.toml`? `.gitconfig` lives at root; `.cargo/config.toml` is nested. Repo root is more discoverable; nested keeps the project root clean. Lean: repo root (`.mache.toml`) for the leading file, room for `.mache/` directory later if we add e.g. smell-rules subdirs.
- Pairs with [[mache-966e22]] (MACHE_SMELL_RULES_DIR discoverability) — both push toward "mache has a project-config story." The smell-rules dir could become `[smell-rules].external-dir` in TOML rather than its current env-var-only surface.

## Acceptance

- ADR: name the design choice (toml vs yaml vs cli-only, where the file lives)
- Wire viper into Cobra in cmd/root.go
- Migrate at least `serve --http`, `serve --schema`, `serve --backend`, and `MACHE_SMELL_RULES_DIR` to the new resolver
- `mache config` subcommand mirrors `git config --list --show-origin`
- Tests: per-source override precedence; TOML round-trip; missing file = graceful default

Paired beads: [[mache-96341d]] (smell-rule categories), [[mache-966e22]] (smell-rule dir).

comments.text: ADR-0018 (mache-e1b6c8) merged 2026-05-19, references this bead as a future substrate dependency (annotated "bead, not yet shipped"). Specifically: the ADR's `.mache/drift-counts.toml` schema + the deferred `.mache.toml [drift-rules.overrides]` block both want this viper+TOML config hierarchy. v1 of the ADR ships without it (per-rule defaults + CLI flags only); v2 picks it up when this bead lands.

title: Prototype shelling out to leyline-mcp-descriptor for server.json generation, once notme proves cross-language adoption
description:
Investigated (background agent, 2026-07-29) whether mache should adopt LLO's shared `leyline-mcp-descriptor` crate instead of hand-maintaining `tools/server-json-gen/main.go`.

Findings:
- The crate ships a CLI binary (`src/main.rs`) specifically designed for cross-language invocation: reads a JSON Descriptor on stdin, writes server.json on stdout, non-zero exit + stderr reason on failure. Same shell-out pattern mache already uses for the `leyline` binary itself (internal/leyline/binary_pin.go), released as one of LLO's per-arch release assets since v0.12.1+.
- mache's own OCI-identifier bug (mache-03745c, fixed) is structurally unrepresentable under LLO's generator now — render() hard-rejects any oci_image containing ':'/'@' and any empty oci_version (lib.rs:337-357). LLO's CHANGELOG (ley-line-open-04300f) names mache as the reference implementation it copied the fix from.
- The session-per-transport gap (mache-e28a9f) is resolved by relocation, not a blocker — see that bead.
- Zero cross-language precedent exists yet: every current adopter (just LLO itself, in rs/tools/server-json-gen) calls the Rust library directly. notme is the next adopter in line (notme-450c3c) but is still blocked on a cloister-side consumer (cloister-02dd65) landing first.
- mache's server.json has fields with no slot in LLO's generic schema (remotes[] with a port variable, the _meta transports block, tiered tool buckets, required-deps version pin) - would need to keep hand-assembling those around the binary's output via _meta extension.

Do NOT adopt yet. Wait for notme to prove the cross-language shell-out pattern in production first (bar to clear), then prototype: shell out to leyline-mcp-descriptor for the coverage-validated core (tool/group validation + base server.json rendering), keep mache's _meta extensions hand-assembled around it same as today.

Files: tools/server-json-gen/main.go, Taskfile.yml (gen:server-json target)
acceptance_criteria: Re-evaluate once notme-450c3c (or cloister-02dd65) closes, confirming a working cross-language (non-Rust) consumer of leyline-mcp-descriptor exists. At that point, either prototype the shell-out or record the concrete reason not to.

title: Plan graphForSession's root-path correlation for when mcp-go drops Mcp-Session-Id (MCP protocol 2026-07-28 / SEP-2567/2575)
description:
MCP protocol revision 2026-07-28 (SEP-2567/SEP-2575) removed protocol-level sessions (the Mcp-Session-Id header mechanism) from the spec entirely — found investigating mache-e28a9f.

mache's multi-tenant graph-sharing design depends on it today: cmd/serve_registry.go keys the actual graph/db build by repo root path (`graphs sync.Map // rootPath -> *lazyGraph`), with session ID used purely as the correlation key to discover which root path a given client connection belongs to (via ListRoots on first contact, cmd/serve_registry.go:227 resolveSession). This is what avoids building N separate dbs for N sessions open on the same repo. mark3labs/mcp-go's Streamable HTTP transport (server/streamable_http.go:619 etc.) reads Mcp-Session-Id directly off the wire to populate session.SessionID().

NOT currently broken: mache pins mcp-go v0.57.0 (latest published as of 2026-07-29), whose LATEST_PROTOCOL_VERSION is "2025-11-25" — it has not adopted protocol 2026-07-28 yet, so Mcp-Session-Id is still present end-to-end.

This is a forward risk to track, not an active bug: before ever bumping mcp-go to a version that adopts protocol 2026-07-28, mache needs a replacement correlation mechanism for graphForSession/resolveSession. The spec's stated direction (per LLO's ley-line-open-4ec276 discussion) is a server-minted handle passed as an ordinary tool argument rather than a transport-level session header — that's a materially different flow (explicit handle exchange on first call vs. transparent ListRoots-on-connect) and would need real design work, not a drop-in swap.

Files: cmd/serve_registry.go, go.mod (mcp-go pin)
acceptance_criteria: Before bumping github.com/mark3labs/mcp-go past whatever version first adopts MCP protocol 2026-07-28 (check LATEST_PROTOCOL_VERSION in mcp/types.go on each upgrade), confirm a replacement correlation mechanism for graphForSession's root-path dedup is designed and tested, or confirm mcp-go's own SDK still provides a connection-scoped identifier we can use even without the wire-level Mcp-Session-Id header.

title: Clear the smell gate on the LLO v0.10.4 typed-wire branch (long_function + a real new clone)
description:
`feat/mache-llo-v0.10.4-typed-wire` passes `task test` but fails `task check` (EXIT=201) on the smell ratchet with 2 NEW findings above baseline. Both are genuine and branch-caused — neither is a v0.10.4 grammar shift, and neither should be baselined:

1. `[long_function] internal/leyline/sheaf_subscriber.go:457` — `SheafSubscriber.dispatch` grew to 103 lines (threshold 81) when the branch added the narrow-envelope decode that works around `ley-line-open-3e2492` (LLO v0.10.4 emits `seq` as a JSON number while its exported Event mirror marks that field `,string`).
   Fix: extract the region-alias resolution block into `resolveInvalidatedRegions(json.RawMessage) ([]int, error)`, sited next to its existing `decodeRegionAlias` helper. dispatch → 74 lines.

2. `[duplicate_code] cmd/cache.go:838` — cmd/cache.go is NOT touched by this branch. Line 838 is `bytesEqual([]byte)`, and the branch's new `equalRegionIDs([]uint32)` is a structurally identical Type-2 clone of it, so the ratchet flags both members of the new clone group. Regenerating the baseline here would have grandfathered a real duplicate.
   Fix: delete `equalRegionIDs`, use stdlib `slices.Equal` at the single call site (go 1.26; `slices` already imported across internal/leyline).

Verified out of scope: all four v0.10.4 SHA pins in binary_pin.go match the live release assets exactly, so the LLO CDC/signing work has not re-cut them.

Gate command: `task check` must reach EXIT=0 with docs/smell-baseline.json UNCHANGED — an unchanged baseline is the proof both findings were real defects rather than grammar drift.
acceptance_criteria: `task check` exits 0 on feat/mache-llo-v0.10.4-typed-wire with docs/smell-baseline.json unmodified vs origin/main; `go test ./internal/leyline/ -run 'TestResolveInvalidatedRegions|TestSheafSubscriber' -count=1` passes; `grep -c equalRegionIDs` over the tree returns 0.

title: feat: .macheignore for ingest-policy overrides on top of .gitignore
description:
Today mache's ingestion respects .gitignore via RespectGitignore=true (engine.go:233). Binary toggle — either you trust git's view of 'what matters' or you index everything. A .macheignore would let users override:

1. Skip files git tracks but you don't want indexed (vendored deps, generated *.pb.go, large fixtures, captured fixtures in testdata/, etc.)
2. Include files git ignores but you want navigable (local notes, scratch dirs, generated artifacts you're indexing temporarily)
3. Different rules per schema (index .go but not .proto)

Design sketch:
- .macheignore at the mount root, same syntax as .gitignore
- Layered semantics: .gitignore filters first (RespectGitignore), then .macheignore applies overrides:
  - Pattern in .macheignore = exclude (in addition to .gitignore)
  - Negation pattern (!path) = re-include something .gitignore would have excluded
- engine.go gains a second matcher; check .macheignore in same loop where .gitignore is checked (engine.go:359, :371)
- Watcher: load .macheignore alongside .gitignore via WithGitignore (rename to WithIgnoreMatchers?)
- Schema-driven: a Topology could declare extra ignore patterns via api.Schema if per-schema overrides are wanted

Not urgent. .gitignore covers ~95% of cases today. File this as the next-level granularity once a real user pain point lands.

comments.text:
Refinement per user: .macheignore should also be usable as a STANDALONE ingest policy, not just an overlay on .gitignore. Three modes worth supporting:

1. .gitignore only (current default — RespectGitignore=true, no .macheignore present)
2. .macheignore overlays .gitignore (load both, .macheignore can override either way via negation)
3. .macheignore replaces .gitignore (when .macheignore is present, ignore .gitignore unless explicitly opted in)

Mode 3 is the user's ask. Use case: agentic workflows that don't want git's tracking to dictate what mache sees — they want a clean, declarative ingest policy independent of source control state. Especially relevant for agent dispatch into worktrees where git's view of 'tracked' is messy or irrelevant.

Implementation note: introduce a small policy struct (e.g. IngestPolicy{ UseGitignore bool; Macheignore *Matcher }) instead of stacking booleans. .macheignore presence + a sentinel (e.g. first line '# standalone') OR a flag could opt into mode 3.
comments.author: jamestexas

title: Cyclomatic memo oracle doesn't exercise LIMIT truncation or hashless occurrences
description:
Follow-up on mache-238673 phase-1 (branch feat/mache-238673-incremental-cyclomatic, PR #504, commit 7d6cbc9). The "byte-identical to full scan" claim for runCyclomaticComplexityMemo (cmd/smell_incremental.go) is proven by a differential oracle (cmd/smell_findings_incremental_test.go), but the oracle has two coverage gaps that weaken the claim before phase-2 wiring:

1. LIMIT truncation never exercised. Every test call uses `oracleLimit = 100000` (smell_findings_incremental_test.go:149), always exceeding the fixture's finding count, so the `out[:limit]` truncation branch (smell_incremental.go:156-158) and the SQL `LIMIT %d` truncation (smell_findings.go:48) are never both hit with real truncation. Go's `sort.Slice` (unstable) and SQLite's `ORDER BY` could disagree on tie ordering if the (metric, source_id, start_byte) tuple is ever non-unique in real data; a truncation-boundary divergence would currently go undetected. Real callers that will eventually drive this path pass small limits: cmd/find_smells_cli.go:244 (findSmellsLimit), cmd/serve_find_smells.go:121 (limit), cmd/smell_digest.go:68 (digestScanCap).

2. Hashless occurrences never exercised. Every fixFunc in every test (smell_findings_incremental_test.go, find_smells_bench_test.go) sets a non-nil hash. The `f.hashHex == ""` branch in runCyclomaticComplexityMemo (smell_incremental.go:90-107, the per-occurrence "local" map path) and the `hasHash == false` branch in scanASTFunctions (smell_incremental.go:171-178) — the "standalone db, no node_hash column" backward-compat case the code comments explicitly claim to handle correctly ("correctness never depends on the producer emitting a hash") — are asserted but never tested.

Recommend adding oracle cases for both (a small-limit run against a >limit fixture, and a fixture with no node_hash column / mixed hashed+hashless rows) before this is wired into a real limit-bounded caller.

comments.text: Addressed in commit 3387a56 (PR #504). Added four oracle cases in cmd/smell_findings_incremental_test.go: LimitTruncation (out[:limit] with a tie group straddling the boundary), HashlessAndMixed (f.hashHex=="" nil-node_hash path, asserts hashless recomputed every scan), SourceScoped (sourceID!="" WHERE clause), NoHashColumn (hasHash==false — no node_hash column at all, asserts memo.hits==0). All green; parity byte-identical to the full scan in each. Closing.

title: smellMemo needs a concurrency + eviction story before phase-2 daemon wiring
description:
Follow-up on mache-238673 phase-1 (cmd/smell_incremental.go). `smellMemo` (smell_incremental.go:49-53) is a plain, unsynchronized `map[string]int64` plus two bare `int` counters (hits/misses), incremented without any mutex/atomic. The type's own doc comment (smell_incremental.go:27-30) explicitly anticipates "a long-lived caller (e.g. a future sheaf-subscribe daemon) holds the memo across scans." Per CLAUDE.md, mache's MCP HTTP mode serves concurrent stateful sessions per client — the natural home for a long-lived daemon. If a future integration shares one `*smellMemo` across concurrent scan requests (concurrent runCyclomaticComplexityMemo calls), the unsynchronized map read/write in the hit/miss decision loop (smell_incremental.go:89-107) and the writes in the compute-result loop (smell_incremental.go:113-120) are a data race — `go test -race` would only catch this if a concurrent test exists, and none currently does.

Separately, there's no eviction: every distinct node_hash ever seen accumulates in `memo.metric` forever, so a long-lived daemon watching an evolving codebase grows the memo unboundedly across the process lifetime (renamed/deleted functions' hashes are never purged).

Not a phase-1 blocker (current usage is single-threaded, in-process, per-test/bench, no production caller exists yet — confirmed via grep, only test/bench files call runCyclomaticComplexityMemo). File so the concurrency + eviction design is decided explicitly before phase-2 wires this into a daemon, rather than discovered via a race panic in production.
