title: cross-lang refs: second scheme (npm or git remote-hint) to prove generalization
description:
## What

Register a second `Resolver` implementation to prove the registry generalizes cleanly. Adding a new scheme should require **two lines of wiring**: one `RegisterAddressRefQuery` call (in `internal/ingest/engine_languages.go`) and one `Registry.Register` call (in `cmd/serve.go`), with zero changes to the core graph or MCP plumbing.

## Pick one

**Option A — `NPMResolver`**: extracts `npm:<pkg>@<version>` tokens from `package.json` `dependencies`/`devDependencies`. Resolver looks for `node_modules/<pkg>` adjacent to the source; if present, ingests the package directory as a sub-graph (mirrors `LocalPathResolver` shape). If absent, returns `ErrNotResolvable` with a structured `RemoteHint` pointing at the npm registry URL.

**Option B — `GitResolver` stub**: extracts `git::https://...` tokens from Terraform remote module sources. Does **not** clone in V1 — returns `ErrNotResolvable` with a structured `RemoteHint` containing the clone URL, target ref, and any subpath, so the calling agent can decide whether to clone. Validates the `RemoteHint` payload shape for future remote-clone work.

Recommendation: start with Option B (no fetch, no credentials, no network I/O at test time) — proves the registration plumbing without taking on remote-fetch complexity.

## Why this is its own bead

The architect's bead #5 — validates that adding a scheme is genuinely cheap. If this bead requires touching the core graph, MCP plumbing, or the resolver interface, the abstraction is leaking and we need to revisit before scheme #3.

## Tests

For Option B: register the resolver, call `resolve_ref(token="git::https://github.com/foo/bar")`, assert response has `remote_hint` with the parsed clone URL / ref / subpath, and `graph_path` is absent.

## Depends on

`mache-bd97d9` (the Registry interface). Can run in parallel with `mache-be0b9f` after `mache-bd97d9` lands, since this doesn't touch the mount path.

## Files

New: `internal/resolve/<scheme>_resolver.go` (option-dependent). Modify: `internal/ingest/engine_languages.go` (one new `RegisterAddressRefQuery` call), `cmd/serve.go` (one new `Registry.Register` call).

title: MCP annotation defaults leaked: read tools advertised destructiveHint=true + openWorldHint=true (mcp-go NewTool seeds them true)
description:
## Found via post-merge real-binary verification (follow-up to mache-974697)

After mache-974697 added `readOnlyHint=true`, a `tools/list` probe of the installed binary showed EVERY tool also carrying `destructiveHint=true` and `openWorldHint=true`. Root cause: `mcp.NewTool` pre-seeds the annotation struct with the MCP spec defaults (destructive=true, openWorld=true), and the single-field `WithReadOnlyHintAnnotation` override left those defaults intact. The `/mcp` badge was fixed (clients ignore destructiveHint when readOnlyHint=true), but the raw annotations were dishonest — a read-only tool shouldn't advertise destructive, and `list_directory` isn't open-world.

## Fix

Replace per-tool single-field overrides with three `WithToolAnnotation(ToolAnnotation{...})` presets (which REPLACE the whole struct, wiping leaked defaults): `readTool` (readOnly=true, destructive=false, openWorld=false), `readToolExternal` (same but openWorld=true for the 4 daemon-touching tools), `writeTool` (readOnly=false, destructive=true). Verified on the installed binary: destructive=true only on write_file; openWorld=true only on semantic_search/get_type_info/get_diagnostics/get_sheaf_status.

## Guard

`TestMCPRegistry_AnnotationHintsHonest` pins destructiveHint (only mutatingTools) and openWorldHint (only openWorldTools) per tool, so a leaked default can't slip back.

title: Rich-fixture mode for e2e tool harness (mache-on-mache + tunable size)
description:
Surfaced post-PR (DefsMap/RefsMap memoization). The current e2e harness fixture (`writeE2EFixture` in `cmd/all_tools_e2e_test.go`) is a 4-package toy Go project. Findings on it are real — DefsMap/RefsMap rebuild cost surfaced clearly — but they're tiny (single-digit MB heap deltas) on a fixture that doesn't match production workloads.

## What this enables

A rich-fixture mode that runs the harness against:

1. **mache-on-mache** — invoke `leyline parse` on mache's own source dir at test time, use the resulting `.db` as the fixture. ~241 files, full cross-reference graph, real god-functions (e.g. `mount.go`, `serve.go`).
2. **Synthetic-medium** — generate N packages × M functions on the fly. Tunable via `E2E_FIXTURE_SIZE=medium|large`. Deterministic, no external deps.

Selection via env var:
- `E2E_FIXTURE=toy` (default) — current 4-package fixture
- `E2E_FIXTURE=synthetic-medium` — 25 packages, ~4 funcs each
- `E2E_FIXTURE=synthetic-large` — 100 packages, ~10 funcs each
- `E2E_FIXTURE=mache` — leyline parse on mache's source (skip if leyline missing)

## Why we want it

DefsMap/RefsMap memoization (just-shipped) reduced heap deltas 30-45% on the 4-package toy. That's real but small absolute numbers (a few MB → a few less MB). On a real workload:

- `DefsMap` size scales with construct count (10K+ on real repos)
- `RefsMap` size scales with cross-reference density (50K+ tokens common)
- Each rebuild allocates one slice per token — millions of allocs on a real workload

A bigger fixture surfaces:
- Whether more memoization candidates exist beyond DefsMap/RefsMap
- Whether the harness CI runtime stays acceptable (target: <30s on synthetic-large, <120s on mache-on-mache)
- Real-world god-function shapes for `fan_out_skew` cross-checking

## Acceptance

- `task profile-tools-pprof E2E_FIXTURE=synthetic-medium` runs in <30s
- `task profile-tools-pprof E2E_FIXTURE=mache` runs in <120s when leyline is on PATH; skips cleanly otherwise
- Heap-delta numbers grow proportionally with fixture size (sanity check that the pipeline is still measuring the right thing)
- `.e2e/INDEX.md` records which fixture was used

## Out of scope

- Vendored open-source repos (k8s controller, tokio crate, etc.) — that's mache-d332b5's territory (cross-runtime fixtures, gated on CGO removal)
- Per-tool baseline regression detection — separate follow-up

## Refs

- Surfaced after DefsMap/RefsMap caching PR
- Pairs with mache-d332b5 (hetero) — both extend the e2e harness in different directions
- Builds on mache-6b6da6 phase 1-3 (e2e harness + pprof + flamegraphs)

title: Service-ify mache: user unit with declared startup ordering against the leyline daemon
description:
Twin of ley-line-open-4bd5e0 (LLO's LaunchAgent/systemd-user-unit bead), from the user's directive 2026-07-30: LLO and mache must be TRULY OPERATIONAL SEPARATELY — two independent daemons sharing an IPC/ABI surface (LLO's control file + UDS ops), with process lifecycle and startup ordering owned by the init system, not by one process exec'ing the other.

Context: LLO's daemon used to exec 'mache serve --control <ctrl>' as a child; mache removed --control, so the spawn was starting a child that exits on an unknown flag on every daemon start (LLO bead 620c3f — the dead spawn is now removed on LLO's integration branch). The replacement architecture:

1. mache ships its own service unit(s): LaunchAgent plist (macOS) + systemd user unit (Linux), same deliverable shape as LLO-4bd5e0.
2. Startup ordering DECLARED, not improvised: systemd After=/Wants= the leyline user unit; launchd has no hard ordering, so use its on-demand/KeepAlive mechanics (or socket-activation on the UDS path) so mache tolerates starting first and connects when leyline's control surface appears — which mache's DiscoverOrStart posture already leans toward.
3. The IPC contract stays the coupling: mache discovers/attaches to the leyline daemon's ctrl + UDS; exec-coupling exists in NEITHER direction (mache's autoInvokeLeylineParse shelling to 'leyline parse' for one-shot projection is fine — that's a CLI invocation, not daemon lifecycle management).
4. Coordinate the unit install path with mache-341784 (install/PATH first-classing) so units reference binaries at their real installed home.
acceptance_criteria: mache ships a LaunchAgent plist + systemd user unit; startup ordering against the leyline daemon is declared (systemd After=/Wants=; launchd KeepAlive/on-demand equivalent); the leyline IPC contract (ctrl + UDS) is consumed via discovery, never via exec-coupling in either direction

title: Structural test gates: golden projection-parity + scale/query-count regression gate (hybrid)
description:
Motivation: the O(nodes²) projection regression (mache-4f3840) shipped through green CI, and the fix's correctness was proven by a HAND-BUILT byte-diff of nodes/node_refs/node_defs (old vs new binary) — not a test. Separately, PR-B (mache-37ae8b) DELETES sitter_walker.go, killing the only cross-backend parity gate (ASTWalker vs SitterWalker) right as the projection is rewritten — no second backend remains to diff against.

Data (measured 2026-07-20): test LoC cmd 24,891 (81 files) / ingest 6,610 / graph 8,981 / lattice 1,444 / testfixtures 504. Golden-replaceable "assert projection shape" surface = only ~8 of 81 cmd files. "golden reduces LoC" is directionally true but NARROW; LoC is the wrong metric — goal is catching unknown-unknowns (drift + complexity). Decision: HYBRID (user-approved).

Plan — 3 layers:
1. Golden projection-parity harness (replaces the dying cross-backend gate): project a small COMMITTED fixture corpus (real .go exercising functions/methods/types/imports/consts/vars + cross-construct calls + address-refs + a non-Go file for language-tagging) through leyline+ASTWalker → normalized sorted dump of nodes(id,record)/node_refs/node_defs → diff vs committed golden. `-update` regen MUST print a human-readable added/removed summary so regen forces review, not rubber-stamp. Codifies the mache-4f3840 hand-diff.
2. Scale/perf regression gate: project ~100-200 files; assert a QUERY-COUNT budget (sharper than wall-clock — O(n²) shows as query explosion independent of machine speed; instrument a counter on the read db / sql hook). Secondary generous wall-clock ceiling. Would have failed on mache-4f3840.
3. Keep + SHARPEN intent tests (backstop against a bad golden regen): methods/ root when receiver methods present; method→callee cross-ref in node_refs (dead_code FP fix); non-Go routed to _project_files/. Few, sharp, WHY-commented. NOTE: the FCA versions are being migrated by a Fable subagent (the 4 stale PR-B cmd tests → mache pack --infer path); layer 3 reconciles with wherever those land.

Sequencing: build on the SETTLED projection AFTER PR-B tests are green (depends on the 4-test fix + PR-B landing). Related: mache-4f3840 (perf, done), mache-37ae8b (PR-B). See memory feedback_perf_and_parity_gates_missing.
acceptance_criteria: `task test` green with new gates present: (1) a golden projection-parity test that diffs normalized nodes/node_refs/node_defs of a committed fixture corpus against a committed golden and fails on any un-regenerated drift; (2) a scale gate that projects ~100-200 files and fails if the read-side query count exceeds an O(nodes)-linear budget (would fail on the mache-4f3840 O(n²) pattern); (3) the load-bearing intent tests (methods/ root, method→callee cross-ref, non-Go language-tagging) preserved as sharp named-invariant tests. Verify the scale gate actually trips by temporarily reverting the mache-4f3840 fix.

title: Schema-driven projection from external type systems (provider schemas, CRDs, JSON Schema)
description:
## Problem

Mache currently projects data by syntax (tree-sitter AST) or by mache's own
topology schemas. But many data formats have external type systems that define
semantics: Terraform provider schemas, Kubernetes CRDs, Helm values.schema.json,
JSON Schema references.

## Proposal

Ingest external schema definitions to inform projection:

1. **Terraform provider schema** — `terraform providers schema -json` outputs
   complete JSON schema for every resource type. Use it to project HCL resources
   into typed directories with field-level documentation as context files.

2. **Kubernetes CRDs** — OpenAPI schema defines custom resource structure.
   Project YAML manifests into semantically-typed trees.

3. **Helm values.schema.json** — defines the shape of values.yaml.
   Validate writes against schema, not just YAML syntax.

4. **JSON Schema ($schema)** — any JSON/YAML with a $schema reference
   can be projected with schema awareness.

## The Insight

These schemas are type systems for config. If mache ingests them:
- Project by semantic type, not raw syntax (aws_lambda_function is a
  first-class directory, not just an HCL block)
- Validate writes against the schema, not just tree-sitter syntax
- Show documentation — provider schemas include field descriptions,
  which become context files
- LSP-like awareness without an actual LSP

## Implementation Path

Build a schema-aware walker that joins AST nodes with their external
schema definitions. Start with Terraform (richest schema, clearest mapping).

title: Wire file watcher → SheafInvalidator.InvalidateWithCascade (the missing first link)
description:
## What

Today `cmd/serve.go:414-421` `onChange` does:

```go
onChange := func(path string) {
    store.DeleteFileNodes(path)
    if reErr := engine.ReIngestFile(path); reErr != nil { ... }
}
```

Purely local — `store.DeleteFileNodes` + `engine.ReIngestFile`. The ley-line daemon is never told a file changed. So the LLO sheaf cascade (which is real and gated, per audit) never runs in response to an edit.

`internal/graph/sheaf_invalidate.go` already has `SheafInvalidator.InvalidateWithCascade(id, membership)` — looks up the node's region, calls `sheaf.Invalidate`, fans out to all affected nodes. **It has zero production callers today.** This bead wires it in.

## Why this is load-bearing

From the audit (`docs/audit/sheaf-incremental.md`, written under [[mache-49bf9a]]): step 1 of the 7-step chain is fsnotify → daemon notification. Without it, **the entire downstream chain is dead**, no matter how well the daemon side and the cache layer are wired. This is the upstream-most gap on the mache side.

## Sketch

1. After `buildServeGraph` finishes, capture the resulting `*CommunityResult` (from the most recent `find_smells`-style run, or a build-time community detection over the refs map — TBD design call).
2. Construct `si := graph.NewSheafInvalidator(store, leyline.NewSheafClient(sock), result)` once at serve startup.
3. Change `onChange` to call `si.InvalidateWithCascade(nodeID, nil)` for each node affected by the path change.
4. Open question: how to map `path` → set of node IDs (mache's `Store` interface needs a method, or we walk the in-memory store post-reingest).

## Dependencies

- Daemon side already real (LLO PR #16, merged).
- `SheafClient.PushTopology` already runs in `cmd/serve_handlers.go:865-879` — but only after `find_smells` is invoked. May need to push topology at serve startup so the cascade has something to cascade through.

## Verification

- New test in `internal/graph/sheaf_invalidate_test.go` style: spin up a fake `SheafBackend` with deterministic affected-region output, edit a file, assert all expected node IDs got `Invalidate(id)` calls.
- Eventually subsumed by the cross-runtime e2e in [[mache-8e7794]].

## Pairs with

- [[mache-49bf9a]] (the audit that surfaced this gap)
- Sibling P1 bead filed alongside: subscribe to sheaf.invalidate events
- Blocks [[mache-33ffb0]] (pre-injection epic — depends on the cascade actually firing)
- Blocks [[mache-8e7794]] (cross-runtime e2e)

title: Subscribe to sheaf.invalidate events and flush MCP-tool caches (steps 5-6 of audit)
description:
## What

`internal/leyline/socket.go:371` defines `SocketClient.Subscribe(topics []string) (<-chan map[string]any, error)` — a generic event-bus subscribe over UDS. The LLO daemon emits `sheaf.invalidate` (with `{invalidated, count, generation}` payload) and `sheaf.topology` events on every cascade run.

**Today nobody calls Subscribe.** `grep Subscribe\(` across the repo finds only the definition and tests. The event bus is live; mache is not listening. This bead wires a consumer.

## Why this is load-bearing

From the audit (`docs/audit/sheaf-incremental.md` under [[mache-49bf9a]]): steps 5 (daemon → mache notification) and 6 (MCP cache flush) are both ✗ on the mache side. They're the same wiring: a subscribe loop that translates `sheaf.invalidate` events into `Graph.Invalidate(nodeID)` calls so MCP-tool result caches drop the stale entries.

Without this, even if the watcher wires up correctly (sibling bead), agent edits would still return stale `find_callers` / `find_definition` / `get_overview` results from cache until the FIFO ages them out.

## Sketch

1. At serve startup, after `SocketClient` is dialed, spawn a goroutine that calls `sock.Subscribe([]string{"sheaf.invalidate", "sheaf.topology"})` and loops over the event channel.
2. On `sheaf.invalidate`: parse `{invalidated: [regionIDs], generation: uint64}`, map regions → member node IDs via current `*CommunityResult`, call `store.Invalidate(nodeID)` for each.
3. On `sheaf.topology`: refresh cached `CommunityResult` (or re-run community detection).
4. Track the latest `generation` for `get_sheaf_status` ([[mache-4a0c05]]) to report.

## Open design questions

1. **Where does the goroutine live?** Probably in serve startup, alongside the watcher.
2. **Lifecycle on socket reconnect**: if `SocketClient` reconnects after a daemon restart, the subscribe needs to re-establish. Today `Subscribe` is one-shot — may need a wrapper that re-subscribes on EOF.
3. **CommunityResult freshness**: the subscribe loop needs the current `*CommunityResult` to map region IDs → node IDs. If `find_smells` hasn't run yet (or community detection is stale), the loop has nothing to fan out to. Decision: skip silently, or run community detection at startup?
4. **Concurrency**: `store.Invalidate(id)` must be safe to call concurrently with reads. `MemoryStore` and `SQLiteGraph` both have RWMutex around their caches today, so this should be fine — verify.

## Verification

- Test using fake `SocketClient` (already exists in `internal/leyline/socket_test.go`) that pushes a synthetic `sheaf.invalidate` event; assert subscriber called `Invalidate(id)` for expected node IDs.
- Cross-runtime test in [[mache-8e7794]].

## Pairs with

- [[mache-49bf9a]] (audit that surfaced this gap)
- Sibling bead just filed: watcher → SheafInvalidator wiring (the symmetric upstream gap)
- Depends on [[mache-8e2e92]] only for typed bindings (nice-to-have, not blocking)
- Blocks [[mache-33ffb0]] (pre-injection epic)
- Pairs with [[mache-4a0c05]] (get_sheaf_status MCP tool — same subscriber tracks generation)

## Scoping: evolve-simplify-engine (internal/ingest/engine.go, 1884 LOC)

### Research
Five related beads searched (mache-d28eb1, mache-9c830b, mache-acc7dd, mache-ad3f75, mache-28c9a1): all CLOSED. No active blockers. Template extraction (mache-28c9a1) already done via PR #362 — render.go living in internal/template/. Coverage-gate tool search returned 0 results (no tool-specific issues found).

### File Map

**Core ingestion orchestrator** (Engine struct):
- internal/ingest/engine.go: 1884 LOC, 40 functions mixing orchestration, file filtering, walker dispatch, tree-sitter parallelism, schema recursion (processNode), doc extraction, refs/defs storage, diagram utilities

**Related extraction points**:
- internal/ingest/interfaces.go (37 LOC): Walker/Match interfaces, stay as-is
- internal/template/render.go (245 LOC): Template rendering, already extracted
- internal/lang/lang.go: Language registry, independent

### Decomposition Candidates (10 extracts)

1. **engine_filter.go** (150-200 LOC): ShouldSkipDir, ShouldSkipFile, isBinaryFile (lines 179-227, 390-403)
2. **engine_extract.go** (150-200 LOC): extractDocComments, byteOffsetToLine, extractGoPackageName, location metadata (lines 1684-1745)
3. **engine_refs.go** (100-150 LOC): bufferingTarget impl, batch file-children, recordJob/recordResult types (lines 74-95, 710-765)
4. **engine_walk.go** (400-450 LOC): processNode, collectNodes, processRecord, parentAwareMatch — core recursion (lines 1204-1343, 1356-1681)
5. **engine_walkers.go** (100-150 LOC): langForExt, schema introspection, walker selection (lines 123-141, 274-297)
6. **engine_ingest.go** (300-350 LOC): Ingest dispatcher, tree-sitter walk phase, gitignore (lines 309-425, 660-717)
7. **engine_treeitter.go** (250-300 LOC): Job scheduler, result processing, ingestTreeSitter, ingestRawFile (lines 426-659, 766-975)
8. **engine_sqlite.go** (150-200 LOC): SQLite streaming + parallel record processing (lines 1097-1203)
9. **engine_diagram.go** (80 LOC): Diagram cache, FuncMap, RenderContentTemplate (lines 1790-1838)
10. **engine.go** (200-400 LOC, irreducible): Constructor, walker lifecycle, state, public API

### Verification

**Source**: Taskfile.yml (lines 49-322)
- **Lint**: task lint → golangci-lint run ./...
- **Test**: task test → go test -tags boltdb -race ... ./...
- **Fmt**: task fmt → gofumpt -w -extra .
- **Vet**: task vet → go vet ./...
- **Check**: task check (CI equivalent)

**Coverage Gate**:
- task coverage-gate BASE=origin/feat/godfile-decomposition
- Target: ≥80% on new/modified code

**Not found**: No type checker beyond Go compiler; no custom pre-commit hooks beyond standard Go linting.

## Team
- Scale: 2-agent (generator + evaluator)
- Generator: principal-agent (extraction + refactoring)
- Evaluator: skeptic-agent (circular import audit, coverage gate, test validation)
- Rationale: 1→8 files, high extraction complexity, --simplify flag, needs careful review

## LOC Tolerance & Irreducible Floor

**Target range**:
- **engine.go**: 1884 → 250-400 LOC (orchestrator floor)
  - Irreducible: Engine struct (state), NewEngine, Ingest entry, walker lifecycle, SetASTWalker, public API (SetFileIndex, ReIngestFile, PrintRoutingSummary)
  - Cannot extract: RootPath, Store, Schema, childSeen dedup (reset per-Ingest), gitignore lifetime, fileIndex (incremental re-ingest state)

- **Total extracted**: 1900-2100 LOC across 8 new files
- **Net delta**: -50 to +200 LOC (slight expansion from package-scope signatures, offset by reduced engine.go size)

**Irreducible state** (stays on Engine):
- Schema, Store, RootPath, RespectGitignore
- childSeen map (shared dedup across all walker types, reset per-Ingest)
- gitignore matcher (lifetime tied to Ingest call)
- sitterWalker, astWalker (shared cache across file set)
- fileIndex, fileIndex map (incremental re-ingest tracking)
- diagramOnce, cachedCommunities, cachedRefs, diagramFuncMapOnce (lazy evaluation)

## Known Tool-Issues Surfaced

- mache-d28eb1 (closed): find_callees returned empty — lang Properties missing. **Engine scope**: processNode line ~1428, fixed in PR #373. No extraction impact.
- mache-28c9a1 (closed): Template extraction already done. render.go lives independently. No extraction conflict.
- No coverage-gate-specific issues found.

## Risk Assessment

- **Circular imports** (MEDIUM): engine_walk.go needs Match interface, walkers need Engine. **Mitigation**: Interfaces already in interfaces.go; export if needed.
- **State fragmentation** (LOW): All state remains on Engine struct; extracted functions receive state via receiver or params.
- **Test compatibility** (LOW): engine_test.go uses public APIs only (NewEngine, Ingest); indirect testing of extracted code paths via integration tests.
- **Performance regression** (LOW): No async overhead; call-stack depth unchanged; inline if profiling shows hot spots.

## Plan (14-step extraction sequence)

1. Audit test coverage → task test baseline
2. Extract engine_filter.go → skip logic, file-type detection
3. Extract engine_extract.go → doc comments, byte tracking, location metadata
4. Extract engine_refs.go → bufferingTarget, batch writes, ref/def accumulation
5. Extract engine_walk.go → processNode, collectNodes, processRecord (core recursion)
6. Extract engine_walkers.go → walker dispatch, schema introspection
7. Extract engine_ingest.go → Ingest dispatcher, walk orchestration, gitignore
8. Extract engine_treeitter.go → tree-sitter job scheduler, result processing
9. Extract engine_sqlite.go → SQLite streaming + parallel record processing
10. Extract engine_diagram.go → diagram cache, FuncMap, RenderContentTemplate
11. Consolidate engine.go → verify imports, no circular deps
12. Full test suite → task test ./..., task validate, task parity (if leyline available)
13. Coverage gate → task coverage-gate BASE=origin/feat/godfile-decomposition
14. Review prep → document extraction boundaries, state rationale, test impact

## Exit Criteria

- All tests pass: task check (fmt, vet, lint, test, validate, docs:lint)
- Coverage gate: ≥80% on new/modified code
- No circular imports (audit via import graph)
- engine.go: 250-400 LOC irreducible orchestrator
- 1 atomic commit (no intermediate squashing)

## Questions for Human

None — scoping complete. Principal-agent can proceed to implementation.

title: _ast smell dogfood blocked: leyline _ast baseline isn't reproducible across darwin/linux (CI mismatch)
description:
The _ast smell dogfood (mache-46af85 part 2) was split out of PR #516 (preserved on branch wip/mache-46af85-dogfood-ast-rules) because a docs/smell-baseline-ast.json generated locally on darwin does NOT match the linux CI run: the CI smells:ast step reported many NEW long_function findings (socket.go:210, tools/mcp-fetch/main.go:54, tools/notion-fetch/*, tools/server-json-gen/*, tools/coverage-gate/*, tools/sheaf-subscribe-probe/main.go:28, several test files) that the darwin baseline lacked.

The lane already builds from TRACKED files only (git ls-files → cpio) for parity within a platform, and uses the pinned leyline. Two candidate causes to determine:
  1. Cross-platform leyline variance (darwin-arm64 vs linux-amd64 v0.7.0 producing different _ast / long_function line-spans or function sets) — if real, a committed baseline can't be authored on darwin. Depends on/relates to ley-line-open determinism.
  2. Local baseline was generated from an incomplete tracked-file set (some tracked tools/*-probe were physically moved out during the session, so cpio skipped them even though git ls-files listed them → those files absent from the baseline; CI's clean checkout has them → NEW).

Resolution paths: (a) verify (2) by regenerating with a fully-present tree and diffing; (b) if (1) is real, generate the baseline IN CI (a `task smells:ast:baseline` job that commits the artifact) or normalize the metric to be platform-stable; (c) confirm leyline _ast output is byte-stable across platforms (file an LLO bead if not). Also note: mache's community-detection quotient test (internal/ingest/quotient_test.go:704) flaked on the same linux run — a separate determinism flake to watch.

Close condition: `task smells:ast` passes in linux CI against a committed baseline, and the baseline is reproducible (0 NEW) from a clean checkout on the platform CI uses.

comments.text:
ROOT CAUSE FOUND — it's cause (2), a cpio portability bug, NOT cross-platform leyline variance:

`git ls-files -z | cpio -pd0 "$SRC"` copies 0 files on macOS (BSD cpio doesn't handle -0/null-delimited stdin the way GNU cpio on Linux/CI does). So the baseline was generated from an EMPTY tree (0 findings baselined); CI's GNU cpio copied all tracked files → every finding was NEW. I misread the earlier "tracked tool present? NO (bad)" + "0 parsed" as working.

FIX confirmed: replace cpio with `git archive HEAD | tar -x -C "$SRC"` — fully portable (git+tar everywhere, no flag ambiguity). Local test: copies 770 tracked files, leyline parses 696, long_function = 103 INCLUDING the 5 CI-flagged files (socket.go, mcp-fetch, notion-fetch, server-json-gen, coverage-gate). git archive HEAD uses the COMMITTED tree = exactly CI's checkout → exact parity. Minor nuance: local runs then gate HEAD, not uncommitted working-tree changes (acceptable for a ratchet).

Residual risk: git archive equalizes the FILE SET; if leyline ALSO has darwin↔linux output variance (masked until now by the empty baseline), the regenerated darwin baseline could still differ from linux CI — handle by generating the baseline in CI if that surfaces. But the primary blocker (cpio) is resolved.

Next: on top of LLO v0.7.1 (#517), swap cpio→git archive in smells:ast:run, regenerate a REAL baseline, verify smells:ast 0 NEW, re-open the dogfood PR.

title: Ingestion silently drops constructs on in-record name collision (14.6% loss on Rust)
description:
`collectNodes` (internal/ingest/engine_walk.go:83-172) — the streaming path taken by `mache build` via engine_sqlite.go:41 -> processRecord -> collectNodes — performs NO dedup. It renders `name` from the schema template, computes `id := toNodeID(currentPath)`, and appends to `result.nodes`. Two matches within the SAME record that render the same name produce the same node ID, and the last one written to the store wins. The earlier constructs are lost with no error, no warning, and no diagnostic.

The store-based dedup at engine_walk.go:222-229 does NOT cover this. It lives in the OTHER path (`walkNode`), and even there the suffix is derived solely from `dedupSuffix(sourceFile)`, so it disambiguates ACROSS files but never WITHIN one — N>2 same-named constructs in a single file collapse to the same suffixed ID.

REPRODUCTION (minimal, deterministic):

    // /tmp/rsfix/lib.rs
    pub struct A { pub v: u32 }
    pub struct B { pub v: u32 }
    pub struct C { pub v: u32 }
    impl A { pub fn new() -> Self { A { v: 1 } } }
    impl B { pub fn new() -> Self { B { v: 2 } } }
    impl C { pub fn new() -> Self { C { v: 3 } } }

    mache build --schema examples/rust-schema.json /tmp/rsfix /tmp/rsfix.db
    sqlite3 /tmp/rsfix.db "select id, record from nodes where name='source' and id like 'functions/%';"

    -> functions/new/source | pub fn new() -> Self { C { v: 3 } }

Three distinct methods, ONE node, holding C's body. A::new and B::new are gone. No `.from_` suffix was applied at all.

SCALE (measured against ley-line-open rs/, 228 files):
  ground truth `fn new(` in source ......... 63
  captured as functions/new ................  1
  ground truth all fn items ................ 4210
  captured functions/*/source .............. 3597
  -> 613 constructs lost (14.6%), silently

Go is unaffected in practice because its schema nests by package AND names methods `{{.receiver}}.{{.name}}`, so collisions cannot arise. Any language whose schema uses a flat, bare-name namespace is exposed. The Rust schema is the concrete case (see the sibling schema bead).

WHY P0: this is silent data loss in the core projection path. mache's primary claim is that it presents a faithful structural view of a codebase; a 14.6% silent shortfall makes find_definition / get_overview / callers quietly incomplete, and nothing in the pipeline surfaces it. A caller cannot distinguish "not present" from "dropped".

FIX (two parts, this bead is the first):
1. `collectNodes` must never emit a duplicate ID. Track IDs seen within the record and disambiguate deterministically (source order is stable for a given file, so a counter is reproducible). Losing data must be impossible by construction.
2. Emit a WARN naming the schema node and the colliding name, so the schema author learns their name template is not unique rather than having the engine paper over it. The suffix is a safety net, not the intended outcome — the schema fix is the real one.

Explicitly NOT acceptable: keeping last-writer-wins, or deduping only across files.

Discovered while running the F4 per-language generality benchmark (mache-544659) against the ley-line-open Rust workspace.

comments.text:
ROOT CAUSE CONFIRMED — and it corrects two claims in the original description. Do not act on the description's attribution; use this.

WRONG (original): "`collectNodes` performs NO dedup ... the streaming path taken by `mache build` via engine_sqlite.go:41".
RIGHT: `mache build` on source takes `processNode` (engine_walk.go:179), NOT `collectNodes`. Instrumenting both paths and rebuilding the repro emitted `[PATH-processNode] id=functions/new files=1` three times and ZERO `collectNodes` hits. A first fix attempt placed in `collectNodes` changed nothing, which is what exposed the misattribution. `collectNodes` may well have the same latent gap, but it is not the path that produces this bug and is not where the fix belongs.

ALSO WRONG: I speculated the survivor was nondeterministic because workers are parallel. It is deterministic — 5 consecutive rebuilds all yielded C's body. Within one record, matches are walked in source order and the last one wins. Do not write a test asserting nondeterminism.

ACTUAL MECHANISM — the dedup guard at engine_walk.go:222-229 is DEAD CODE on this path:

    if len(schema.Files) > 0 && sourceFile != "" {
        if existing, err := store.GetNode(id); err == nil && len(existing.Children) > 0 {
            suffix := dedupSuffix(sourceFile)   // never reached

Probing the guard's own condition on the 3-collision repro:

    [PROBE] id=functions/new ABSENT  err=node not found     <- match 1
    [PROBE] id=functions/new EXISTS children=0              <- match 2
    [PROBE] id=functions/new EXISTS children=0              <- match 3

The node EXISTS by match 2, but reports zero children, so `len(existing.Children) > 0` is false and the suffix branch is never taken. That is why no `.from_lib_rs` node appears anywhere in the output — the store ends with a single `functions/new` holding C's body, with A's and B's silently discarded. Full store dump confirms: only `functions/new/source` exists under `functions/`.

Why children reads 0 at check time is the remaining sub-question. processNode builds `node` with `Children: existingChildren` re-fetched from the store, then attaches files via `bufferingTarget.AddFileChildren`, which appends to `parent.Children` in memory and republishes the parent via `AddNode`. The file nodes themselves are buffered for a later `ReplaceFileNodes` atomic swap (engine_refs.go:31-69). Something in that publish/swap sequence means the parent's Children are not observable to the next match's `GetNode`. Confirm this before fixing — it determines whether the guard is repairable in place.

FIX GUIDANCE (revised)
Do NOT simply repair the children check. It is order-dependent and couples collision detection to the file-buffering lifecycle — the exact coupling that made it silently dead. Detect the collision on the thing that actually collides: the FILE node ID (`functions/new/source`). That is unambiguous, needs no knowledge of publish order, and is checkable in one place.

Also note the guard is unreachable for a second, independent reason: even when it does fire, `dedupSuffix(sourceFile)` is a function of the source file ALONE, so N>2 same-named constructs in ONE file all render the identical suffixed ID and collide again. Both defects must be fixed together, or a 3-way collision still loses one.

Preferred end state: the engine makes loss impossible AND reports the collision at WARN naming the schema node and the name, so the schema author learns their template is not unique (Rust methods lack a receiver qualifier — mache-c777ef, which is the real fix). The suffix is a safety net, not the intended outcome.

REPRO IS EXACT AND FAST (~3ms). /tmp/rsfix/lib.rs with three `impl {A,B,C} { pub fn new() }` -> one node. Keep it as the regression fixture.

Verified on branch docs/mache-0ca7e6-required-gates with a locally built ./mache; working tree left clean (all instrumentation reverted).

FALSIFICATION PASS — four tests run against the finding. It survives, the mechanism is confirmed to 99.8%, but ONE framing claim was overstated and ONE scope claim was wrong in the direction that makes this worse. Corrected numbers below supersede both the description and the previous comment.

T4 — DOES COLLISION ACTUALLY EXPLAIN THE GAP? (the decisive test)
If bare-name collision is the mechanism, then captured should equal the number of DISTINCT bare names, not the number of functions.

    adjusted ground truth (fns with a body) .. 4193
    distinct bare names ..................... 3605   <- predicted capture
    mache actually captured ................. 3597
    residual unexplained ....................    8   (0.2%)

Collision explains 99.8% of the loss. The mechanism is confirmed, not inferred. The 8 residual are worth a look but are not the story.

T3 — GROUND TRUTH WAS INFLATED. 35 of the matches I counted were bodyless trait method DECLARATIONS (`fn foo(&self);`), which mache is CORRECT to omit — they have no body to project. Corrected loss: 588 constructs (14.0%), not 613 (14.6%). Use 588.

T1 — "SILENTLY DROPPED" WAS TOO STRONG FOR RUST. For methods inside `impl` blocks the bytes are still in the db, inside the coarse `implementations/<Type>/source` blob:

    implementations/A/source | impl A { pub fn new() -> Self { A { v: 1 } } }
    implementations/B/source | impl B { pub fn new() -> Self { B { v: 2 } } }

So for Rust impl methods this is ADDRESSABILITY loss, not byte loss: `functions/` is missing 588 entries and find_definition / get_overview / callers are correspondingly incomplete, but the source is recoverable from a coarser node. Retrieval correctness bug, not corruption. Downgrade the language in the description accordingly.

T2 — "GO IS UNAFFECTED IN PRACTICE" IS FALSE, AND GO IS THE WORSE CASE.
The description claims Go is safe because it nests by package and qualifies methods. That is wrong for FREE functions, and the guard's own documented purpose is to handle exactly this ("This handles cases like multiple init() functions across Go files") — it does not work:

    3 files, each `func init()`, one package  ->  ONE node, holding c's body

Critically, Go has NO coarser parent to fall back to — there is no impl-block equivalent holding the whole region. The other two bodies are nowhere in the database. For Go this is TRUE, IRRECOVERABLE BYTE LOSS.

Demonstrated on mache's OWN source (self-hosting):

    `func init()` in cmd/*.go .............. 10  (build, cache, init, infer, config,
                                                 mount, pack, find_smells_cli, schemas, serve)
    captured as cmd/functions/init ........   1  (serve.go's)
    cmd/mount.go's init() body in the db ..   ABSENT

Query proving absence: `select id from nodes where record like '%controlPath%' and record like '%Leyline control block%'` returns zero rows, while `grep -l 'Leyline control block' cmd/*.go` returns cmd/mount.go. mache cannot see 9 of its own init() functions, including the one registering the --schema/--data/--control flags.

Whole-corpus Go exposure is small in RATE but not zero: ~52 of 6683 funcs+methods (0.8%) by name-collision arithmetic, concentrated in init(). Low rate, high severity — irrecoverable, and it hits the flag-registration functions that define the CLI surface.

NET EFFECT ON PRIORITY: stays P0. The Rust headline softens to addressability loss; the Go case hardens to irrecoverable byte loss in the project's own graph. The fix does not change — detect the collision on the FILE node ID, disambiguate deterministically, WARN naming the schema node — but the regression test must now cover BOTH: a Rust impl-method collision AND a Go multi-file init() collision, asserting all bodies are present and distinct.

Also update mache-c777ef: it currently asserts Go is unaffected. It is not.

comments.text:
ROOT CAUSE OF THE DEAD GUARD — FOUND. This closes the open sub-question from the previous comment ("why children reads 0 at check time"). It is not a race and not an ordering problem.

`SQLiteWriter.GetNode` (internal/ingest/sqlite_writer.go:582-637) NEVER POPULATES Children:

    SELECT kind, mtime, record, context, props FROM nodes WHERE id = ?
    ...
    n := &graph.Node{
        ID:      id,
        Mode:    mode,
        ModTime: time.Unix(0, mtimeNano),
        Context: context,
    }
    n.Properties = graph.DecodeProps(props)
    return n, nil          // <-- Children is never set. Always nil.

Its sibling confirms the intent: `func (w *SQLiteWriter) ListChildren(id string) ([]string, error) { return nil, nil // Not used during ingest }`. Children are simply not a readable property of this store during ingest.

`mache build` writes through SQLiteWriter (wrapped in bufferingTarget — confirmed at runtime: `storeType=*ingest.bufferingTarget`). Therefore `len(existing.Children) > 0` at engine_walk.go:223 is ALWAYS FALSE on this path, and the dedup branch is structurally unreachable. Not dead by accident of ordering — dead because it interrogates a field the store never fills.

Runtime trace proving the write is not the problem (3x `impl {A,B,C} { fn new() }` in one file):

    [G] guard id=functions/new ABSENT
    [F] AddFileChildren node=functions/new files=1 nowChildren=1     <- node HAS 1 child
    [G] guard id=functions/new children=0                            <- refetch says 0
    [F] AddFileChildren node=functions/new files=1 nowChildren=1
    [G] guard id=functions/new children=0

AddFileChildren correctly sets Children=1 on the node it holds; the refetch through GetNode drops it. The write is fine; the READ is lossy.

SECOND CASUALTY — the same nil Children silently disables a DIFFERENT feature. engine_walk.go:236-241:

    // Create/Update Node — preserve existing children when merging
    // multiple files into the same node (e.g. multiple .go files in one package).
    var existingChildren []string
    if existing, err := store.GetNode(id); err == nil {
        existingChildren = existing.Children      // always nil on this path
    }

That preservation is also inert. It survives in practice only because the parent-child wiring at engine_walk.go:326-338 keeps its own IN-MEMORY set (`e.childSeen`) rather than trusting the store. That is the pattern the dedup guard should have followed.

SO THERE ARE NOW THREE INDEPENDENT DEFECTS, all of which must be fixed together:
  1. The guard reads Children from a store that never populates it -> never fires. (this comment)
  2. Even when it fires, `dedupSuffix(sourceFile)` is keyed on the FILE alone, so N>2 same-named constructs in one file all render the identical suffixed ID and collide again.
  3. The name being disambiguated is the wrong identity in the first place — bare, unqualified (mache-c777ef).

FIX DIRECTION (revised, and now concrete)
Do NOT teach SQLiteWriter.GetNode to return Children just to feed this guard — that adds a per-node query to the ingest hot path to answer a question the engine can answer in memory for free. Follow the `e.childSeen` precedent: keep an in-memory set of claimed construct IDs for the current build and check that. It is O(1), needs no store round-trip, and cannot be defeated by a store that does not track children.

Better still, make the collision impossible rather than detected: key construct nodes on LLO's `node_id`, which is unique per definition (4137 distinct node_ids == 4137 function_item nodes, exact) instead of a rendered bare name. See mache-c777ef for that measurement and the caveat that `node_defs.token` alone is NOT sufficient (Go's init() tokens are bare; identity needs node_id).

Working tree left clean; all instrumentation reverted.

title: Rule-polarity generalization: extend smell-rules engine to host must-hold rules (cloister done-rules) as a second polarity
description:
## Framing (user, 2026-05-21)

> "Polarity belongs in mache. That's why I mention tool repo. Like mache should compose enough, right? Cloister then uses it."

mache already owns the rule-engine surface (smell-rules with SQL evaluator, severity tiers per ADR-0018, `MACHE_SMELL_RULES_DIR` external loader, find-smells CLI + GH Action). Cloister has `done-rules/*.json` driven by `scripts/done-runner.mjs` — a shell-evaluator with overlapping but inverted semantics. The shape is unified by adding a polarity flag to mache's rule schema and a shell evaluator alongside the SQL one. **Cloister consumes mache as a tool (per ADR-0026 / cloister-cf7a3b); cloister stops maintaining its own engine.**

## The polarity, concretely

| | smell-rule (mache, today) | done-rule (cloister, today) |
|---|---|---|
| Assertion | findings = drift; "must NOT be present" | exit 0 = pass; "must hold" |
| Evaluator | SQL template over `_ast`/`nodes`/`node_refs`/`node_defs` | shell command |
| Loader | `cmd/smell_rules.go` + `cmd/smell_rules_external.go` | `scripts/done-runner.mjs` (cloister) |
| Severity | `off` / `warn` / `error` (ADR-0018) | `block` / `warn` |
| Gate | `--fail-on` selects severities | `block` short-circuits the runner |
| Fields | `{ ID, Languages, Description, Requires, ScopeColumn, Query, DefaultMinMetric, Severity, Tags }` | `{ id, description, severity, run }` |

Both are "rule whose findings cross a gate." Adding `polarity: must-hold \| must-not-hold` and a pluggable evaluator collapses them to one shape mache hosts.

## Proposed unified schema (sketch — to refine via ADR)

```jsonc
{
  "id": "lint-passes",
  "description": "task lint exits 0",
  "polarity": "must-hold",        // NEW — defaults to "must-not-hold" for back-compat with smell-rules
  "evaluator": {                  // NEW — was implicit (SQL only)
    "kind": "shell",              // alternatives: "sql", later "wasi-component" once cloister-c2a7c3 ships
    "run": "task lint"
  },
  "severity": "error",            // unified to ADR-0018 enum; map cloister "block" → "error"
  "tags": ["ci", "fast-gate"],
  "requires": []
}
```

Smell-rules today carry SQL via top-level `Query` + `ScopeColumn` + `Requires` — move those into `evaluator.kind: "sql"` for the new shape, keep the existing top-level fields as a back-compat reader.

## What mache ships

1. **ADR** — pick the unified schema; align severity vocab (kill the `block` alias or formalize it as a per-call gate alias for `error`).
2. **Evaluator interface** in `cmd/` — Go interface with `SQL` + `Shell` impls; `find_smells` becomes evaluator-agnostic.
3. **Back-compat** — existing `smellRegistry` entries + external `MACHE_SMELL_RULES_DIR` rules continue to load. New `polarity` field defaults to `must-not-hold` if absent.
4. **CLI** — `mache find-smells` already exists (mache-hupl). Probably rename to `mache check` or `mache rules` since it's no longer smell-specific, with `--polarity=both|must-hold|must-not-hold` filtering. (Naming decision is part of the ADR.)
5. **MCP tool surface** — `find_smells` either renames or gains a sibling `check_rules`. Either way it returns findings tagged by polarity so consumers (cloister done-runner) can interpret correctly.

## Why this benefits "tools that compose"

Cloister's `done-runner.mjs` becomes a 30-line wrapper that:
- Loads cloister/done-rules/*.json (and any other repo's rules dir cloister has been told about by `cluster.toml`)
- Calls `mache check --polarity=must-hold` (or the MCP tool) with that rules-dir as input
- Reports findings + exit code

cloister no longer maintains an engine. mache becomes The Rule Engine for the ecosystem. The tools-repo template (cloister-c1b77e) ships `rules/*.json` (collapsed name once this lands) that mache picks up regardless of which tool authored them.

## Related work

- `mache-6z2e` (Sibling 'machelint' tool: rules engine over mache + LSP diagnostics) — broader generalization. This bead is narrower (just polarity + shell evaluator); machelint adds the LSP-diagnostic dimension. Decide at ADR time whether this work ships INSIDE mache or initializes machelint.
- `mache-3f8w` (extract find_smells to ext/machelint when product split is right) — decides physical home. Polarity work should land before the physical split, so the extraction happens with the unified shape already in place.
- `mache-hupl` (find-smells CLI, closed) — CLI surface this bead extends.
- `mache-0yy4` (find-smells PR commenter GH Action, closed) — advisory pattern that's compatible; just gains a "Required checks" group for `must-hold` rules that fail.
- `cloister-cf7a3b` (ADR-0026 tool composition implementation arc) — the resolver that lets cloister consume mache.
- `cloister-c1b77e` (tools-repo template, just filed) — the template ships `rules/*.json` in the unified shape this bead defines.
- (Closed) `cloister-c1123d` — previously held this work in the wrong repo; closed with redirect.

## Future evaluator: wasi-component

Once cloister-c2a7c3 (Ring Seam reference impl crate) ships, a rule's `evaluator.kind` can be `"wasi-component"` — the rule itself is a sandboxed unit reading findings from the host via the Ring Seam. This is the elegant endgame; not in scope for v1, but worth not foreclosing in the schema.

## Files (asserted scope)

- `docs/adr/` — ADR for the unification
- `cmd/smell_rules.go` — adds polarity + evaluator interface
- `cmd/smell_rules_external.go` — back-compat reader
- `cmd/serve_find_smells.go` — handler dispatch by evaluator
- `cmd/find_smells_cli.go` — CLI flags
- (Maybe) `cmd/run_shell_rule.go` (new) — shell evaluator
- `examples/smell-rules/` — add a must-hold example

title: rust-schema.json: methods are not receiver-qualified and impl blocks are one blob
description:
Two related defects in examples/rust-schema.json, both visible by comparing it to examples/go-schema.json.

DEFECT 1 — methods lose their receiver, producing a flat global namespace.

go-schema.json has a dedicated `methods` node whose child name template is `{{.receiver}}.{{.name}}` with selector `(method_declaration receiver: (parameter_list (parameter_declaration type: (pointer_type (type_identifier) @receiver))) name: (field_identifier) @name) @scope`. Result: `api/methods/Topology.ResolveIncludes/source`.

rust-schema.json has no `methods` node at all. Its `functions` node matches every `function_item`, including those inside `impl` blocks, and names them by bare `{{.name}}`. Result: `functions/new/source` — with no receiver and no module path, in ONE global namespace shared by all 228 files of the corpus.

This is what feeds the silent-drop bug (mache-c725e9): 63 `fn new(` in ley-line-open rs/ collapse to a single `functions/new` node. Fixing the engine stops the data loss but leaves the names wrong — `new.2`, `new.3` are not useful identifiers. `Cell.new` is.

DEFECT 2 — `implementations/<Type>/source` captures the entire impl block as one blob.

  implementations/CellComplex/source   46,314 bytes
  implementations/TsLanguage/source    27,132 bytes
  implementations/JjIntegration/source 20,716 bytes

versus Go's per-method granularity:

  api/methods/Topology.ResolveIncludes/source   114 bytes
  cmd/methods/OCIClient.SetToken/source          63 bytes

A 46KB "construct" defeats the entire point of construct-granular retrieval — reading it costs more than reading most whole files. It also double-stores content already captured (badly) under `functions/`.

FIX
- Add a `methods` node selecting `function_item`s inside `impl_item`, named `{{.receiver}}.{{.name}}`, mirroring go-schema.json's shape. Cover the cases Rust actually uses: inherent impls (`impl Foo`), generic impls (`impl<T> Foo<T>` — type is `(generic_type type: (type_identifier))`), and trait impls (`impl Trait for Foo`, which has both `trait:` and `type:` fields).
- Restrict `functions` to free functions so it stops double-capturing impl methods.
- Decide `implementations`' role once methods exist: either keep it as a thin index of the impl header (trait + type, no bodies) or drop it. Do NOT keep a 46KB body blob.

Verify with tools/token-bench against ley-line-open rs/ — the F4 numbers (median 62.57x) were computed on the current, lossy projection and will need regenerating once the corpus is complete.

comments.text:
AUTHORITATIVE MEASUREMENT + A MUCH CHEAPER FIX THAN THIS BEAD PROPOSES. Supersedes the description's fix guidance.

TWO CORRECTIONS TO THIS BEAD
1. The description asserts Go is unaffected ("Go avoids it via {{.receiver}}.{{.name}}"). FALSE for free functions — 3 `func init()` across 3 files in one package collapse to ONE node, and unlike Rust there is no enclosing impl blob to recover the bytes from. See mache-c725e9 for the proof on mache's own cmd/ (10 init(), 1 captured, mount.go's body absent from the graph).
2. The proposed fix — hand-author a `methods` node with tree-sitter selectors covering inherent/generic/trait impls — is unnecessary work. LLO already computed the qualified names.

THE FINDING: LLO's `node_defs` ALREADY CARRIES RECEIVER-QUALIFIED NAMES

    sqlite> select token, canonical_kind from node_defs limit 3;
    TEMP_NONCE        | constant
    FsBlobStore       | type
    FsBlobStore::open | function     <-- fully qualified, already done

Schema: node_defs(token, node_id, source_id, container_node_id, canonical_kind, node_hash).

mache's rust-schema.json discards this. Its selector `(function_item name: (identifier) @name)` re-derives a BARE identifier from the AST, throwing away the qualification LLO computed during parse. That discard is the entire bug.

EXACT NUMBERS — matched pair, no regex anywhere. Built with:
    leyline-v0.10.3 parse -l rust -o /tmp/rs_ast.db <ley-line-open>/rs     (245 files, 245 sources)
    mache build --schema examples/rust-schema.json <ley-line-open>/rs /tmp/rs_matched.db

    _ast function_item nodes ............... 4137
    _ast function_signature_item ...........   37   (bodyless trait decls; correctly omitted)
    node_defs canonical_kind='function' .... 4889
    DISTINCT QUALIFIED tokens .............. 4330   <-- what mache COULD address
    DISTINCT BARE names (after ::) ......... 3597   <-- prediction
    mache actually captured ................ 3597   <-- actual
    residual ...............................    0

The prediction "mache captures exactly the set of distinct BARE names" holds to ZERO residual. The collision mechanism is confirmed by the parser's own index, not inferred from a regex.

CORRECTED MAGNITUDE: 4330 - 3597 = 733 addressable constructs lost, 16.9%. This supersedes every earlier figure on both beads (613 regex, 588 regex-adjusted, 540 function_item-based). All earlier numbers were derived from a line-based regex over source text; that instrument over-counted by ~1.4% and was the wrong tool for auditing a tree-sitter pipeline. Use 733 / 16.9%.

REVISED FIX — cheap, language-agnostic, no new selectors
Name construct nodes from `node_defs.token` (already qualified, already keyed to node_id and node_hash) instead of re-deriving a bare `@name` in each language's schema. This:
  - fixes Rust methods (FsBlobStore::open) without writing impl/generic/trait selectors;
  - fixes Go init() the same way, if Go's node_defs qualifies by file/package — VERIFY THIS before assuming, it is the one untested leg;
  - removes the per-language naming logic that made this a per-language bug;
  - is what LookupDef already relies on (internal/graph/sqlite_graph_lookupdef_test.go asserts both bare and qualified forms resolve), so the qualified form is already a first-class identity in the codebase.

Open question to settle first: is `node_defs.token` unique per definition, or can it still collide? 4330 distinct qualified tokens vs 4889 rows means ~559 rows share a token — likely trait impls of the same method on the same type across modules, or generic monomorphisation. Whatever the engine ends up doing about residual collisions (mache-c725e9), it must not silently drop.

DEFECT 2 (impl blocks as 46KB blobs) stands unchanged and is independent of the naming fix.

comments.text:
CORRECTION — my "LLO already has the address half" claim was TOO STRONG, and LLO said so with evidence. Do not implement against it as written.

I reported that ley-line's LSP projection already builds the semantic address, citing walk_symbol at rs/ll-open/lsp/src/project.rs:1028 building `{parent_id}/{name}` recursively, and concluded the ask shrank to "key the tree-sitter walk by name like the sibling projection does".

The keying observation stands and is genuinely useful prior art. The conclusion does not. From ley-line-open-2037b4:

1. THE LSP ADDRESS IS SYNTACTICALLY DERIVED, NOT CANONICAL. The container segment is the
   RAW IMPL HEADER TEXT — `impl fmt::Debug for Hash` — embedding the trait path exactly
   as written. Rewriting `fmt::Debug` to `std::fmt::Debug` changes the address without
   changing the code's meaning. An address that moves under a no-op edit is not an
   address.

2. THE ROOT IS `symbols/`, NOT THE FILE. So source_id is absent from the id entirely —
   the LSP form cannot even locate the construct without a separate join.

3. LSP CANNOT BE THE SUBSTRATE IDENTITY at all: it is an enrichment pass requiring a
   live language server, so it is not reproducible from source alone the way
   tree-sitter is, and coverage is per-language. It can be the AUTHORITY the
   tree-sitter walk is validated against — a conformance direction — but not the
   source of truth.

So: prior art for the KEYING (name, not ordinal), not a canonical semantic path to
adopt. The ADR must define the canonical form; it cannot lift the LSP form verbatim.
That is more work than my "shrinks to a keying change" framing implied.

ALSO SETTLED, and it closes an open question I raised: my four INSERT OR REPLACE
candidate sites (Hash::fmt, ArenaLock::try_acquire, HotSwapGraph::flush_to_arena,
SqliteGraphAdapter::serialize) were found via a tree-sitter proxy over node_defs, and I
flagged the proxy might be void if DocumentSymbol nests impl blocks separately.

It does. LLO ran `leyline lsp` with rust-analyzer against an impl Display / impl Debug
fixture:

    symbols/impl fmt::Debug for Hash/fmt      method
    symbols/impl fmt::Display for Hash/fmt    method

Distinct parents, no collision. And Rust cannot reach it through impls at all —
duplicate method names inside ONE impl block are illegal, so same-name pairs always live
in different impls and therefore always get different parents. C++ overloads remain the
open risk case and are untested.

My container_node_id correction was accepted on their side too: it is NOT universally
NULL (Rust 91/6126, Go 383/4707) and is populated only for FUNCTION-LOCAL items, so it
tracks lexical enclosure by a definition rather than membership in a type or module.
Consequence for whoever implements ley-line-open-23377a: the obvious "just populate the
column that already exists" fix would OVERLOAD a column that already means something
else. Do not do that.

NET EFFECT ON THIS BEAD: unchanged in scope, but the upstream half is a real ADR with a
canonical-form decision pending, not a small keying fix. The #570 suffixes stay
load-bearing longer than I estimated. Do not start mache-side schema work assuming
qualified names arrive imminently.

title: Test constructs are indistinguishable from production ones (Rust #[cfg(test)] vs Go _test.go)
description:
mache has no way to tell a test construct from a production one, and the difficulty differs by language in a way the schemas do not currently account for.

Go colocates nothing: tests live in separate `_test.go` FILES, so `source_file` alone is a reliable discriminator even though no schema marks it.

Rust colocates everything: tests live INSIDE the production file under `#[cfg(test)] mod tests { ... }`, with individual `#[test] fn`s. `source_file` is therefore useless as a discriminator, and today those functions land under `functions/` alongside production code with nothing to distinguish them.

MEASURED (ley-line-open rs/, 228 files):
  files containing #[cfg(test)] ......... 112 of 242  (46%)
  bytes from the first #[cfg(test)] on ... 1,746,867 of 5,060,752  (34.5% of all source)
  functions/test_* captured .............. 66
  modules/* captured .................... 135

So roughly a third of the Rust corpus by bytes is test code that mache presents as if it were production code.

WHY THIS MATTERS BEYOND TIDINESS

1. Benchmark validity. tools/token-bench arm A charges whole-FILE bytes. Rust files carry their tests; Go files do not. That inflates Rust's arm A by 1.53x (20,912 B avg with inline tests vs 13,693 B without) purely as an artifact of packaging convention. The F4 headline of 62.57x vs Go's 25.89x is therefore not like-for-like — on a tests-excluded basis it is ~41x. The finding (Rust wins bigger) survives, but the raw gap is part language and part convention, and the published baseline should say which.

2. Smell rules. Rules that count production API surface, or flag "referenced only by tests", cannot be written correctly for Rust while test functions are indistinguishable from production ones. This is a prerequisite for mache-0715f4 (advisory smell for production APIs referenced only by tests) working on anything but Go.

3. Retrieval quality. An agent asking "show me the functions in this module" should not get test helpers mixed in unasked.

SCOPE TO DECIDE
- How to detect. In tree-sitter-rust, `#[cfg(test)]` is an `attribute_item` that is a SIBLING of the `mod_item` in the enclosing declaration_list, not a child of it — so a naive descendant query will not associate them. Confirm the actual node relationship before designing the selector; a sibling-aware selector or a post-pass over `_ast` may be needed. `#[test]` on individual functions has the same sibling shape.
- How to represent. Options: a separate top-level `tests/` subtree; a boolean property on the node; or a naming convention. A property is the least disruptive to existing paths and the most useful to rule SQL.
- Whether token-bench excludes test code. Recommend adding an explicit `-exclude-tests` flag and reporting F4 BOTH ways rather than silently changing the published baseline — the tests-included number is the honest answer to "what does it cost to read this repo", and the tests-excluded number is the honest answer to "how do these two languages compare".

Do the same for Go for symmetry (mark `_test.go`-derived nodes), so the discriminator is one concept across languages rather than a Rust special case.

Raised by the user while reviewing F4 results: "detecting cfg testfiles vs test files that are explicitly defined is another".
acceptance_criteria: A Go test ingests a Rust fixture with a `#[cfg(test)] mod tests` containing two `#[test]` fns plus production code, and asserts the test constructs are distinguishable from the production ones by the chosen mechanism; the equivalent Go fixture with a `_test.go` file asserts the same discriminator works there. Plus `tools/token-bench -exclude-tests` reports both figures and docs/benchmarks/token-efficiency-baseline.json records which basis each number uses.

title: Smell rules assume the mache Go-schema node_id taxonomy — silently wrong on ALL leyline projections (dead_code inert, types/methods misclassified)
description:
Generalization of mache-22fecf (fixed narrowly for Rust in PR #505). The node_defs-based rules (dead_code, duplicate_definitions, and any rule matching `functions/`/`methods/`/`types/`/`constants/`/`variables/`/`imports/`) encode the mache Go-SCHEMA node_id taxonomy — which is produced ONLY by mache's own tree-sitter + examples/go-schema.json. leyline's AST-native projection uses tree-sitter KIND paths instead (`method_declaration_N` for Go, `impl_item_N/.../function_item_M` + `function_signature_item` for Rust, `class_definition`/`function_definition` for Python, `method_definition`/`class_body` for JS) with NO category segments. Verified empirically via `leyline parse` (2026-07-09).

Consequences on leyline-parsed .db (the find-smells GHA / cross-repo path):
- duplicate_definitions: bare-token methods across N types collide → false positives. Confirmed on Rust (PR #505 fixed impl_item/function_signature_item) AND on LLO-Go (`method_declaration_N` — NOT yet covered; PR #505 should be broadened).
- dead_code: INERT on leyline projections — leyline leaves nodes.source_file empty, so the `source_file != ''` filter drops every row (misses real dead code). If source_file WERE populated, the `types/`/`constants/` exclusions wouldn't match Rust `struct_item`/`const_item` → struct/enum false positives.
- Python/JS: leyline extracts ZERO node_defs for them (ley-line-open bead) → rules silently find nothing.

This is the concrete first instance of the analysis-as-substrate-query thesis (mache-463612): rules must derive their category/method taxonomy per-language from a producer-agnostic signal (node_kind via _ast join, or a rule-as-contract kind map), not hardcode go-schema path strings. Options: (a) join _ast for node_kind and classify by kind (breaks the node_defs-only backend contract — weigh it); (b) a per-projection taxonomy map; (c) restrict path-taxonomy rules to the mache-go-schema backend and write kind-based variants for leyline.

Close condition: dead_code + duplicate_definitions produce correct results on a leyline-parsed Go AND Rust fixture (no method/type false positives, real dead code found), verified by tests using real leyline node_id shapes. Depends on the ley-line-open extraction-fidelity bead for Python/JS coverage.

Gated on the LLO v0.7.0 adoption + empirical verification tracked in the new mache adoption bead: check whether tokens are qualified, source_file is populated, dead_code is no longer inert, and whether the #505 impl_item/method_declaration exclusion is still needed. Re-scope (update or close) this bead based on those findings.

Now urgent because dead_code is no longer inert.
3. Deeper fix (the real one): derive the taxonomy per-language from a producer-agnostic signal (node_kind via _ast join, or a rule-as-contract kind map) rather than enumerating path strings — mache-463612. The enumeration in (1)/(2) is the pragmatic stopgap; the kind-based classifier is the durable fix.

title: Local integration recipe: compose.dev.yaml pairing mache + llo-daemon for end-to-end testing
description:
Filed 2026-05-12. Re-filed from `ley-line-open-69072b` after the architectural reconsideration: LLO is a substrate; the compose recipe for "how to run mache against LLO" belongs on the consumer side (here in mache), not on the substrate side.

## Why this is the right shape

mache is the canonical Go-side consumer of LLO's UDS + MCP protocol. After mache PR #372 lands typed `clients/go/leyline-schema/v0.3.0` decoders, the natural validation is "stand up mache + a real LLO daemon, run a query through mache's MCP surface, verify the typed decode path works end-to-end." That's the demonstration shape — and mache is where it should live.

LLO already has `task image:smoke` for its own substrate-local validation (single-service, daemon boots, MCP `tools/list` responds). That's the right LLO-local validation.

## Scope

Ship a `compose.dev.yaml` (or similar — match mache's existing orchestration patterns) at the mache repo root that:

1. **Brings up a mache container** (uses the post-#372 mache image with typed decoders) — MCP HTTP on a host port.
2. **Brings up an LLO daemon container** (uses `ley-line-open:0.3.0` from agentic-research/ley-line-open) with a shared volume for the UDS + ctrl + arena files.
3. **Wires mache → LLO** via the shared `default.sock` socket (mache's `--control` flag pointing at the volume mount).
4. **Parses a fixture repo** — small embedded Go source tree (LLO PR #14's `tests/fixtures/sample-repo/` is the suggested starting point — moving to mache as part of this bead). One-shot `reparse` op against LLO, populates `nodes` + `_ast` + `node_refs` + `node_defs`.
5. **Smoke-tests the integration** via a `task cluster:smoke` target: bring up, run a query through mache's MCP (e.g., `udsGraph.ListChildStats` or `find_callers`), assert response is well-formed and Int64 fields are correctly decoded.

## Sample-repo fixture sketch (from the original LLO-side scaffold)

```
tests/fixtures/sample-repo/
├── go.mod      # module github.com/agentic-research/mache/tests/fixtures/sample-repo
├── main.go     # entry point, calls Greet() from greet.go
├── greet.go    # defines Greet(name string) string, calls formatGreeting
├── util.go     # formatGreeting(template, name string) — leaf of the call graph
└── README.md   # what each file is for; what gets exercised
```

Three small Go files, cross-file references, no external imports — exercises `node_refs`, `find_callers`, `find_callees`, `read_content`. README explains each file's role in the smoke test.

## What this bead is NOT

- Not a replacement for `task image:smoke` in LLO (that tests LLO standalone — substrate-local validation).
- Not cloister's `cluster.compose.yaml` (cloister's bundled UX could grow LLO + mache as a cluster — that's a separate cloister-side concern).
- Not production deployment scaffolding. Dev/test only.

## Coordination + sequence

1. mache PR #372 merges → typed Go bindings adopted in mache
2. mache cuts a release image with #372's typed decoders
3. This bead's PR brings up the cluster recipe + smoke test using that image
4. `task cluster:smoke` becomes the canonical "see mache talk to LLO end-to-end" command

## Reference work

- Original LLO-side scaffold (closed): https://github.com/agentic-research/ley-line-open/pull/14 — contains compose.dev.yaml + Taskfile targets + sample-repo fixture as a starting reference. Adapt to mache's repo conventions.
- LLO bead `ley-line-open-69072b` (will be closed pointing here)
- mache PR #372 (`mache-a5ad09`) — the typed-bindings adoption that unblocks this

## Files (suggested)

- `compose.dev.yaml` (new, mache repo root)
- `Taskfile.yml` or equivalent (new `cluster:dev` / `cluster:smoke` targets matching mache's existing pattern)
- `tests/fixtures/sample-repo/` (new — fixture Go source tree)
- `README.md` (new "Local integration cluster" section)

title: MCP tool: mache_embedding_similarity — sqlite-vec nearest neighbor for BDR dedup
description:
## What

Add a new MCP tool `mache_embedding_similarity(text, k)` that computes MiniLM 384D embedding of input text and returns the k nearest neighbors from sqlite-vec.

### Interface

```
Tool: mache_embedding_similarity
Input:
  text: string      -- text to find similar items for
  k: int            -- number of nearest neighbors (default 5)
  item_type: string -- "bead" | "symbol" | "any" (default "bead")
Output:
  results: [{item_id: string, score: float, item_text: string}]
```

### Implementation

1. Use leyline-embed to compute 384D MiniLM embedding of input text
2. Query sqlite-vec: `SELECT item_id, distance FROM vec_items WHERE embedding MATCH ? ORDER BY distance LIMIT ?`
3. Convert distance to cosine similarity
4. Return results with item text for context

### Why in mache

- mache already has ley-line integration (ley-line populates mache's SQLite)
- mache already has sqlite-vec loaded
- Keeps the AGPL rosary / closed-source ley-line boundary clean
- rosary queries this over MCP (~50ms per call, acceptable)

### Consumer

rosary's BDR enrichment pipeline Stage 2 (dedup check) calls this to find semantically similar existing beads.

title: cmd/cache.go's _ast DDL has drifted from ley-line's — no node_hash, NOT NULL lost on row/col
description:
Found while deriving the pinned producer's real schema for mache-7555da (internal/fixturedb).

`cmd/cache.go:759` CREATEs `_ast` when hydrating a pulled cache entry. Diffed against ley-line-open v0.13.0's own `sqlite_master`, mache's copy has drifted in two ways:

    -- ley-line v0.13.0 (ground truth, `leyline parse` + SELECT sql FROM sqlite_master)
    CREATE TABLE _ast (
        node_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, source_id TEXT NOT NULL, node_kind TEXT NOT NULL,
        start_byte INTEGER NOT NULL, end_byte INTEGER NOT NULL,
        start_row INTEGER NOT NULL, start_col INTEGER NOT NULL,
        end_row INTEGER NOT NULL, end_col INTEGER NOT NULL
    , node_hash BLOB REFERENCES node_content(node_hash))

    -- cmd/cache.go:759
    CREATE TABLE _ast (
        node_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, source_id TEXT NOT NULL, node_kind TEXT NOT NULL,
        start_byte INTEGER NOT NULL, end_byte INTEGER NOT NULL,
        start_row INTEGER, start_col INTEGER, end_row INTEGER, end_col INTEGER
    )

Two differences, one of which is behavioural:

1. **No `node_hash`.** A cache-hydrated .db therefore has NO content identity on its AST rows, so every node_hash-dependent consumer degrades silently on it: `ensureCanonicalViews` emits `NULL AS node_hash`, `v_test_nodes` cannot join `_ast.node_hash -> node_content.token` and so returns EMPTY, which means Rust `#[cfg(test)]` / `#[test]` constructs are judged as PRODUCTION code on a hydrated cache entry but as test code on a freshly-parsed one. Same repo, same rules, different answer depending on whether the .db came from `leyline parse` or from `mache cache pull`. There is also no `node_content` table at all on that path.
2. `NOT NULL` lost on start_row/start_col/end_row/end_col. Cosmetic today (the writer always supplies them) but it is drift, and it is the kind that stops being cosmetic when a partial write appears.

This is direct evidence for mache-e64f36 (delegate materialisation to LLO rather than re-typing its schema). `cmd/cache.go` is the first entry in `lloWriterAllowlist` precisely because of this, and the allowlist comment says "do not re-justify, delete" — so the preferred fix is delegation, not patching the DDL.

If delegation is not close, the interim fix is to derive the DDL from `internal/fixturedb`'s conformance-tested snapshot (or to move that snapshot somewhere production can read) so there is ONE statement of ley-line's `_ast` shape in the repo rather than two.
acceptance_criteria: A test asserts that the `_ast` (and `node_content`) tables a cache-hydrated .db carries match the pinned ley-line producer's shape — ideally by reusing internal/fixturedb's derived snapshot rather than a second hand-written literal. Concretely: `go test ./cmd/ -run TestCache` passes with an assertion that v_test_nodes is non-empty on a hydrated .db containing Rust `#[cfg(test)]` constructs, i.e. the same answer as on a freshly-parsed one. Alternatively, closed by mache-e64f36 removing the hand-written DDL entirely.

title: god_file's threshold is corpus-relative, so the smell ratchet false-positives on unrelated PRs
description:
Found while landing mache-7555da (PR #592).

`cmd/rules/god_file.json` thresholds against the CORPUS MEAN:

    proj AS (SELECT AVG(n) AS mu FROM per_file)
    ...
    WHERE pf.n >= 10 AND CAST(pf.n AS REAL) > 3.0 * p.mu

`mu` is computed over EVERY file in the projection, including files the rule then refuses to report (it excludes `*_test.go` from the OUTPUT but not from the MEAN). So the finding set for file X depends on every other file in the repo.

**Observed, deterministic, twice:** adding `internal/fixturedb` (seven small non-test .go files) lowered `mu` enough to push `testdata/snapshots/medium-rust-rosary/src/dispatch/session.rs` — a file the PR does not touch, in a vendored Rust snapshot — over the threshold. The `task smells` ratchet then reported it as a NEW finding and failed the pre-push gate. A later commit in the same PR (which added a few more files) pushed it back UNDER, so the baseline regeneration removed the entry again.

Verified it is the corpus effect and not daemon jitter (reference_leyline_daemon_pollution): built HEAD and origin/main each into their own one-shot `mache build --backend leyline` .db, diffed the god_file finding sets, got exactly `+testdata/snapshots/medium-rust-rosary/src/dispatch/session.rs`. Re-ran twice, identical.

**Why it matters:** the ratchet's contract is "you broke it, you fix it". A non-local threshold breaks that — a PR that adds any small file can be told to absorb a baseline delta for a file it did not touch, in code it does not own. The author's only move is to regenerate the baseline, which is exactly the habit a ratchet exists to prevent: it trains people to regenerate on red rather than to read the finding.

**Options, roughly in order of preference:**
1. Compute `mu` over the same population the rule REPORTS on (exclude `*_test.go`, generated files, and `testdata/` from the mean, not just from the output). Still relative, but at least the population is the one being judged.
2. Exclude `testdata/snapshots/**` from the gate entirely — vendored third-party snapshots are corpus for the parser, not code this repo owns, and they currently contribute ~35 of the god_file baseline entries.
3. Make the threshold absolute (or a fixed high percentile computed once and pinned), so a file's verdict depends only on that file.

Whichever is chosen, the gate should be verified to stay stable when N unrelated small files are added — that is the falsifiable property.
acceptance_criteria: A test demonstrates the invariant directly: build a fixture corpus, record god_file findings, add N small unrelated files, rebuild, and assert the finding set is UNCHANGED. It must be shown to fail against the current corpus-relative threshold (mutation: revert the fix, observe red) before the fix lands. `task smells` stays green on a PR that only adds files.

title: Audit what the pinned-leyline test gates missed while lltest resolved the dead legacy binary path
description:
PR #592 (mache-7555da) fixed the mechanism; this is the follow-up question it raises.

`internal/lltest/pinned_unix.go`'s `pinnedBinaryOrSkip` resolved `~/.mache/bin/leyline` — the LEGACY UNVERSIONED path — and `t.Skipf`'d when it was absent or reported a version other than the pin.

mache-0acdf6 namespaced the binary cache BY PIN (`~/.mache/bin/leyline-v0.13.0`) and, per `internal/leyline/binary_cache_path.go`'s own comment, the legacy path "is still READ ... but it is never WRITTEN". So after that change nothing creates or updates the file lltest was looking at. On any machine that had moved past it — including a clean CI checkout, which downloads to the NAMESPACED path — `StartPinnedDaemon` / `UsePinnedDaemon` skipped UNCONDITIONALLY.

Observed on this machine: `~/.mache/bin/leyline` reports 0.10.2; the pin is v0.13.0; `~/.mache/bin/leyline-v0.13.0` exists and is fine. Every lltest-gated test skipped.

Fixed in #592 by exporting `leyline.CachedPinnedBinary()` (a wrapper over the production `resolveCachedPinned`) and `lltest.PinnedBinaryOrSkip(t)`, so the gate resolves the pin exactly the way production does.

**What this bead is for:** a skipping gate is indistinguishable from a passing one in the summary line, so we do not yet know what these tests would have said. Someone should:

1. Enumerate the `lltest.UsePinnedDaemon` / `lltest.StartPinnedDaemon` consumers and RUN them now that resolution works. Expect findings — that is the point.
2. Work out how long the window was (`git log -S` on the namespacing change vs. the lltest helper) and whether CI ever had a legacy binary at the pin, i.e. whether this was local-only or repo-wide.
3. Consider making SKIP LOUD in CI. A gate that can silently turn itself off is the same failure mode as an unenforced rule — cf. the `regexpAllowlist` / LLO-boundary framing ("a rule that is off enforces nothing"). Options: fail rather than skip when `CI=true`, or emit a summary line counting skipped pinned gates.

Related: the LLO boundary rule had a sibling defect found in the same PR (`writesTable` could never match a table starting with `N`, so `node_content` was never enforceable). Two silently-disabled gates in one afternoon suggests the class is worth a sweep, not just two point fixes.
acceptance_criteria: Every lltest-gated test has been run against the pinned binary at least once with resolution working, and any failures are filed. Plus a mechanism so a pinned gate cannot silently disable itself again — either it FAILS instead of skipping under CI, or the run emits a counted summary of skipped pinned gates that a human sees. Verify by deleting the cached pinned binary and observing the loud signal (`go test ./... 2>&1 | grep -i "pinned"`), not a silent pass.
